en: Chapter 4, Section 1 // Now begins the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.

[======= JNys_4,1.I: The Section on Repetition =======] I take refuge in that Lord of Śrī, by resorting to the shade of whose lotus feet the liberated ones, having attained bliss, rejoice eternally. // 1 //
The commentary states that "the fruit is declared in this chapter. To the question, "What is the connection now for this definition of the fruit? he says: "Samanvaya... [etc.].

When the reality has been established through both positive concomitance and non-contradiction, and when all possible means of proof have been specifically examined in their entirety; (1) Mānava 4.1.1.
That which must always be done, the means that will inevitably come to pass, is first considered therein... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.2a-c]
Once the reality in the form of the Supreme Brahman and so forth has been established through the first and second chapters— by means of "concordance" (samanvaya) and "non-contradiction" (avirōdha)—
then, regarding the means of attainment (sādhana), that is, the subject matter of the means, [the discussion proceeds] in the third chapter.
When all the means for liberation have been examined without exception,
the occasion has arrived for the presentation of the result.
Since other matters that were intended to be investigated have already been examined, this alone remains;
therefore, the remainder of the sentence is: "Thus, the fruit characterized as liberation is declared in this chapter alone.
Furthermore, he will explain the subject matter to be presented by each of the four quarters and their mutual connection all together in one place for the sake of brevity.
Consequently, it is stated that in this chapter concerning results, the result known as the destruction of karma is declared in the first quarter (pāda).
He states an exception to that [general rule]: "In particular," and so forth.
In this regard, within the first quarter of the fourth [chapter],
the means of proof itself is first considered by certain sūtras.
How so?
It should be performed especially with supreme reverence, constantly and without interruption. Why?
Since this is absolutely certain for the accomplishment of liberation,
the following is what is meant:
it is established here at the outset that among those very means of realization examined in the third chapter, some must be practiced with supreme devotion and continuity.
Because liberation exists only when one practices in this way, and does not exist otherwise;
it is for the sake of making this known that, although this was not stated in the third [chapter], it is stated here.
For in that case, its distinction from that [other fruit] is understood through its not being mentioned;
and by its being mentioned in the definition of the fruit, its status as an internal factor of the fruit is established.
Furthermore, the arrangement of chapters and so forth is justified because it is based on what is generally the case. *12,11*
Oṃ. There is repetition [of the path], because of the repeated instruction. Oṃ.
He shows the cause for the arising of the legal dispute (adhikaraṇa) with the words: "from hearing and so forth."
There must be repetition because of the repeated instruction;
[otherwise] there would be a single performance of hearing and so forth. (BBs 4.1.1–2d)
Or is there a return? Such being the doubt... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.3a]
First, the word "therein" (tatra) is understood from the context.
Since it is seen that "it is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, and it is to be meditated upon," hearing and the other stages are enjoined for the purpose of realization.

When a doubt arises as to whether these—such as hearing—are to be performed once, like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others, or whether they are to be repeated, like the threshing of rice and similar acts; [the following is stated].
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that "and when there is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that [the rite] is performed once" is to be included.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced."
The seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) should be understood clearly from the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*. He explains the Sūtra: "It must be performed" (*kartavyā*).
...for repetition must indeed be performed;
for the instruction "That thou art" and so forth is given precisely more than once.
[The phrase] "of hearing and the rest" is understood to carry over from the previous context.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the well-known status of the instruction "That thou art.

For if repetition were not to be performed by the disciple, then the teacher's repeated instruction would be purposeless. By this it is known that repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*) must be performed. *12,13*
By this, the necessity of repetition for the hearing [of the Veda] is established.

Having cited the sūtra *liṅgācca* (and because of an indicative mark), which establishes the repetition of all three [stages of study], he demonstrates the intended indicative marks by means of scriptural statements themselves, beginning with the words "because of an indicative mark" (*liṅgāt*).
And from a sign:

"From the sign [of his lineage], from Lātavya, and because he was previously a Brahmin of pure conduct for a hundred years, one named Ugratapas heard that he was worthy of the station of Rudra. (Mānava Ānuvākya 4.1.4)
For half a parārdha, he remained constantly and devotedly intent upon the qualities of Viṣṇu; for one-third of that time, he performed worship with a concentrated mind.
It is to be received, it is to be accepted, and it is to be attended upon by disciples;
therefore,
[the suffix] *tasi* is applied after the genitive plural form *brahmatvataḥ*.
"Prior to a hundred Brahma-kalpas" is an epithet of Ṛju;
that is to say, from this present Brahma-kalpa until a hundred Brahma-kalpas have passed, he will attain the state of Brahmā.
In the phrase "along with half a Parārdha," the accusative case is used to denote continuous duration.
Of that time for hearing, one-third part;
that is, during the third part of the time,
[one should practice] *upāsā*, which consists of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*).
"With collected mind" means one whose mind is fixed upon the very object that is to be cultivated. For ten *manvantaras*, he was fit for the station of Śakra;
from Garuḍa, who was fit for that station, he heard [the teaching] from Sumanas, named Sunanda.
He performed worship with diligence for four sets of Manvantaras.
They were as radiant as the sun and the moon, worthy of their station, and possessed of great splendor;
one was handsome and the other was tranquil in form, and they spent four *manvantaras* with well-disposed minds, listening to the teachings and honoring the *manvantara*.
Then all those [sages], such as Bhakti, Ugratapas, and the others,
having been thus addressed by Viṣṇu himself in the work known as the *Sattattva*, beheld the Supreme Viṣṇu, ever nourished by His grace. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.1.8)
The period in which there are ten *manvantaras* is described as such. Regarding the phrase "from the one worthy of Garuḍa’s station": it means from that which is suitable for the station of Garuḍa.
"Endowed with splendor" means indeed possessing excellent wisdom, not being dull-witted;
"aśṛṇvatām" means "of those who do not hear. The doubling of the verbal suffix occurs according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* ("there is extensive transposition").
With well-disposed minds,
let them worship for the duration of a Manvantara— that is, for the period delimited by a Manvantara.
This is a Vedic modification of the vowel.
Indeed, in this case, only the multiplicity of the time for hearing and so forth is understood,
not repetition.
"It is indeed the repeated hearing of the very same statement," and so forth—
this is not correct.
For *śravaṇāvṛtti* (repetition of hearing) is the repeated comprehension, by means of that same [statement] or by another, of the reality already understood through a single statement.

This is because "repetition of reflection" (mananāvṛtti) is intended to mean the repeated application of one reasoning, or the application of other [reasonings] as well, to that which has already been investigated.
[Objection: But if this is so, is this not already covered by the statement "it is based on all Vedānta texts"?
[Response: True.
It has already been stated that this section is commenced again in order to demonstrate the absolute necessity of that very [practice].
This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
Thus ends the section on Repetition (*āvṛttyadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_4,1.II: The Section on the Acceptance of the Self =======] *12,18* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the acceptance of the self.
"Oṃ! They indeed approach [the view] that there is a self, and they cause others to grasp it, Oṃ!"
In order to explain this sūtra, he first states the meaning of the word "self" (ātman): "Self... [and so forth].
"But they approach it as 'the Self' and cause others to grasp it as such;
for the name 'Self' is indeed declared to be that of Nārāyaṇa himself. (Manu 4.1.9ab)

Since the name "Self" (ātman) is directly stated as referring to Nārāyaṇa in its primary sense, and it is not appropriate to resort to a secondary sense when the primary one is possible, therefore even in this sūtra, the connection is with what will be stated later: "The Self is Janārdana; Janārdana is denoted by the word 'Self'. *12,20*
To the question, "What is the purpose of stating that the word 'Self' (ātman) is a name of the Blessed One? he says: "The Self... (ātmeti).
The Self, Brahman, the Great One, the Savior, the Supreme Lord, of pure renown.
"Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Ananta—thus is the Lord of Śrī proclaimed.
So says the Piṅga-Śruti, as does the Parama-Śruti.
Thus, by these names;
Paiṅgi-Śruti declares the word "Self" (ātman) to be a name of the Blessed Lord.
The word "and" (ca) serves to include other scriptural passages.
The word "only" (eva) signifies that this is indeed Śruti and not a designation composed by a human being;
therefore, one should not suspect any contradiction with such [Vedic] passages as "The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Self (ātman), the Person (puruṣa)."
"Om, the Self"—this is the supreme Vedic revelation.
Om, the Self is the Lord Viṣṇu; the Self is bliss, the imperishable, the self-ruling sovereign;
the protector of the universe, Nṛsiṃha, the unborn, Nārāyaṇa, the wide-striding one. (Manu 4.11)
In the same way, Anasūyā bore to Atri sons free from blemish, born of Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā: Datta, Durvāsas, and Soma. (Manu 4.12)
Thus it is also stated in the Bhāgavata; therefore, Janārdana is the Self.
"Ātmānandā" is a single name taken as a whole.
Furthermore, in the *Bhāgavata*, the word "ātman" is used specifically for the Lord;
the phrase "tathaiva" (in the same way) serves there to connect it with what has been previously mentioned.
*jajñe* means "he caused to be born" (*janayāmāsa*). Here, the root *jani-* either has the sense of the causative (*ṇic*) implied within it, or it possesses the causative meaning directly.
The term *sambhava* means those who arise together with Ātman, Īśa, and Brahmā, or with Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Brahmā.
In this context, the two *sambhavas* are Viṣṇu and Śiva themselves, along with Datta and Dūrvāsas.
Soma is coexistent with the Brahmin;
its property is attributed to the other two as well by figurative usage, just as in the expression "the men with the parasols. *12,25*
Even if the word "Self" (ātman) refers to Viṣṇu, what then is the meaning of the Sūtra? To this, he explains the proposition "as the Self" with the words "Therefore":
"Therefore, Viṣṇu is to be known by the virtuous as the one always to be worshipped. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.1.13cd)
Since the word "Self" (ātman) refers to Viṣṇu, this is the meaning of the proposition:
Viṣṇu is the Self; thus, the Self should always be known, worshipped, and meditated upon by the virtuous.
He explains the portion concerning the reason (hetvaṃśa) with the words: "In that very same way."
In that very same way the virtuous worship, and in that very same way they instruct.
By this, it is stated that the word "ātman" does not recur [in the subsequent sections] and that the word "tu" (but/however) serves the purpose of restriction; thus,
it is established by the scriptural passages cited in the Commentary that instruction regarding meditation applies only to those [entities] that truly exist.
"They approach" is stated for the purpose of knowledge and for the purpose of worship (*upāsana*).
Among these, the purpose of knowledge is clear; thus, only one meaning has been explained.
For this very reason, it was previously stated that [the Self] is both to be known and to be worshipped. *12,27*
[Objection: But surely, by this it would be said that Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon as "Viṣṇu.
What, then, would be achieved by this? For meditation on him as not being Viṣṇu is certainly not what is relevant here. To this, he says: "ādāna... (beginning with "taking up").
Moreover, because it has the sense of "taking hold," this word *ātman* denotes the husband. (Manu 4.14cd)
This word "self" (*ātman*) found in the Sūtra may also denote a master.
How so?
Because it has the sense of being the agent of grasping (*ādāna*), that is, because its meaning is the state of being the doer of grasping.

From the root *dāñ* preceded by the prefix *ā*, the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule *āto manin kvanip* (Pāṇini 3.2.74); there is the elision of the vowel *ā* and the substitution of *t* for *d* due to the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*).
Thus it has been said: "That which he attains and that which he takes," and so forth.
For a husband indeed takes his servants as his own. *12,28*
To the question "What follows from that?", he explains the meaning of the sūtra as follows: "The Master," etc.
"Viṣṇu alone is my lord"—this indeed should be constantly and truly meditated upon.

In this Sūtra there are two occurrences of the word "ātman": the first is for the purpose of restatement, and the second is for the purpose of an injunction. Both instances in the phrase "one should meditate on the Self as the Self" refer to Viṣṇu.
In this regard, the first [usage] functions as a mere name (*saṃjñā*) whose constituent parts are not intended to be expressed;
the second intends to express the meaning of its constituent parts and denotes the Lord (*svāmin*).
Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that "the Self is Viṣṇu, the Self is the Lord, the Self is the one to be meditated upon. This is the sense.
"Directly and with the utmost reverence.
But has this not already been covered by the statement, "Indeed, these [qualities] such as bliss and so forth belong to the Principal"?
True.
The repetition is for the purpose of making known that He is to be worshipped in every way;

this is what is meant by the words "eternally and directly" (*nityadaivāñjasā*). To the question, "What is the proof for His being to be worshipped in every way?", he says: "He is the Master" (*svāmī*).
The meditation "Viṣṇu is the Lord" should be performed by means of the qualifier and the qualified;
this must be done in every way and should never be forgotten.
Thus, the truth concerning the principles of existence and the supreme discourse on the six qualities:
"My lord is Hari, who is eternally the master of all"—thus should the imperishable Lord Viṣṇu be meditated upon at all times. (Manu 4.16)

The meaning is as follows: "as qualifier and qualified" refers to the relationship of qualifier and qualified itself—wherein lordship is the qualifier and Viṣṇu is the qualified—and not that lordship is an incidental (taṭastha) secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) of the qualityless Viṣṇu.
"In any way" means even when mental or physical afflictions exist.
The word "supreme" (param) means "higher.
By the phrase "my master," he precludes the notion of limitedness that might arise, stating "of all."
Thus ends the section on the "Approaching of the Self" in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_4,1.III: The Section on Quotations =======] *12,30* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning quotations (pratīkādhikaraṇa).
Oṃ! [The Self] is not in the symbols, for He is not that; Oṃ.
The worship of symbols such as the mind (*manas*) as Brahman—established by scriptural passages such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman"—is here prohibited.
In this context, one might think that the locative case in the word *pratīke* denotes location;
however, it is entirely appropriate for the meditation upon Brahman to have the symbol as its locus.
Therefore, he explains the proposition otherwise, saying: "In the form of a representative part" (pratīka).
Not in a symbol, for he is not that;
one should not perform the meditation on Viṣṇu by taking a symbol as the object.
The third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakṣaṇe).
The meaning is that one should not perform worship in such a form as "This mind and so forth is Viṣṇu.
He explains the reason for this with the word "pratīkam" (symbol): for [Viṣṇu] is not [merely] a symbol.
Viṣṇu is not even a mere representative part [of that]. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.17c //
Since that which is a "pratīka"—
that is, a representative image of Brahman, such as the mind and so forth— [is not Brahman itself].
"He is not indeed Viṣṇu; therefore [it is not so]"—this connects with the preceding statement.
Now, one might object: "This reason is irrelevant.

For it is the absence of non-difference between the image (pratīka) and Viṣṇu, as well as the cognition thereof, that precludes non-difference, and not the mere mental cultivation (bhāvanā) of non-difference. To this he says: "It is false" (mithyā).
For false worship indeed yields no benefit.
For that Viṣṇu is not the mere symbol;
therefore, the contemplation of non-difference between the two is a false form of worship,
and it is indeed a cause of misfortune.
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect intended by the author of the Sūtra is precisely that [the action] "should not be performed," and not directly [as a separate statement].
Consequently, there is no inconsistency. *12,31*

To explain why false worship is a cause of misfortune, he clearly articulates the very intention of this Sūtra, beginning with "He who [perceives] otherwise... and ending with "...the Lord of Lords": "He who perceives the Self and the Lord as other than what they truly are—what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own soul? (Manu 4.18).
"What sin is not committed by that thief who steals the Lord, who represents the Self as something other than what it truly is? He who represents Viṣṇu, who exists in one way, as being otherwise— "
What sin has not been committed by that thief who practices celibacy?
Otherwise, [he would be] existing in a manner different from being a mere symbol (pratīka) and so forth;
[he is] the Lord of the selves, that is, the individual souls (jīvas);
otherwise, [he would be perceived] as a symbol and so on.
One practices, knows, and meditates;
this is an explanation of "thievery" itself as that which "steals the self.
Indeed, if there were no distinction [between them], there would be only one remaining.
In that regard, when meditation is performed upon a symbol (*pratīka*), there is clearly a denial of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Even when the symbol is dissolved, because of the negation of divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), it remains a denial of the Supreme Self alone—
the Self who is the Supreme Self.
These three statements are obstacles to meditating on Viṣṇu as a mere symbol (*pratīka*);
however, there is no obstacle to meditating on a symbol as being Viṣṇu himself. For this reason, the statement "one's own self" (*svātmānam*) is cited:
"One's own self, or even an image, or indeed another deity..."
Whatever else one might meditate upon, whether conscious or unconscious, if one thinks "I am Keśava," what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals the Lord? (Manu 4.1.21)
"He who [thinks] 'another'—these three [terms] have a dual meaning.
He who meditates upon or knows Viṣṇu as another, that person shall sink into blinding darkness from which there is no emergence anywhere. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.22)
He who meditates on Viṣṇu as being something else, or thinks that Viṣṇu is something else,
sinks into the great darkness by reason of the fault of such erroneous meditation.
He who meditates on Viṣṇu as being something other, or on something else as being Viṣṇu,
has no emergence at all from the great darkness into which he has sunk.
"In which [case] one has fallen":
otherwise-contemplation itself is the fault; thus, "otherwise-contemplation-fault.
The words "whatever it may be" and so forth serve as *kaimutya* (a fortiori) arguments for the very same primary meaning.

Whatever exists in one way, if it is directly meditated upon as otherwise, it causes great harm to the meditator; how much more so in the case of Hari, the Lord of All? Whatever exists in one way, if it is directly known as otherwise...
If even Viṣṇu causes great harm, how much more so the Lord of all lords?
Whatever exists in one way but is perceived directly in another way causes misfortune in this world; how much more so the Lord of all lords?
Nothing whatsoever should be known or meditated upon by him as being otherwise;
how much less could Viṣṇu, the supreme of all, ever be known as inferior?
Therefore, an object should always be known and meditated upon exactly as it is;
for it is the cause of human purpose, and never otherwise.

If even something like the water of the Gaṅgā, which is inherently pure, would immediately cause great harm to the meditator if meditated upon as something else—that is, as impure—how much more so would it be for Hari, the Lord of All? For him, such a state of being "not preeminent" would lead to disaster.
Therefore, on the strength of the evidence stated in the Śrutis and Purāṇas, he cannot be a mere symbol (pratīka).
For it is sometimes to be meditated upon as Viṣṇu, since false knowledge brings about misfortune.
Intending this, the Blessed Lord said, "For he is not [the son]. (Manu 4.1.31ab)

Thus, by the force of the statements in the Śruti and Purāṇas, false knowledge is understood to be the source of misfortune; therefore, because it is the cause for [the objection that] the symbol (pratīka) of Viṣṇu should not be meditated upon, the Blessed Sūtrakāra, intending to show the relationship of cause and effect through this traditional sequence, states the reason "for indeed it is not so" (na hi saḥ).
Consequently, there is no lack of logical connection—this is the meaning.
Because both types of meditation (*dhyāna*) are equal in the manner that will be described hereafter, it is said "by way of power.
Since meditation is also a specific form of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is a mention of them as being conflated.
To the question, "In that case, what is the meaning of such scriptural passages as 'The mind is Brahman'? he says: "As a symbol" (*pratīka*).
Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon as being present in the various parts [of the body], and not otherwise.
There is extensive transposition: the nominative occurs in seven cases,
and the accusative in six.

The sense is that, based on such traditional Smṛti texts, the Śruti passages should be interpreted by transposing the case endings so as to convey the meaning of the locus (adhikaraṇa). Thus ends the section on Pratīka in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_4,1.IV: The Section on the Vision of Brahman (brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇam) =======] // Now begins the Section on the Vision of Brahman in the illustrious Nyāsudhā.
Oṃ, the vision of Brahman [arises] from excellence; Oṃ.

In this context, it is stated that "the vision of Brahman is to be practiced. When the question arises as to *where* this is to be done, it follows from proximity that it refers to the *pratīka* (symbolic object). However, that is rejected because of a lack of suitability.
Therefore, he explains the expectant statement of the proposition with the words: "Brahman, and so forth."
The vision of Brahman arises from excellence;
and the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon directly as "Brahman" at all times. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.32ab)

And here, by the employment of the word "ca" (and), there is a connection of this [word] with "ātman" (self) through fitness, even though it is separated; moreover, the word "ātman," which is introduced as ending in the nominative case,
has here the sense of the locative case.
The change of case endings occurs for the sake of the sense;
thus it is indicated that the word ending in the locative case is to be understood here.
The intended meaning is that the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, is Brahman, who is to be meditated upon.
This is not the literal meaning [of the word *sadā*].

Now, one might object that this has already been established by the statement, "The greatness [of the Self] is superior, like a sacrifice" (*bhūmnaḥ kratuvajjyāyastvam*). To this, it is said: "always directly" (*sadāñjasā*). The reason for this is "because of its excellence" (*utkarṣāt*).
In that case, it is not known whose excellence [is intended];
therefore, he explains: "excellent" (utkṛṣṭa).
The meaning of the word "Brahman" is supreme... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.32c //
The word "yataḥ" (from which) is connected here as well with what is to be stated later.
By the author of the Sūtras, it was stated that excellence (*utkarṣa*) is the ground for the application of the term *brahman*;
however, by the author of the Anuvyākhyāna, it was asserted that that which possesses excellence is the denotation of the term *brahman*.
In effect, however, the meaning is one and the same.
To the question, "How is excellence (*utkarṣa*) the ground for the application of the word 'Brahman'? he says:
"Because fullness (*pūrṇatva*) is the state of being Brahman (*brahmatā*). (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.32d)

From the root *bṛh*, meaning "to increase," the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well"; by the force of the inclusion of the word "is seen" (*dṛśi*), the augment *am* is added to the root.
"Increase" (*vṛddhi*) and "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*) have one and the same meaning. The state of being Brahman (*brahmatā*) is the ground for the application of the term "Brahman."
Perfection itself is excellence;
and the relationship of cause and effect has already been established in the commentary.
To the question, "What is the proof for the fact that Brahman-hood is in every way the object of meditation? he says: "Suffering from mental anguish and physical disease," and so forth.
"Even for one whose mind is distracted by the causes of mental or physical affliction,
the nature of Brahman should always be meditated upon through uninterrupted devotion to Viṣṇu"—
this is the statement uttered by Viṣṇu in the *Prakāśikā*. (MAnu 4.1.33)
*Ādhivyādhi* is a dvandva compound treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*).
That [suffering] and its cause—by that [means].
The genitive case is used according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*.
By the word "ca" (and), he includes the statements cited in the Bhāṣya.
Thus ends the section on the "Vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā. [End of Section 4.1.V:
The Section on the Acceptance of the Self (*ātmopagamādhikaraṇa*)].
Now, in the *Śrīmanyāsudhā*, the refutation of alternative explanations regarding the section on "The Self’s Arrival" (*Ātmopagamādhikaraṇa*).

Some explain the three sūtras— “But they [the Upanishads] approach [the Self] as the Self and cause [others] to grasp it,” “Not in a symbol, for he is not that,” and “The vision of Brahman [is to be applied to the symbol], because of its excellence”— in a different manner.
For instance, when the doubt arises as to whether the Supreme Self should be apprehended as "I" or as "other than me," it follows that it should be apprehended as "not I."
Why?
Because the Supreme Self possesses qualities such as being free from evil,
whereas the embodied self possesses qualities contrary to those.
Therefore, how could there be non-difference between the two?
If the Lord were identical with the transmigrating soul, it would follow that the Lord does not exist, and consequently, the scriptures would be purposeless.
Conversely, if the transmigrating soul were the Lord, there would be no one eligible for instruction, and thus the scriptures would likewise be purposeless.
Furthermore, there would be contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge.
This being the case, we reply:
the Supreme Lord is to be understood as the Self alone.
For instance, in the *Parameśvaraprakriyā*, the Jābālas approach Him as their very Self, saying:
"I am indeed You, O Blessed Deity; You are indeed I, O Deity."
In the same way, other assertions of selfhood, such as "I am Brahman" and so forth, are to be understood;
moreover, Vedic statements cause one to grasp the Lord precisely as the Self.
“‘This is your Self, which is within all,’ ‘That thou art,’ and so forth; and, ‘Now, he who worships another deity [thinking,] “He is one and I am another”...’”
Scripture, beginning with such passages, also refutes the perception of difference.

As for the claim that it is impossible for two things possessing contradictory qualities to be of one another's nature, that is incorrect; for their possession of contradictory qualities is merely illusory.
Nor does it follow that there would be an absence of God;
for it is not the transmigratory state of God that is being established, but rather Godhood [is established] through the exclusion of the transmigratory state.
Furthermore, there is no lack of a qualified person [for the practice], nor is there any contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition.
This is because, prior to awakening, one accepts the state of being a transmigrating being (saṃsārin),
and because empirical transactions such as perception and so forth have that [state] as their object;
however, upon awakening, there is simply the absence of perception and the like.
If it is argued that, in that case, there would also follow the non-existence of the scriptural teaching of the non-duality of reality (*satyādvaita*), we reply:
this is indeed accepted.
Therefore, the meaning of the first sūtra is that one should fix the mind on the Lord as being simply the Self (*ātman*).

Regarding meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," a doubt arises: should the grasping of the Self (ātmagraha) be performed in these cases as well, or not? What is the initial position?
It is argued that even in those cases, the grasping of the Self alone is appropriate.
Why?
Because Brahman is the Self, and since the symbols (pratīkas) are also transformations of Brahman, it is logical that they possess the nature of the Self insofar as they are Brahman.
We reply:
one should not fix the notion of the Self upon the symbols;
for that worshipper is not [merely] the symbols, since he would have to regard those symbols as being the Self.

Furthermore, the claim that symbols (pratīka) possess the nature of Brahman—and consequently the nature of the Self—because they are modifications (vikāra) of Brahman, is incorrect; for it would entail the non-existence of the symbols themselves.

This is because, by means of the sublation of the specific nature of a modification, one would necessarily resort to the view that the entire class of things beginning with names is nothing but Brahman.

Furthermore, if the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the name and so forth were to be sublated, how could they possess the nature of a *pratīka* (symbolic representation) or serve as the grasping of the Self?
Moreover, just as there is no identity between a golden necklace (*rucaka*) and a svastika cross,
because both are modifications (*vikāra*).
The same applies to the symbols (pratīka) and the Self as well.

We have already stated that if there were identity between the symbol and the Self through the nature of Brahman—just as there is identity through the nature of gold—it would follow that the symbol would cease to exist.
Therefore, the meaning of the second sūtra is that one should not practice the contemplation of the Self upon symbols. *12,46*
Regarding those very same examples, another doubt arises:
should the meditations on the sun and so forth be applied to Brahman, or should the meditation on Brahman be applied to the sun and so forth?
This is because grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is possible in both ways.
In this regard, there is no restriction, because there is no scripture that imposes such a restriction.
Alternatively, the very meditations on the sun and so forth should be performed upon Brahman;
for in this way, Brahman becomes worshipped.
When it is argued that the meditation on Brahman must be fruitful, we reply:
the vision of Brahman alone should be applied to the sun and other such objects.
Why?
Because of their excellence;
thus, by way of excellence, the sun and other luminaries are perceived,
and in this way, the worldly principle is followed.
Indeed, the view of the king is applied to the steward, but the view of the steward is not applied to the king, because in such a reversal there would be the consequence of sin.
As for your claim that meditation on Brahman is appropriate because it possesses a fruit, that is incorrect;
for it is established that meditation on the sun and other objects likewise possesses fruits.
Furthermore, Brahman alone, because it is the presiding overseer of all, will bestow the fruit;

and this very meditation on Brahman consists in viewing [Brahman] within the sun and other such objects, just as one views Viṣṇu and others in images and the like—this is the meaning of the third sūtra.
Regarding that, he first refutes a misinterpretation of the first sūtra with the word "no" (na).
The Sūtra "not the Self" establishes that the Lord is the individual soul.
In this context, "cognition" (pratipatti) is intended by the opponent to mean nothing other than valid knowledge (*pramiti*),
since [the author] refutes it by suspecting it to be a mere perception (*pratīti*).
Therefore, [the phrase] means "that which establishes the state of being cognizable as a living being."
And the meaning is one and the same: that which establishes the state of being alive.

Why is this not so? Because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words, [the author] first refutes the word-meaning with the phrase: "the word 'ātman'."
Since the King of the Vedas, taking the word "self" as the reason, excluded the individual soul (jīva),
and likewise did not mention the vital breath (prāṇabhṛt) because of the word "own" (sva).

The construction is as follows: since the King of the Vedas (the Upanishads) himself, by using the word "Self" (*ātman*) as the reason, excluded the individual soul (*jīva*)—on the grounds that it was not mentioned even by its own specific term—it follows that Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the word "Self" and no other, namely the individual soul.
This is what is meant:
this would be the meaning of the Sūtra if the word "Self" were a synonym for the individual soul.
But it is not so; for by the very force of the author of the Sūtra’s statement, it is understood that it does not denote that [meaning]. To explain:

Having cited the passage beginning with "In which the heaven," a doubt arises as to whether the *pradhāna*, the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is here spoken of as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. When the *pradhāna* and others are initially proposed, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached:
"The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is the Supreme Self], because of its own word" (*svaśabdāt*).
This is because of its own word: "Know Him alone as the one Self. (*tamevaikaṃ jānatha ātmānam*)

Thus, because the word "Self" (ātman) is heard in reference to the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, it follows that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self alone. Therefore, having refuted the Pradhāna by the sūtra "Not the inferable [Pradhāna], because of the absence of its designation," the following was formulated as a sūtra for the purpose of refuting the individual soul (jīva).
Regarding the phrase "and [the word] *prāṇabhṛt*":
here, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to draw forward both the word "not" (*na*) and the reason "because of its own word" (*svaśabdāt*).
Consequently, the meaning is that the individual soul (*jīva*) is also not [denoted] because of the word "Self" (*ātman*).

Since the author of the Sūtras has thus refuted the individual soul (jīva) by employing the word "Self" as the reason, we understand from the impossibility of any other interpretation that the author intended the word "Self" not to denote the individual soul. And so, how could he now act in a manner contrary to his own established position? (12.51)
He clarifies this very point with the words "If... (yadīti).
If the word "Self" (ātman) applies even to the individual soul (jīva), how could it exclude [Viṣṇu]?
Therefore, he who is denoted by the word "Self" is Viṣṇu alone, and no other.
The implication is that it is the intention of the author of the Sūtras that [the term "self"] applies to the living being (*jīva*) as well.
If so, how could the author of the Sūtras exclude the *jīva* by using the word "self"?
For indeed, a jar cannot be excluded on the grounds of its possessing fragrance.

Alternatively, if the word "Self" (ātman) were to apply even to the individual soul (jīva), then how could that word "Self" exclude the individual soul? On the contrary, it would establish it; such is the construction [of the argument].
He also cites a scriptural statement on this point: "As the Self... (*ātmeti*).
Words such as "Self" (ātman) and "Brahman" do not denote that immutable Viṣṇu,
because perfection in all qualities is never found in them;
for the Vaiṣṇava teaching states that the supreme Self resides in Nārāyaṇa alone.

They do not say [these names] refer to anything else because words such as "Ātman" and others denote fullness (*pūrti*); by those other [entities], the state of being full of qualities has never been attained at any stage. Furthermore, if they were to have the sense of some limited kind of fullness, it would result in their being used in a non-primary (secondary) sense.
Even the word "Ātman" is derived from the root *tan* preceded by the prefix *ā*, formed with the suffix *manin* and the elision of the *ṭi*-portion; thus, it is a term expressing fullness.
"Since there is such a statement, for that reason also"—this connects with what was stated previously.
Now, he refutes the meaning of the sentence with the word "yadi" (if).
If one considers the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), how can one logically exclude the word "Self" (ātman) from the latter? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.37)
If one thinks that in that sutra [the term] "self" refers to that living being (jīva), then how does it exclude the word "self" from that living being?
To the question of where it has excluded it, it is said: "by means of reasoning."
The meaning is that this is stated as a logical argument for the refutation of the individual soul (jīva).
This is what is intended:

by stating that "because of the hearing of the word 'Self' (ātman), the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not the individual soul," the author of the Sūtras provides the word "Self" as the reason for excluding the individual soul; thus, it is understood that the word "Self" excludes the individual soul.
It is like [the argument]: "This person is not [a cow] because he has horns.

For it is not logical that the negation of that [cow-nature] should be established by means of something residing therein; otherwise, it would follow as an absurd consequence that "this is not a cow because he has horns."
Furthermore, in the first Sūtra, it was accepted that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Lord and not the individual soul (jīva), on account of the word "Self" (ātman);
for otherwise, it would be impossible to establish that [the Supreme Lord] by means of that [word].
In that context, if the author of the Sūtras had held the view that the individual soul and the Lord are one and the same reality, [he would not have used the term "Self" in this way].
Thus, it is said that by him the word "self" both applies and does not apply to that very same thing;
and it is not reasonable to claim that the author of the Sūtras speaks in contradiction.
Therefore, it is understood that his view is not that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are identical.
Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication:
the Supreme Lord is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
It should also be understood that the two propositions—that [the self] is not the living being (*jīva*)—are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, he states the contradiction with other sūtras: "of the difference," etc. (*bhedasya*).

The Lord of the World, with full intention, has stated the reason for the firmness of distinctions—namely, the designation, the maintenance, and the consumption [of food] according to those distinctions. (Manu 4.1.38)

If the Lord of the World, the author of the Sūtras, considers the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), then how is it that he himself states the designation of difference in the sūtra “Because of the designation of difference” (*bhedavyapadeśāt*) and provides the reasons for establishing the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord with full intent through the sūtras “And because of abiding and eating” (*sthityadanābhyāṃ ca*), which describe both their coexistence and their distinct functions?
Since the distinction has already been established previously, it is described here as being "firm.
Furthermore, because multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been presented here as well, it possesses a definitive intention (*satātparya*).
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever here.

For even though the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are one in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there exists a conventional distinction (vyāvahārika-bheda); with that [distinction] in view, those Sūtras [were composed].

However, this [present work] is from the perspective of the ultimate truth; thus, with the intention that such a systematic arrangement (vyavasthā) is logically consistent, he raises an objection: "vyāvahārika... and so forth.
If it is a conventional distinction... // MAnu 4.1.39a //
Here, by the term "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*), that which is established through delusion (*bhrānti*) is intended,
because it is a restatement of what was previously said [in the verse], namely, "prior to awakening.
One who asserts that the distinction between the individual self (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established through delusion should be questioned as follows:
Is this very distinction established by error, or is it merely a distinction?
Not the first,
because it would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).
He states the fault in the second [case] with the words: "Where? (kveti).
... where is that which is beyond worldly convention? (Manu 4.1.39b)

Because error must be preceded by non-error, if the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) were merely imagined through error, some true distinction would have to be admitted somewhere;
but where could it be? Nowhere at all.
The sense is that if one were to admit the reality of difference anywhere, even the superimposition of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) would be impossible.
This might be argued:
there is no difference whatsoever that is real.
Nevertheless, the delusion of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) is possible;
for delusion depends upon mental impressions (saṃskāra),
and mental impression is nothing but cognition (jñāna).
Therefore, because each preceding [moment] is unconditioned, each succeeding error arises;
and this saṃsāra is beginningless.
This is not so.
Indeed, this conceptual construction is tenable only if difference (*bheda*) itself is known to be false;
but that is not the case.
For the very thesis that "all difference is illusory" is itself undermined.
Intending to show that the presentation of formal proofs is far removed [from this context], he asks, with supporting arguments, "Is it conventional? (vyāvahārikam).
The very statement "it is conventional" is itself conventional.
But in the case of the alternative "or not," ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.40a //
The remainder is "merely a distinction. The meaning is simply: "let the other matter rest for now. Thus, in the case of the two-fold alternative (pakṣadvaye).
In the case of a conflict (*dvaidhe*),
the ellipsis is "which side should one rely upon?
In all these instances, by the word "statement" (*vacana*), its meaning is indicated through metonymy (*lakṣyate*).

The meaning of the sentence is that every distinction is imagined through delusion; the sense of the question is whether this [sentence-meaning] itself is imagined through delusion or is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). He raises the first alternative with the words "If... (*yadīti*).
"...if it were merely conventional. The phrase "this statement" carries over from the previous context.
Here too, we ask: is this meaning of the sentence to be set aside or not?
If the position is "no," then it could not even be imagined by delusion;
for if that which is never, anywhere, or by anyone sublated were imagined by delusion, then Brahman itself would necessarily fall into the same state.
He first raises this doubt with the words: "tasya" (of that).
If even that [scripture] were subject to sublation... // MĀnuv 4.1.40c //
The meaning is that not only would that statement be a construction of error, but it would also be subject to sublation. He refutes this with the words "difference" (bheda).
... there would be an ultimate distinction.
If the meaning of the statement "all difference is erroneous" were itself erroneous or sublatable, then every difference would be ultimately real.
He raises the second objection: "It is non-conventional."
If it is argued that [it] is not subject to worldly transaction...
The phrase "of that statement" carries over [from the previous context].
He refutes it with the words: "Difference."
... this distinction has attained the status of truth. // MAnu 4.41b //
Let it be for now that there is no other [objection].
If the meaning of the sentence were real, then there would be a difference between that [sentence-meaning] and Brahman;

and since the reality of the sentence-meaning is untenable if the word-meanings are unreal, there would also be a mutual difference among the word-meanings, as well as a difference between them and the sentence-meaning and Brahman.
Thus, that [distinction] has become real.
The meaning is that in either case, the meaning of the sentence is contradicted.
It was stated that if the meaning of the sentence—namely, "all distinction is erroneous"—were itself erroneous or sublatable, then all distinction would necessarily be real.
Why is that? To establish this, he first states the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "of one" (*ekasya*).
For when one of two contradictory things is unreal, by what means can it be prevented that the other must indeed be real? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.41c–f)
Between two things that are mutually contradictory, if one is false, the other must necessarily be true; by what can this pervasion (*vyāpti*) be refuted?
By nothing at all, because there is an absence of both a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
There is no such rule that if the object standing before one is not a person, it must necessarily be a post.
Since the state of being an anthill is also possible [in that case],
it was stated "of two contradictory [things] only.
The term "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is employed to avoid the charge of redundancy regarding the qualification "of two" (*dvayoḥ*).
It is stated that whichever object possesses the unreality of one of two contradictory things must possess the reality of the other.
He provides an illustration: "that which is impermanent."
When it is said, "I have not spoken an untruth," people understand that truth has been spoken;
but when it is said, "I have not spoken the truth," they also understand the lack of truth. (Manu 4.1.42)

When a trustworthy person says something untrue, people know that what was said is true when they hear "it is not untrue"; likewise, when a deceiver says something true, they recognize its falsity when they hear "it is not so.
Thus, truthfulness and untruthfulness are both mutually exclusive opposites.

The meaning is this: therein, when there is no falsity in the matter spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), the existence of truth is established; and when there is no truth in what is spoken by one who is not reliable, the existence of falsity is established.
The phrase "thus it has been said" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its being cognized through valid means of knowledge (*pramita*).
By the expression "people know," [it is indicated that]...
This pervasion is established even among cowherd women and sheepherders, not only among investigators; this he indicates.
[Objection: But surely, having seen "there is a jar here" in a dream, one also sees "there is no jar here.
In that case, both the jar and its absence are false.
Therefore, because there is a failure of pervasion (vyāpti), he says: "No."
Even in a dream, duality is false...
To the question, "Is both of these true? he says: "In that regard... (tatra).
... for in that case, there is indeed only one truth. (Manu 4.1.43b)
In that regard, between the jar and its absence:
when the absence is unreal, then the jar is indeed real;
and when the jar is unreal, then the absence is indeed real—this is the meaning.
Therefore, the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that there is no breach of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Why is it that neither of the two is false? To this he says: "bhāva... (existence...). "How could both existence and non-existence be false in that case? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.1.43cd).

The meaning is that there is an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) such that whatever is the absence of something, and whatever is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of an absence, both cannot be non-false at the same time and in the same place.
The point is: how could a pot and its absence exist in such a manner even in a dream?
Furthermore, with the intention of showing that it is contradictory to describe both existence and non-existence as being non-existent, he says: "For of an existent thing... (bhāvasya hi).
For when an entity is negated, there is no negation of its non-existence.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason:
because when the negation of existence has been performed, non-existence itself is thereby established;
furthermore, it is not possible to negate that non-existence again, due to contradiction.

Thus, when the negation of non-existence has been made, since existence itself—or that which is pervaded by it—is established as the non-existence of non-existence, it is not again proper to negate existence, because that would be contradictory. [The opponent might say: "Let there be such a pervasion; what of it? To this he says: "By one's own words."
If the unreality of one's own words were to follow from that, then the reality of difference would be established.
By the word "own" (sva), the opponent is denoted;
[the object] is the meaning of their speech, namely, the falsity of all distinctions.
Therefore, because pervasion exists, falsity and truth are two contradictory properties.
The meaning is that if there were a distinction between the two,
then, in the absence of falsity, truth would necessarily exist by virtue of the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*). He concludes the present topic with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, the difference between the individual soul and the Lord is understood through the reasoning already stated.

Since a false difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is impossible, it is established by the aforementioned reasoning and the *dyubhvādi* sūtras that there is indeed an ultimate difference between them.
Thus, it is proven that this sūtra does not teach non-difference, as that would contradict such [evidence].
As for the scriptural texts (*śruti*), they have already been correctly explained above.
The truth of contradictory qualities has been established;
the incapacity of perception and other means of knowledge to reveal ultimate reality has also been refuted;
and the undesirability of the falsity of the Śruti has been supported—thus, the meaning of the Sūtra has indeed been stated.
Thus concludes, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the refutation of alternative explanations regarding the section on the acceptance of the Self (*ātmopagamādhikaraṇa*).

*12,71* [======= JNys_4,1.VI: The Section on the Symbolic Parts (*pratīkādhikaraṇa*) =======] Now follows, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the refutation of alternative explanations regarding the section on the symbolic parts (*pratīkādhikaraṇa*).
Having thus refuted the false interpretation of the first sūtra, he now refutes that of the second as well, beginning with the words "etasmāt" (from this).
Therefore, this word "ātman" should be understood as a designation for the Supreme Self.
From this aforementioned reasoning, this word "Self" (*ātman*) occurring in the Sūtra must first be an expression for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), that is, a designator of the Supreme Self alone.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "As a symbol" (*pratīka*).
The visualization of Viṣṇu upon a representative object would not be that [true meditation].

Therefore, since the word "Self" (ātman) occurring in the preceding sūtra denotes the Supreme Self (paramātman), the meaning is that the proposition "it is not a symbol" (na pratīkaḥ) cannot mean that one should perform the visualization of Viṣṇu upon a symbol; this is what is being stated. In the phrase "it is not a symbol," the word "Self" (ātmeti) must be carried over from the preceding sūtra.
Otherwise, the statement of the proposition would be incomplete;

furthermore, it has been established in the preceding Sūtra that the word "Self" (ātman) refers to Viṣṇu. Therefore, this prohibition must be explained as referring specifically to the meditation on Viṣṇu through a symbolic object (pratīka).

However, regarding the explanation of the proposition that "one should not fix the notion of the living self (*jīva*) upon symbols (*pratīka*"), it would follow that one abandons the subject at hand and accepts what is not the subject at hand.
As for what was stated— that [the Self] exists as a symbol in the sense of the meaning of such scriptural passages as "The mind is Brahman"—
that too is not outside the scope of the Sūtra.
However, the word *pratīke* (in the symbol) is repeated as a locative case ending.
Of these, the first, being a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), is connected with the word *na*;
the second, being a locative of locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), refers to the explanation of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

Intending that the two words "in both cases" and "the self" (ātmeti) are carried over from the preceding sūtra, he explains the second [word] by way of context: "as a representative symbol" (pratīke).
"Because [the perception] of Viṣṇu must be performed with respect to the symbol (pratīka), therefore worship should indeed be performed [in that manner].
This is the meaning of the Vedic passage; the word "therefore" (tasmāt) implies that the perception of Viṣṇu is not to be made by treating the symbol as the primary object.
By the use of the particle "hi," he indicates that it is well known among grammarians that the first case ending can express the sense of the seventh case.
For this reason as well, he states that this is not the meaning of the proposition: "And not... (na ca).
And Viṣṇu is not that which is the image; therefore... // MAnu 4.47ab //
Since Viṣṇu is the symbol—

and by the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] that he is not [the symbol] of the individual soul (jīva)— therefore, the meditation on the symbols as "Self" or as "individual soul" does not apply; this is the remainder of the sense.
This is the meaning:
for a prohibition can only be stated when there is a possibility of occurrence;
however, in the case of the secondary symbols (pratīkas), the worshiper's perception of them as the Self does not arise, because there is no cause for such a misconception.

As for that which was stated as the reductio ad absurdum— the selfhood of Brahman and the fact that the symbols (pratīka) are modifications of Brahman— both of these are unauthoritative and contrary to valid means of knowledge;
for a reductio cannot be established by means of something that is utterly fallacious,
as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, because there is no possibility [of the object being Viṣṇu], the negation is meaningless.
He does not refute the explanation of the reason "for it is not that"; rather, he says: "and Viṣṇu is not that which is the symbol (pratīka)."
For the word "that" (tat) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, and it is the Self (ātman) that has been previously mentioned;
furthermore, it has been established that the word "Self" denotes Viṣṇu alone.
Thus, the meaning results as follows: because He, Viṣṇu, is not a mere symbolic representation (pratīka), therefore [it is so].

For it is not the case that the lay follower (*upāsaka*) is meant by the term "limbs" (*pratīka*), since such an interpretation would entail abandoning the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) to refer instead to something irrelevant (*aprakṛta*).
Thus ends the refutation of the alternative explanation of the section concerning the "limbs.
[======= JNYS_4,1.VII: Section on the Meditation on [the Self] as Brahman (brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇa) =======]
Now follows the refutation of alternative interpretations regarding the section on the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇa*).
Now, he provides a refutation of the erroneous interpretation of the sutra "the view of Brahman" (brahmadṛṣṭi): "Not the Self" (nātmeti).
...the meditation [on the Self] as "not the Self"—this is the position when the perception of Brahman here is contradicted. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.47b–d)
By citing this partial statement, "the meditation [on Brahman] as 'not the Self'," he restates the meaning of the entire sūtra: "Not in a symbol, for he is not that.
One should not perform meditation on symbols as the Self—that is, as the individual soul (jīva).

The position that "that lay follower [does not perceive] the symbols" is explained by the previous sūtra as "when [he thinks] 'this is indeed [Brahman]'; when that is so, then here the perception of Brahman in the symbols would be contradicted.
The word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of excluding a false interpretation and for conjunction.
He explains this with the words "He... (*sa*).
The reasoning that "it is not so" is also contradicted by what was stated previously.

Regarding the point that you stated— that the reasoning characterized by the absence of identity (tādātmyābhāva), expressed as "not this" (neti), applies to the fact that one should not perform meditation on symbols (pratīka) as the Self—

that same reasoning applies equally to the case of Brahman and its symbol; therefore, when the Sūtra is explained as meaning that the vision of Brahman (brahmadṛṣṭi) must be applied to the symbols, it becomes contradictory to the reasoning you have stated.
This is what is meant:
the interpretation of the Sūtra that "the vision of Brahman should be applied to the symbols" is incorrect;
a symbol is not to be meditated upon as being Brahman itself.
Because it is not Brahman;
for it would contradict reason to hold that what is not something should be meditated upon as that very thing,
and this reasoning is not invalid.
For the inadmissibility of meditating on symbols (pratīka) as the Self was already presented by the opponent in the preceding sūtra;
otherwise, that [reason] would not be a valid proof due to its lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntya).
Furthermore, there is no non-difference between Brahman and the symbol, because Brahman is real while symbols are merely imagined.
If it is argued that there is at least an absence of ultimate difference [between Brahman and the world],
then it would follow that such an absence does not exist even between the individual soul (*jīva*) and its representative image (*pratīka*), and thus [the reason] would be unestablished (*asiddhi*).
This might be so.

The reason "not that" (*na hi saḥ*) is not intended by the author of the Sūtras as being without qualification, such that the viewing of the symbols as Brahman would contradict the stated reasoning; rather,
it is to be qualified by the phrase "provided there is no attainment of excellence for the object of meditation."
However, in the case of meditating upon the limbs as Brahman, there is the attainment of excellence;
therefore, even in the absence of that [Brahman-nature], meditation is appropriate. To this he says: "If..."
For even if it is performed merely for the sake of excellence, such worship may indeed be practiced even toward that which is not [the ultimate reality].
In the first [verse], the word "api" (even/also) serves to include the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The word "hi" (for/since) is to be construed with the second half-verse.

If, having explained the specific cause, one were to accept the meditation on the mantras as being Brahman merely because they attain excellence—even though they do not possess that nature and are not Brahman—[then the following would follow].
Therefore, its worship even as the Self must be accepted and not rejected.
Why? To this he says: "Because of excellence."
There may even be an elevation of oneself [through this], because it is conscious, unlike that which is unconscious.
Because, as in the case of Brahman, there is also an exaltation of the self from its representative symbol (pratīka).
How so?
Because the self is conscious.
The symbol (pratīka) is indeed insentient;
[the opponent argues that] by meditating upon it as the Self, one would attain excellence.
To avoid such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he states the conclusion by way of a counter-argument: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, it is the opinion of those who know the Veda that unreality is not to be meditated upon.
Because, if the cause were explained as being distinct [from the Self], there would be a lack of proof regarding the previous Sūtra;
consequently, just like the meditation on Brahman, the meditation on the individual self (ātman) would also result in being treated as a mere symbolic representation (pratīka).
Therefore, it is not the reality.

Whatever is not [the object] itself should not be meditated upon as that in its true nature; this is precisely the general principle intended by the author of the Sūtras, and not the addition of qualifiers.
Consequently, the proposition "the perception of Brahman [in other objects]" is indeed contradicted by the reasoning he himself has stated.

In this context, it must be stated that the intention of the reason (*hetu*)—which is described as being "without qualification" (*nirviśeṣaṇa*)—lies precisely in its being without qualification; the mention of pervasion (*vyāpti*), however, is for the sake of clarity. Having refuted the explanation of the proposition (*pratijñā*), he now refutes the explanation of the reason "because of elevation" (*utkarṣāt*) with the words: "Because of elevation."
If, through meditation on Brahman as superior, a fruit were to arise quickly,
why would no misfortune not arise from meditating on Brahman as inferior?

Since it is observed that in the meditation on Brahman there is an elevation [of the result] due to the elevation of the meditative objects (*pratīka*), if there were a direct fruit consisting of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
then that very same [result] would follow from meditating on the inferiority of Brahman; therefore, why would a disadvantage not arise?
"It is indeed born," [he says], because its result is equal to its expenditure; thus, this is truly not something to be done.
This statement regarding the equality of expenditure and result was made while provisionally accepting it;
in reality, however, it is not a human goal (puruṣārtha), but rather a misfortune. To this effect, he says: "of the insentient."
Brahman is never pleased by meditating upon an insentient object as Brahman;
rather, like people in the world, Brahman becomes angry when a lowly person meditates upon himself as being identical with Brahman.

And because there is an absence of satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*), there is consequently no attainment of the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*). By the phrase "in some cases," [the author] indicates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that whatever is insentient is devoid of satisfaction characterized by the desire to benefit others.
Brahmā becomes angry due to the meditation upon his own self as being identical with a lowly person.
Furthermore, it bestows misfortune;
in this regard, the analogy is "as in the world.
Just as in the world, when a stone or similar object is meditated upon as being a king or the like, it does not become gracious, nor does it bestow any human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

The meaning is that just as a king, when meditated upon as a *caṇḍāla*, becomes angry and bestows misfortune, so it is here. By this, the argument that "even though the remedial means (*pratīka*) are insentient, Brahman alone will grant the fruit because He is the supervisor of all" is refuted; for [Brahman] becomes angry at him on account of this meditation [on a lowly object]. (12.82)

We do not say that one should meditate on Brahman as a mere symbol (pratīka), for if that were so, an angry Brahman might bestow misfortune; rather, we maintain that one should meditate on the symbol as being Brahman itself, and from that, the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) follows. To this, he says: "a Caṇḍāla."
When it is said "the outcaste is the king," or "the king is the outcaste," what distinction could possibly exist once the king has been fully recognized? (Manu 4.51)

If, with reference to a *caṇḍāla*, one says "the king is a *caṇḍāla*," or with reference to a king, one says "the king is a *caṇḍāla*," and this is recognized by the king such that misfortune ensues, what difference could there possibly be? None whatsoever.
Here, by the word "spoken" (*ukta*), meditation (*dhyāna*) is indicated.
It has been stated that a king who worships without knowing [the true nature of the object] does not bring about misfortune, because he is recognized as a king.
Likewise, the remainder of the passage implies that there is exactly the same misfortune whether one worships the *pratīka* (the symbol) as Brahman, or worships Brahman as the *pratīka*.
Now, one might object: "The perception of the king in the charioteer (*kṣattr*) is fruitful."
If it is argued that the sight of the king by the gatekeeper was seen to be a cause of misfortune,
and therefore how can the similarity of both cases be asserted— [we reply] no,
because in that case there was an absence of [such] sight.
The mere statement, however, is used figuratively, just as one says, "Devadatta is a lion.
But with the intention that even in such a case, there is an identity of purpose regarding what is seen, he says: "In front" (*purataḥ*). (12.83)
If a Caṇḍāla is honored before a king like a king himself, why would the king not feel anger? For the king indeed observes this in the world.
If the king is honored in such a manner,
would he not then be free from anger?
This is stated to demonstrate the intensity of his wrath, as one observes that [anger] exists in the world when such things are present.
Because one's status is elevated through worship, it is said that "he is worshipped.
It is not only when the worship elevates his vision that the king’s anger arises, but also when such speech is uttered; thus he says: "But of the king... [rājñastu].
But when it is said before the king, "The king is a Caṇḍāla," he becomes as if enraged, thinking, "He says that about me. (Manu Smṛti 4.153)
Speech uttered without being understood generates anger; therefore, it was said, "in the presence of the king.
Even if one says "O King" to a Caṇḍāla, the king still becomes angry even when told, "I am not speaking figuratively, but indeed according to the actual fact.
For he [the king] feels as if he himself has been called a Caṇḍāla; the meaning here is that it is exactly as if he had been addressed with emphasis.
This verse is intended for the sake of discernment (*viveka*) in order to dispel the doubt that "worship alone is the cause of anger, not the sight [of the deity].
Having thus accepted the two-fold nature [of the deity] as stated in the rules for the preliminary invocation (*uddeśavidhāna*), their equality was described in terms of the result.
Now he says, "without distinction," to show that even that [equality] does not exist.
If there is no difference between these two, what distinction is there in their meditation or even in their speech?

If meditation on these two symbols of Brahman is accepted as non-different, not only is there equality in the result, but what difference is there even in the words? The meaning is that the significance of both statements is indeed without distinction.
He provides an illustration for this very point with the word "this" (*ayam*).
Whether it be said of a Caṇḍāla or a king, "This man is a king" or "This man is a Caṇḍāla," the resulting defilement is indeed exactly the same.
The objection that a refutation might be avoided by means of a difference between individuals is addressed by the word "this" (*ayam*).
The refutation consists in the characteristic of inferiority;
indeed, a refutation is possible in meditation precisely through the non-difference of the two.
But this is not the case;
for it is the symbol that is meditated upon as being Brahman, and not Brahman as being the symbol. Therefore, he says: "meditated upon."
But when one person meditates and that state arises for him, why does that same state not arise for another? (4.55ab)

When one of those two symbols (*pratīka*) is meditated upon as being that—that is, as having the nature of Brahman—why should the other [symbol] not also be meditated upon as having that nature, the nature of Brahman?
This is what is meant:
this would be a valid resolution if [the symbol were]...
The position might be that its status as Brahman is to be meditated upon through the destruction of its own nature;
but this is not so,
because the opponent himself has stated that it would result in the absence of any object of meditation (pratīka).
Nor is it the case that this resolution is intended on the basis of both difference and non-difference;
for how could there be mutual difference and non-difference such that "the pot is non-different from the clay" and yet "the clay is different from the pot"?
Therefore, it is rightly said that when the symbol (pratīka), whose own nature is not sublated, is meditated upon as Brahman, then Brahman itself is indeed meditated upon as the symbol.
Now, one might argue that in this meditation, harm would occur if Brahman were known, but not if it were unknown;
therefore, one will perform the meditation in such a way [as to remain ignorant]. To this, he says: "And indeed not."
And that [knowledge] is never unknown to the omniscient Brahman anywhere.
That is the worship [of Brahman].
To say that "if there is ignorance of Brahman, Brahman alone, as the supervisor of all, will grant the fruit" would be an empty statement.

Anticipating the objection—"But how can misfortune result from the anger of Brahman for one who practices what is enjoined by the Śruti?"—he concludes the refutation of the false interpretation with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, every statement asserting the Brahman-hood of anything else is unseemly.
The word "all" refers to that which takes the form of commentaries on the Śrutis and Sūtras.
By this, it should be understood that the conception of Viṣṇu and others in objects such as the Śālagrāma stone is also refuted.

Thinking that it would be irrelevant to begin with a commentary on the Sūtras and then proceed to refute a misinterpretation, he says "Therefore," with the intention of strengthening his own position.

Therefore, Brahman should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation according to the path as described; for the interpretations of others have been refuted. "According to the path as described" means by the path that proceeds without overstepping the meaning of the Sūtras as stated by us.
Thus ends the refutation of the alternative interpretation of the section concerning the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭyadhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_4,1.VIII: ...adhikaraṇam =======] // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the attainment of that [Brahman].
Oṃ. Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because that is so designated. Oṃ.
The inquiry into the means [of liberation] has been concluded.

Now, the fruit of knowledge called the destruction of karma is being defined in order to dispel the doubt that liberation cannot occur for a knower because of the existence of infinite past and future karmas which act as obstacles.
In this regard, he states the purport of the Sūtra—beginning with the word "tathā"—in order to refute the notion that the destruction of karma occurs through the power of knowledge alone.
Upon the realization of that [Brahman], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof;
likewise, when Brahman is directly perceived through meditation, it reduces all prior evil to ashes and ensures the non-attachment of future evil as well.
...he performs [it] in that manner,
directly, with both earnestness and continuity.
Having worshipped, all sin seen previously to [the arising of] knowledge [is destroyed].
By the word "and" (ca), non-meritorious [karma] is also included—
namely, subsequent sin and non-meritorious merit.
By this, [the phrase] "some say there is another besides these for both" is established.
Thus the purport of the Sūtra has been stated. // Oṃ. For the other as well, there is likewise non-attachment; but at death, Oṃ. //1//

Some knowers of Brahman explain this Sūtra as follows: "Just as for sin, so too for merit, there is a complete exhaustion—that is, destruction—when the fall of the body is imminent. That is incorrect.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy for the phrase "and other than that";
furthermore, the relationship between a commentary and its subject matter would have no other possible basis;
and since it would be sufficient to simply substitute the word "karma" for the word "evil" (*agha*) in the preceding sutra itself, the commencement of a separate sutra would be purposeless.
However, for us, the sūtras beginning with "But [the destruction] of our [past deeds], such as the Agnihotra and so forth," are intended to indicate a distinction even regarding merit.
Since there is no further acquisition of merit after the dawn of knowledge, the word *aśleṣa* (non-clinging) must be explained as meaning destruction.

Thus, mindful that [otherwise] there would be the abandonment of the subject at hand and the acceptance of what is not the subject, he states the intended meaning of the sūtra otherwise: "And of those who hate That."
In the same way, there is no attachment for the other [the one who has fallen] upon his fall;
and likewise for one who hates him, there is both the destruction of merit and non-attachment.
And [the same applies] to those who hate the Brahmins;
just as in the case of one possessing knowledge,
through the fulfillment of hatred, there occurs the destruction of prior merit and also the non-connection of future merit.

Regarding this, the objection is raised that the scriptural passage "that which one knows through knowledge" (yadeva vidyayā) is redundant, because its meaning was already stated previously by the sūtra "on account of that scripture" (tacchruteḥ). To this, he replies: "yadeva... [and so forth].
For in the verse beginning "Whatever by knowledge," it is indeed distinguished from what was stated previously.
In this context, the word "object of cognition" (*prameya*) is understood as the ellipsis;

therefore, there is no fault of tautology—this is the intention of the author. Alternatively, it may mean that the division of the subject matter to be explained is well-known by virtue of the context.
To explain how it is distinguished, he first states the purport of the preceding sūtra: "The former," and so forth.
Previously, for the sake of attaining heaven and other such goals, action was enjoined as being endowed with vigor; [now, however, it is] joined with knowledge... // MDh 4.1.58c-e //
The phrase "heaven and so forth" (svargādi) includes all human goals other than liberation (mokṣa).
He states the purport of the subsequent sūtra with the word "afterwards" (paścāt).
"But it bestows vigor for liberation hereafter. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.1.58ef)
The connection is with the word "afterwards.
The phrase "action conjoined with knowledge" continues to apply.
The "stage of vigor" bestows an excellence of bliss.
The connection is that "it has been urged thus.
Liberation would occur at that very moment upon the destruction of all karma;
however, it is not so.

To resolve the doubt arising from the observation of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the author of the Sūtras stated: "But only those previous [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit."

Then, raising the doubt as to how liberation can occur while prārabdha-karma still exists, it is restated in the aphorism: "But by experiencing [the fruits] through enjoyment, the others being exhausted, he then attains perfection."
Intending to show that this [statement] also does not refer exclusively to one who knows Brahman, he explains it with the words "tataḥ" (therefore).
But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [the state].
Then, having likewise exhausted both merit and its opposite through experience,
the hater of Brahman and the seer of Brahman obtain darkness and liberation, respectively.
Immediately after the exhaustion of those [karmas] not yet begun,
other evil [karmas] remain;
since the karmas already begun are infinite, their exhaustion cannot be achieved through experience alone.
He dispels this doubt with a scriptural statement: "Of the Brahmins."
The destruction of the merit previously begun occurs one hundred kalpas before the end of Brahmā’s life;
for Brahmā himself it lasts for fifty [kalpas],
