for Rudra twenty, and for Indra, the Sun, and the others, ten.
"For others, however, there is the destruction of the commenced [karman] at the end of the life of Brahmā;
and with Brahmā himself, he shall go to the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Thus is the statement regarding the true nature of reality (sattattva) spoken by the Blessed One himself. (Manu 4.1.61)
In the expression "brahmaṇāṃ śatam," there is no elision (aluk) of the genitive case-ending.
Its duration is the "period of a hundred Brahmās" (brahmaṇāṃ śatakālaḥ). Therefore, prior to its completion, the exhaustion of all commenced karma occurs for every person of knowledge.
This is further explained: the very extent of that [time] belongs to Brahmā; it is precisely by a hundred Brahmā-kalpas that there is the exhaustion of karma.
"Brahmaṇaḥ" is the singular used for the class [of Brahmās].
Fifty Brahmās ago, at that time, the destruction of Rudra began.
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction.
The word "twenty" (*viṃśati*) has twenty synonyms.

For the Brahmas, the period for the exhaustion of the commenced karma of Indra is exactly twenty [brahmas], being delimited by that. For the Arkas and others, the period for the exhaustion of the karma of the Arkas and others is ten [brahmas], being delimited by that.
Of the single Brahman alone, who is the measure of all;
henceforth, even after the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma, one shall go to Nārāyaṇa together with Brahman.
Thus [ends the commentary] on the *Anuvyākhyāna*, the well-composed work of the venerable Pūrṇapramati Bhagavatpāda, by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha.
This first quarter of the fourth chapter, consisting of the commentary that explains the meaning of difficult words and sentences, is hereby concluded.

Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā. The commentary (bhāṣya) intended to demonstrate the subject matter expounded in the second quarter states: "In this quarter, the liberation and the departure [of the soul] of the gods are discussed."

In this regard, if the phrase "of the gods" is connected with both liberation and departure [from the body], then it follows that others besides the gods remain only while still possessing their bodies;
or else, one must consider the manner in which they abandon those bodies elsewhere; or, if it is not so considered, the reason for its omission must be stated.
And if it were connected only with liberation, then it would be stated that for the gods there is liberation and for others there is departure (*utkrānti*).
Furthermore, by virtue of the context, "liberation" is understood to mean [liberation] from the body.
Thus, just as it was stated generally that the fruit called the destruction of karma is taught in this [first] pāda, so too it must be said here that departure (*utkrānti*) is taught in this pāda.
Thinking that "by this division, would it not be as if nothing were done?", he says: "And of the gods."
For gods and humans, this much indeed is equal;
however, the paths of departure for gods will generally not occur [in the same way].
That which was considered in the previous quarter— the result known as the destruction of karma— is equal for both gods and humans,
because in the absence of the destruction of karma, the persistence of its results is necessary.
The word "humans" (manuṣya) indicates those other than the gods.
Therefore, what was to be established by the preceding section has been stated in general terms.

Since the departure from the body—which is the subject of this section—and the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), which is to be established in the third section, will for the most part not pertain to the gods, it is appropriate that they are stated separately.
By this [it is shown that] "in this section, both the path and the goal are described."
This indicates that even this commentary should be explained as meaning that the path for all those other than the gods is accessible;
and he will state this clearly:
"The path of departure is that which is to be traversed by the liberated. (12.104)

Let this be established; however, what is the connection (*saṅgati*) for establishing this [specific] chapter? Therefore, by way of a digression, he states the connection for all four chapters as well: "Karma... and so forth.
The exhaustion of karma, the true departure [of the soul], the path, and experience—
these four are declared as the fruit, liberation, taught in sequence within the chapters.
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
By the word "departure" (*utkrānti*), the destruction of the final body—which is common to both deities and others—is indicated;
and by the word "path" (*mārga*), the attainment of Brahman is indicated.
The word *iti* should be joined after the word *bhoga*.
In some readings, the words *proktam* and *uditam* appear; in those cases, the word *iti* remains in its respective place.
In the first case, by way of restating liberation (*mokṣa*), the fact that [the goal] consists of fourfold fruits is what is to be enjoined.
In the second alternative, however, it is the reverse;
the word "in order" (*kramāt*) should be repeated here.
Consequently, this is the meaning:
Indeed, the fruit is what must be defined in this chapter;
and the fruit is liberation (mokṣa),
which consists of four aspects beginning with the destruction of karma.
The ultimate cessation of what is undesirable and the attainment of what is desirable are included within this very [process].
Furthermore, the destruction of karma and the subsequent stages occur in sequence:

immediately upon the arising of knowledge comes the destruction of karma; for one whose karma is destroyed, there is the departure (utkrānti); for one who has departed and traveled by the path appropriate to himself, there is the attainment of Brahman; and from that, experience.

Therefore, since these have been taught in sequence within these sections, the connection (*saṅgati*) is characterized both by inclusion (*antarbhāva-lakṣaṇā*) and by immediate succession (*ānantarya-lakṣaṇā*).
It was stated that there is no path for the gods; does this mean they become liberated right where they reside? To this, he says: "only among the creators" (*sraṣṭṛṣveva*).
But at the dissolution of Brahmā, the entry of those to be created back into the creators is declared to be the path of the gods... // MAnu 4.23a-c //
The word "and" (*ca*) implies that this occurs even in the case of those who are not creators;
thus it is stated in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*:
"When the dissolution of Brahman is imminent, their approaching Him for the purpose of entering [Him] is precisely what is meant by 'going on the path'."
To the question, "In that case, what is the scope of the statement that there is no path for the gods? he says: "No."
... nor the path beginning with light ... // MAnu 4.2.3d //
It has been stated that there is no departure from the body for the gods. Why is that? Because it would follow that they must remain possessed of a body; therefore, he says: "And not... [na ca].
... nor is there any departure.
The phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) should be supplied [to complete the sentence].
By the word "and" (*ca*), he includes the persistence of those who possess bodies.
He explains this very point with the words: "by the Creator" (*sraṣṭrā*).
The body of the Creator, who has become food, shall dissolve therein;
therefore, there can be no departure of the breath from the divine being who is the object of creation.
The body is indeed presided over by consciousness;
therefore, it proceeds from the Creator.
The departure is the body.
The meaning is that even before the emergence of volition (*cetanā*), the body of those things to be created dissolves into the creators;
the reason for this dissolution into the creators is that the creator has become their devourer (*grāsa*).
This is to be connected with the phrase "the body, however" (*dehastu*). (12.111)

It has been stated that there is no path beginning with light for the gods; why is that? With the intention that this is established from the very same reason for which another path was previously mentioned, he states another argument by way of restating that point: "And because of dissolution: 'And because of the dissolution of the worlds, including those beginning with light, how could there be a path for them when they have entered the Supreme by their own nature? (Manu 4.2.5)
The meaning is "even before the release from the deity.
The two genitive cases in "of the worlds beginning with light" (*arcirādīnāṃ lokānām*) are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "for all [of them] too, it would be [the path] beginning with light."
The statement "let them enter from their own [bodies]" is a restatement of what was previously said.

Now, since it was stated "mostly," one might object that the paths of departure for the gods must occasionally be admitted; in that case, there would be a contradiction with the reasoning already stated. To this, he says: "of those who have been born."
For those born in the world of humans and among the gods, there are at times paths for the departure [of the soul]; liberation is not desired in such cases.
Even if it were so for you, liberation is not desired at that time; rather, it is [desired] only together with Brahman.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the aforementioned reasoning.
This is what is meant:

It was stated "generally" with reference only to the commonality of the path of departure (*utkrāntimārga*), and not to the two paths of departure occurring at the time of liberation; for those two are the exceptions to be excluded, as they pertain to the time of non-liberation.
"Since reasoning has liberation as its object, there is no contradiction.
Do only the gods attain liberation along with Brahmā?
We say: it is for others as well.

If that were so, there would be a contradiction with such statements as "He resorted to the base of the feet of the Lord whose banner bears the king of birds"; therefore, he says: "And of others as well."
The conclusion of the scripture is that even for others, liberation shall be attained directly upon reaching that Hari, together with Brahmā;
"direct liberation" is characterized by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
The phrase "even for those who have reached and remain [there]" is to be supplied.
Regarding the word *tam*, it refers to one situated in Vaikuṇṭha and so forth.

According to the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117), since the optative (*liṅ*) even when not expressing a benediction is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the form *bhūyāt* is grammatically correct.
"Thus, [it is] the blessing of the Lord.

since there would be the consequence of contradiction (bādhā) and so forth if any arbitrary movement were taken as the subject (pakṣa), the movement of liberated beings (muktānām gatiḥ) must be taken as the subject.
In establishing that state [of liberation] as being characterized by suffering, you would be contradicting your own tenets,
for you yourselves have accepted that those who are liberated are free from suffering.
Likewise, by asserting the pervasion that "whatever is a state of existence (gati) is characterized by suffering," you must also admit that even Īśvara possesses suffering.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case; from that too, it follows that there is indeed a departure from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

If one accepts that "residing in a body" (*śarīravṛttitva*) is a pervader of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*), then one must also accept that God (*Īśvara*) possesses a body, because He possesses motion (*gatimat*).
And since that would result in a contradiction with one's own tenets (apasiddhānta), he says: "By scripture" (āgama).
Since this consequence applies regardless of whether one follows the scriptures or not, the fault of deviating from a tenet does not exist... [MAnu 4.2.28a-c]

Since we have stated this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the inference of the nature of liberation based on following scriptures such as the Vedas— asking, "If you infer in this way independently of the Vedas and so forth, then why would you not likewise infer it in that other way too?"—
for that reason, the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) does not occur.
In order to inform one who raises the objection of an "unestablished tenet" (apasiddhānta) even regarding a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), he says: "Regarding the reductio... (prasaṅge).
...if that were the case in this context, then there would indeed be an over-extension of the principle... // MAnu 4.2.28cd //
That is the fallacy of abandoning one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
The word "would be a fault" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
To the question "How would there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?", he says: "No."
... there would be no occasion for attachment anywhere.
The word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied at the end here.
The sense is that, since in all possible cases it is somehow possible to raise the objection of an *apasiddhānta* (departure from a tenet), [the opponent's position fails].
By this, the argument that "if the constant upward motion of liberated souls is established, there is a contradiction; otherwise, there is a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*)" is also refuted.
Because one would be forced to admit the counter-position by relying on what is established for the opponent,
he anticipates another qualification, saying "in the world" (*loka*).
If being situated in the space of the world (*lokākāśa*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*)...
[here,] the connection with the space of the world itself is the limiting condition,
because it pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatvāt*).
The term "being a means" (*gatitva*) is a statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). He refutes this with the words, "by the means," etc. (*sādhaneti*).
"...is one who follows the means of accomplishment.
When it is asked, 'Is he also...? one should say: 'What is he...?'"
The argument that "the destination [of the soul] is connected with the space of the world" implies that this limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) follows upon and pervades the probans (*sādhana*).
If it is argued that this is not the case because the limiting adjunct is absent in the state of liberation (*muktagati*), we say no;
for even there, it is established as a destination by virtue of being a movement.
By this, it should be understood that the property of "residing in an embodied being" (*śarīrivṛttitva*) is also established as being pervaded by the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*).

This is what was stated [in the verse]: "When this has been said, one might ask 'What is that?'"—and now, demonstrating the proof for liberation as he himself intends, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
... therefore, it should be that which is declared in the Veda. (MDh 4.2.29d)
... liberation ... // MAnu 4.2.30a //

Because there is a lack of valid evidence for the nature of liberation as taught by the Jina, he refutes the liberation taught by the Buddha as well by extending the previously mentioned faults: "In this way," etc.
Thus, although Viṣṇu himself is the Lord and the knower of all things,
he composed the Buddhist doctrine solely for the purpose of deluding [those who would otherwise follow the path of the Vedas].
Because it is intended for the Asuras who are unfit and yet proceed along the path of the Vedas, that doctrine should never be accepted anywhere, as it pertains to the domain of the Asuras.
Just as the Jaina doctrine is not to be accepted because it lacks authoritative validity (*prāmāṇikatva*), so too that Buddhist doctrine is not to be accepted in certain respects.

To the objection—"But why should this [Buddhist doctrine] not be accepted, since it was composed by Viṣṇu in the form of the Buddha, who is the supreme authority (*paramāpta*)?"—it is said: "by himself" (*svayam*).
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: although Viṣṇu himself composed the Buddhist doctrine (*saugata-mata*), it is nevertheless not to be accepted.
By the term "Lord" (*īśa*), he acknowledges proficiency in the instruments [of action];
by "knower of all" (*aśeṣavit*), he acknowledges knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*).
By the word "hi" (for), he states the reason for accepting [this view]: namely, that it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question, "In that case, why is it not to be accepted?", he says: "It is only for the sake of delusion."
Since he performed that [act] solely for the delusion of the asuras,
it is not to be accepted because it pertains to the domain of the asuras.
"Domain" (adhikāra) means that in which they are authorized (adhikriyante).

The term *asurādhikāra* means the domain (*adhikāra*) of the *asuras*; its state is its essence (*tattva*), and [the delusion arises] from that. As for why the *asuras* are subject to delusion, it is said: "of those who are unfit" (*ayogyānām*).
The phrase "the path of the Veda" is connected both with what precedes and with what follows.
This is what is meant:
although the Blessed Buddha is established by scripture and other means as possessing keen faculties and possessing knowledge of reality;
And one who intends to compose a treatise is not thereby [automatically] authoritative,
because of the possibility of being deceptive.
As it has been said: "Then, when the Kali age has set in, for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods, a son of the Jina named Buddha will appear among the Kīkaṭas.
Therefore, the nature of liberation described by him is indeed to be rejected.
Having thus refuted the Buddhist doctrine in general, he states its specific divisions in order to refute them individually, beginning with the word "four."
And that has been declared to be of four kinds... // MAnu 4.2.32a //
The meaning is that this is due to the difference in the intellects of the commentators.
To the question "How so?", he says: "It is empty."
... consciousness alone is empty;
likewise, the external reality that is to be inferred is [empty], as is that which is perceived externally. MAnu 4.2.32b–d.
Thus ... // Manu 4.2.33a //
One view holds that the reality is solely the solitary, non-dual void (*śūnya*). Another view holds that the reality is consciousness alone (*vijñāna*).
That in which external reality is inferable and not distinct from cognition is described as such.
The meaning is that there is indeed a reality distinct from cognition, but it is inferable; this is the Sautrāntika view, which is different [from the others].
The word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
That which is directly perceived as being external is the Vaibhāṣika view; thus, including these, there are four types.
Among these, the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādins*) are the most ignorant,
because they deny all objects that have been cognized;
superior to them are the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādins*).
Because they accept mere consciousness even while denying form and other [objects],
and because they accept external objects— therefore, the Sautrāntikas are more difficult [to refute] than the Vaibhāṣikas, since they accept that such objects are inferable.
Then the Vaibhāṣikas [respond]:
"Having accepted external objects and having accepted that they are respectively cognizable through perception and other means, this enumeration was made in this sequence in order to make this known.
In that context, he restates the liberation taught by the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
But those who, deluded by ignorance, speak of emptiness therein—
they would describe liberation in such a way, like those who are devoid of shame.

Among those four, those who assert that emptiness alone is the reality would describe liberation exactly as it is; they would speak of it in precisely such a manner. However, there is this distinction:

Out of the conceit that "the Veda of the Māyins is the authority," they harbor doubts regarding such Vedic passages as "he attains supreme equality" and "he enjoys all desires"; having thus provided alternative interpretations, they propound a liberation according to their own preference.
This indicates the quality of darkness (tamas).
Because ignorance is the cause;
for it is said: "Negligence and delusion arise from darkness, as does ignorance itself."
Deluded by that [ignorance], he explains what was stated in general terms more clearly: "not anything at all."
In the state of liberation, there is nothing whatsoever that belongs to a self or to what pertains to a self.
This is an elaboration of the phrase "something":
"either the self or what belongs to the self. Here, "self" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It should be understood that "belonging to a self" refers to these two;
neither of them exists in liberation.
Furthermore, the doctrine of emptiness is also twofold.

There are the doctrine of a single self and the doctrine of multiple selves. Of these, the first alone is the primary tenet; however, the second was introduced for the sake of leading those of dull intellect to enter the path.
Having stated that which is common to both, and desiring to state the distinction, he first states the former: "In one... and so forth.
When one [person] is liberated from saṃsāra, nothing remains.
Some things are conscious and some are unconscious. To the question, "How is this so when there is liberation for only one? he says: "That..."
This distinction between the sentient and the insentient exists only through conventional reality;
upon the destruction of conventional reality, there is nothing but the undifferentiated emptiness.

This collection of objects (*padārthasamūha*), which appears as the manifold of the sentient and the insentient, is seen as a "division" (*bheda*)— meaning it is differentiated— only of that single Self (*ātman*) through conventional ignorance (*saṃvṛti-ajñāna*).
It does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nor is it constructed by multiple ignorances.
Therefore, when the destruction of that very single self’s conventional reality occurs, it is entirely logical that emptiness alone is distinguished as the ultimate truth;
"without distinction" is a description of the essential nature of emptiness.
He will state that liberation is simply the destruction of conventional reality (saṃvṛti). He explains its lack of distinction as follows: "not existence" (na sattvam).
Neither existence nor non-existence is found in the reality of emptiness;
there is neither happiness nor suffering, nor is there any distinction whatsoever.
Existence (*sattva*) has the nature of the highest generality (*parasāmānya*) and so forth;
non-existence (*asattva*) is the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of absence.
What more need be said? Not even the slightest particularity (*viśeṣa*) exists.
Now, it might be argued that liberation (mokṣa) cannot be non-existent, because [otherwise] one would always remain subject to saṃsāra;
therefore, since liberation exists, emptiness (śūnya) must possess some distinction. To this he says: "without distinction" (nirviśeṣam).
It is without distinction, self-luminous, untainted, ageless, and immortal;
it is the void reality, unobstructed, and devoid of various conventional coverings.
That which is free from all defects and beyond the reach of mind and speech is called "liberation" by the wise.
Emptiness itself, when not perceived by the ignorant, is called liberation;
there is no liberation apart from emptiness.
Therefore, it does not possess any distinct attributes.
If that were so, since liberation would exist at all times, the cultivation of emptiness and so forth would be useless; therefore, it is said to be "without distinction" and so on.
This is an elaboration of the term "self-luminous," namely, that it is "beyond the reach of mind and speech.
It is "untainted," meaning free from merit and demerit, and "ageless"; being thus ageless, it is also immortal—ageless and immortal.
"Constriction" (*sambādha*) means being crushed by other things;
"unconstricted" (*asambādha*) means being without a second.
"Faults" (*doṣa*) refers to desire and the like.
Liberation is not merely emptiness; rather, it is characterized by being free from various conventionalities (*saṃvṛti*) and so forth.
Furthermore, meditation and other practices are employed for the sake of perfecting these characteristics. *12,165*
From what [source] does it follow that liberation is nothing but emptiness characterized by the cessation of ignorance and so forth? To this, he says: "Not manifold... (nāna).
... corrupted by various conventional notions.
...is to be understood as existing in the state of transmigratory existence.

The state of saṃsāra should be understood as emptiness itself, corrupted by various conventional designations; therefore, it is logical that liberation is emptiness itself, which is the opposite of that [state].
This is what is meant:
the reality of emptiness is, by its own nature, undifferentiated and one alone.

Of that which is supremely subtle, transcending speech and mind, and self-luminous, there arises a slight coarseness due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which possesses the powers of agency and enjoyership through the fundamental ignorance (mūla-saṃvṛti) endowed with various powers such as obscuration (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa).
From that, by virtue of having a second [entity], it attains a state of being qualified (saviśeṣatā) and thus becomes coarse.
Then, once it enters the domain of mind and speech, it becomes subject to defilement (salepatva) by virtue of falling within the scope of injunctions and prohibitions.
Furthermore, there is the association with defects such as passion (*rāga*).
From that, in connection with the body, the senses, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and objects, a state of greater grossness arises.

Then, for one who possesses the sense of "mine" (*mamakāra*), there occurs a state of extreme grossness characterized by suffering and so forth. Thus, from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), because it is the effect of those [defects], emptiness itself—conjoined with the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) and other factors termed "conventional"—is *saṃsāra*.

When the fundamental conventional reality (*mūlasaṃvṛti*) has been destroyed through the excellence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, and the stream of its effects has dissolved, that which is characterized by it— emptiness alone— is liberation.
Anticipating the objection that "if emptiness alone is both liberation and saṃsāra,
then the words 'liberation' and 'saṃsāra' would become synonyms," and so forth, he says "only conventionally" (*saṃvṛtyaiva*), intending to show that this very point resolves that challenge as well.
...it is distinguished by convention alone;
likewise, both cyclic existence and liberation are characterized by what is established and what is destroyed. (Manu 4.2.39b–d)
Although both saṃsāra and liberation are indeed emptiness,
nevertheless, they are nonetheless distinguished as "saṃsāra" and "liberation.
How so?
The meaning is that,

although there is a difference in referents due to a difference in their defining characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no synonymy (*śabdaparyāyatva*) and so forth between them, whether [the term] is used in its established sense or in its negated sense.
Having thus presented the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmavāda*), he shows the doctrine of multiple selves (*anekātmavāda*) with the words "some" (*kecit*).
Some among them have declared otherwise... // MAnu 4.2.40a //
Regarding those proponents of emptiness:
how is it that [their view] is different from the doctrine of those who maintain a single self? To this he says: "By conventional reality alone. (12.168)
...but conventionally, it is manifold; the great void is divided and designated by various terms such as "person" (pudgala). MAnu 4.2.40b-d.

By the word "tu" (but), he excludes the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmavāda*), the doctrine of multiple selves as inherent (*svābhāvikānekātmavāda*), and the doctrine of multiple selves produced by adventitious conditions (*upādhikṛtānekātmavāda*).
Through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), which is manifold, [the self] is indeed delimited by convention, but not by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).

Since conventional reality and the delimitations produced by it are false (*mithyātva*), it follows that what is designated by the term "multiple persons" (*nānāpudgala*) is so stated; this is the remainder of the sense.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of whom... (yasya).
He for whom the state of being of a single flavor with emptiness departs through knowledge—
he, liberated from the nature of a person (pudgala), shall attain great emptiness.
But conventionally, another [being], being delimited, experiences various sufferings to their full extent.
Thus... MĀnuv 4.2.42a-c.

In that regard, among the many selves, when a particular self— through the knowledge that the self has the single flavor of emptiness and the knowledge of the non-duality of emptiness— becomes free from that conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), the fundamental conventional reality is turned back and other [conventionalities] perish. That person, being liberated from the form of agency and so forth, will, as it were, attain great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatva*).
"But that self which is delimited by conventional reality experiences sufferings as the state of a person (*pudgala*), [yet] through the intellect of ultimate reality alone.
Such is the connection of the words "they say.
Thus do the proponents of the doctrine of a single living soul (*ekajīvatva*) speak, being like magicians. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 4.2.42)
And those held in high esteem by many living beings... // MAnu 4.2.43a //

With the intention that by refuting the liberation favored by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), that favored by the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādin*) will also be refuted, he establishes the similarity of their tenets with the statement "as the proponents of illusion," explaining it as follows: "In this way" means that both the proponents of a single soul (*ekajīvatvavādin*) and those who hold the view of many souls (*bahujīvamatā*)—these two types of proponents of illusion—describe the nature of liberation in exactly the same way as the two types of proponents of emptiness. They are called "proponents of a single soul" because they assert the state (*tattva*) of that which exists in a world where there is but one soul.
That which contains many living beings (*jīva*) is called "many-beings" (*bahujīva*); those who hold that view are the "proponents of many beings" (*bahujīvamatāḥ*).
Now, do not the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādinaḥ*) declare that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is bound by conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), and its cessation is liberation (*mokṣa*)?
Whereas the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādinaḥ*) maintain that this cyclic existence has illusion (*māyā*) as its cause, and its cessation is liberation.
Therefore, to address the objection that there would be inequality, he says: "It is Māyā."
... but for them, conventional reality is illusion.
The conventional reality (saṃvṛti) accepted by the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) is itself the "illusion" (māyā) of those proponents of illusion (māyāvādins).
The sense is that this is because their effects—such as obscuration (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa)—are identical in being characterized by beginninglessness and ineffability.
The proponents of emptiness declare emptiness to be the ultimate reality (tattva), whereas the proponents of illusion declare Brahman to be so.
Therefore, because there is indeed a disparity [between the two], he says: "Because of the absence of distinction."
By the very statement that there is no distinction, we hold that Brahman alone is empty; there is no duality.
There is no difference between these two [concepts]— namely, "Brahman" and "emptiness"—
because they are both stated by words alone to be without distinction.
Indeed, it is dissimilarity that serves as the differentiator of things.
And that this is not the case here is agreed upon by both parties;
therefore, there is merely a difference in words, not a difference in reality.
Now, [the opponent] thinks:

"By the very Vedic texts stating 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite' and 'Brahman is indeed consciousness and bliss,' Brahman—characterized by truth and so forth—is distinguished from everything else; how then can it be said that Brahman is void?
This is true.

With the intention that Brahman is distinguished from everything else by the characteristics of "Being" (sat) and so forth according to the Śruti, but that this is not tenable in the Māyāvāda system, he says: "Being" (sat).
And how could there be truth, consciousness, bliss, and so forth, for one who asserts that [Brahman] is undivided? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.44ab)
And what is "existence" and so forth? The meaning is that it is nothing at all.
To explain: is existence and so forth the very nature of Brahman, or is it something else?
In the first case, there is no relationship between the characterized and the characteristic;
furthermore, multiple terms would be redundant.
Nor is it the second case.

If it is argued: "Since [the definition] is not inconsistent with our own position—just as for you, attributes such as truthfulness, though being the very nature of Brahman, are also its definition, why should this not be the case for me as well?"—we reply:
No, because we accept that [definition] is established through a specific power (*viśeṣaśakti*).
But how could this be maintained by another?
If it is argued that I too accept a distinction [between the two], we say no, because of the principle of non-fragmented speech (*akhaṇḍavāditva*). *12,172*

Although there is no difference in the reality denoted by words such as "Being" (*satya*) and so forth, nevertheless, there certainly exist the things to be excluded, such as non-existence (*asat*) and the like; therefore, since we accept that multiple words denoting those [attributes] apply to Brahman for the purpose of excluding them, how is it that the meaning of the scripture cannot be established in our view? To this, he says: "vyāvartya... (by the exclusion...).
However, for the proponent of emptiness, there exists a distinction consisting merely of what is excluded.
The phrase "only the distinction between that which is excluded" indicates by mentioning a single part the entirety of what has been stated.
This entire method exists even in the view of the Śūnyavādin; therefore, even by this [method], it is impossible to state a difference between Brahman and the Void (śūnya).
As for the statement "it exists even for the Śūnyavādin," what is the point of such an objection?
He says "no," [explaining] that it is because of falsehood and so forth.
For he himself indeed considers the exclusion of falsehood and the other [vices].
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "as the referents of terms such as 'truth' and as qualifiers of emptiness.
The proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādī) holds this view.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates that it is well known that these are Buddhists who maintain that the referent of a term is an exclusion (apoha).
“And it is well known that [Brahman] is that which is opposed to the prior defects of dullness, concealment, suffering, and so forth.
Let alone the demonstration of the distinction between Brahman and the Void, for they are both devoid of distinctions.
The very proposition that "there is a distinction" does not even sustain its own limbs, because it is self-contradictory; with this intention, he says: "Because there is no distinction."
Because they are without distinction, there is no difference whatsoever between Brahman and emptiness.
The ellipsis implies that it simply cannot be admitted.

[Objection: But surely the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin), having accepted the authority of the Veda, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), and its eternity, has provided this interpretation of the Vedic statements;
however, the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) does not even accept the authority of the Veda.
How then can it be said that "only [the object] is to be excluded"?
To this, he says: "Because of its being a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya), etc."
Moreover, the authority and other qualities of the Veda are indeed equal in their results.
The difference lies merely in the words;
however, the meaning is exactly the same for both.
Therefore, it is rightly stated that the accomplishment of the sentence-meaning is also identical.
The point is that the Māyāvādins' prioritization of Vedic statements is merely a pretense, whereas their object of knowledge (*prameya*) is indeed the same.
To the question of how they are the same in result, he says: "because it does not reveal reality" (*atattvāvedaka*).
For that reason, it is said that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which does not reveal reality.
The word "veda" (is known) continues [from the previous context],
or it means "all that is authoritative.
By that [statement], the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin) [is addressed].

It is stated [in the passage] beginning with "the means of valid cognition, such as perception, and the scriptures have for their object those possessed of ignorance," the word "and so forth" being the ellipsis.
To the question, "Even if it is admitted that they do not reveal reality (*atattvāvedakatva*), why are they equal? he says: "*Atattvāvedakatvam*...
"*Atattvāvedakatvam* is that lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) which is accepted by the wise. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.46ef)
For this reason, even though investigators who compose various kinds of definitions for the wise strive precisely to exclude that which does not reveal reality,
one who asserts that "experience is the means of valid cognition" has likewise made no such effort, being content merely with the conceit that there is nothing which fails to reveal reality.
Nor, however, is it with the intention of asserting validity for that which does not reveal reality.
Therefore, what is accepted by the Māyāvādin as the validity of the Veda is in fact invalidity itself;
and since there is an absence of validity, its inherent nature (*svatastva*) is cast far away.
Furthermore, the demonstration of its eternity would be entirely futile.
[Objection: Even if it does not reveal reality (*atattvāvedaka*), there is a distinction: that whose object is sublated even prior to the knowledge of Brahman is invalid (*apramāṇa*);
whereas that whose object is sublated only by the knowledge of Brahman is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that does not reveal reality.
However, the scope of the Veda is sublated only by the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, with the intention that its authority remains intact, he raises the following objection: "Dīrgha... etc.
"If it were to produce long-lasting delusion, it would be a means of knowledge that does not reveal reality.

(MAnu 4.2.47ab) The meaning is: if it is held that whatever produces long-lasting delusion is a means of knowledge that does not reveal reality—why is this stated merely by following worldly convention?
Or is it by mere conventional designation?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "In the case of a rope... and so forth.
The scripture would lack authority even more than the cognition of a snake in a rope and the like,
because it produces a great delusion that cannot be dispelled.
Of the *āgama*, that is, the Veda. Why? Because it bestows a great delusion that cannot be overturned even in a short period of time.

The meaning is that it was stated [in the previous verse] that [the latter is] superior because of the intention to indicate a greater degree of harm caused by that [falsehood], even though there is no difference regarding its lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Regarding the second [alternative], he states the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words "tala... etc.
The cognition of a palm tree, a blue color, and so forth would attain the status of valid knowledge regarding space.
The surface is sapphire; its blueness, like that of the sapphire, is "surface-blueness.
The author of the commentary himself explains the meaning of the first term: "Like an umbrella," and so forth.
The cognition of the form of an umbrella and the notion of the moon being the size of a thumb-tip [are examples of erroneous perception].
The term "space" (ākāśa) is understood to carry over. The phrase "should attain the status of a means of valid cognition" (mānatāṃ vrajet) is connected to everything [in the preceding context].

Since one who establishes the convention of validity for [the Vedas]—on the grounds that they are causes of error that cannot be overturned even in a short time—must also establish the convention of validity for these [other means], as there is no distinction between them.

If it is argued that this convention is established on the basis of having as its object that which is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), and not on the basis of being the cause of an error that persists for only a short time, [we reply:
no, because even by stating that it has as its object that which is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, this very same meaning is intended by the proponent of Māyā (*māyāvādin*).
Otherwise, it would not be said: "Indeed, those who understand from the words 'nāga' or 'naga' an elephant or a mountain do not become deluded."
Thus, how could one demonstrate the knowledge of phonemes, their length, and so forth?
Furthermore, since even the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) accepts the authority of the Veda in such a manner, from where does this distinction arise?
It is not said that the entire Veda fails to reveal reality for the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin).
What indeed is the point regarding the scope of injunctions and prohibitions?

It is certainly accepted that the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which teach the non-dual reality, and the intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) such as "That which is invisible, ungraspable... the Truth," which teach the referent of the term *tat* (*tatpadārtha*) as being without distinction and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), possess the capacity to reveal the ultimate reality (*tattvāvedakatva*).
But this is not the case for the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin);
therefore, how can there be equality? To this, [the author replies]: even the proponent of emptiness accepts exactly this [point].
For the quality of revealing reality (tattvāvedakatva) is nothing other than the absence of non-correspondence with the object.

Intending to show that even the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) indeed accepts the non-contradiction of the meaning of the two statements, [the author] first demonstrates the acceptance of the meaning of the great statement: "But as for the state of being without differentiation..."
Furthermore, he has always admitted that emptiness is characterized by indivisibility.
By using the word "always" (*sadā*), that proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) himself indicates [this] and not by our own imposition.

Showing that the acceptance of the meaning of the intermediate sentence is likewise common to both, he says "existence" (*sattva*) etc., [demonstrating] that their lack of distinction is agreed upon by both parties.
The non-existence of phenomena such as existence and non-existence is the view of both [schools].
The word "of this reality" (tattvasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
It is accepted by both— the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins) and the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins)—
as being real (satyatvam).

With the intention that this is accepted by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), he asks: "How can there be the existence of that which is called 'emptiness' [and is itself non-existent]? To this, he replies: "No," and so forth.
For emptiness is not intended by him to be the state of having an existent counter-correlative.
Non-existence (asattva) consists in having a real counter-correlative or being opposed to the real;
and even by that proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin),
it is said that "emptiness" is spoken of with the intention of signifying the absence of specific distinctions (nirviśeṣatva), not with the intention of signifying non-existence.
The meaning is that this is because [the opponent] accepts it as the reality (*tattva*).

To show that even the state of bliss (*ānandatā*) is admitted by the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), he first restates the bliss accepted by the proponent of Māyā (*māyāvādin*) with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
For bliss is not held to be anything other than the cessation of suffering.
... by a deceitful person. // MAnu 4.2.51a //
The meaning is that blissfulness (*ānandatva*) is simply the state of being opposed to suffering (*duḥkha*), and not some kind of positive attribute (*dharma*).
By the word "for" (*hi*), he indicates its well-known status as being opposed to the unreal (*anṛta*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*), and so forth.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Śūnya... [and so on].
... even in the case of the position of emptiness (*śūnyapakṣa*) ... // MAnuv_4.2.51a //*12,181* The word "is the same as that" (*tatsamānam*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
[It refers to] that which "opposes dullness, conventional reality, the end of suffering, and prior faults."
This is because of such statements as those.
He shows the acceptance of its being knowledge by saying: "knowledge."
... and knowledge is the opposite of dullness.
Furthermore, the Māyāvādin asserts that knowledge is by its very nature opposed to insentience (*jāḍya*);
the meaning is that this is the same for the proponent of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) as well.
This might be so.
The proponent of illusion (māyāvādin) accepts that Brahman is devoid of distinctions and so forth, whereas the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) accepts this of the empty (śūnya).

How, then, can there be equality between them? To this he says: "Not so; for it has been stated that there is no difference between Brahman and the empty. This is expressed by the words "dharmā" (phenomena).
Since no phenomena exist at all, what distinction can there be between those two?
Consequently, since there is no distinguishing factor, what difference could there be between those two—Brahman and the Void—and what would constitute their distinction?

Now, one might object: "The non-dual reality described in this manner is indeed the established doctrine (siddhānta) of the author of the Sūtras; so why is it restated here for the sake of refutation? To this, he says: "Of such as these... [etādṛśānām].
The Lord has already refuted such positions by the very fact that they destroy one's own position...
[of those positions] which are like the "void-position" (śūnyapakṣa).
How?
By means of establishing one's own position which is the opposite of that [position], it follows by implication.
This is what is meant:
Non-duality (*advaita*) is not the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the author of the Sūtras, because it has been refuted by him; for,
through such statements as "because of the separate instruction" (*pṛthagupadeśāt*), he has established a meaning contrary to that [non-duality].

For it is not possible that one who does not perceive the faulty nature of a thing can establish something contrary to it. Not only is the refutation established by implication, but it is also established by the statement beginning with “There is no non-existence, because [it] is perceived”; thus he says: “nābhāvaḥ” (there is no non-existence).
...and because it has been stated that "it is not non-existence. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.52d)

Having thus restated liberation as it is conceived by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) along with its various subdivisions, and having first refuted it by means of a common defect, [the author] now refutes that specific view of the proponent of emptiness who stated that liberation is the destruction of the self, saying: "The self..."—namely, that "for that Protector (*tāyin*), liberation is like the extinction of a lamp. This is what he refutes.
In the absence of a self, what is the goal of man? ... MAnu 4.2.53a
The term "liberation" (mokṣa), which will be discussed later, is also connected here by way of the "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokana) maxim.
If the self were non-existent— that is, if it were subject to destruction— what would liberation be, and to whom would it belong as a human goal?
This is what is meant: Is liberation, characterized by the destruction of the self, a fruit for the self or for that which is not the self?
It cannot be the first.
Because of its non-existence;
for when the possessor of the fruit does not exist, the fruit cannot logically exist,
as is observed in the case of dharma and so forth.
Not the second [alternative],
because when the self is destroyed, the non-self also ceases to exist;
and even if it were to persist, it would follow that it could not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
[It is] non-self because there is no benefit [to it] from that [action].
Now, one might object: "But surely this [agency] belongs to the self alone;
since, like dharma and so forth, it lacks the nature of prosperity (abhyudaya), its being at a different time is also logical. To this, he says: "The self... [and so on].
"What is liberation? It means that it would not be a human goal. He states the reason for this:
"Because the desired [goal] has the self as its limit" (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.53b).
The limit of the succession of desired excellences is that from which everything is desired for the sake of the self (*ātman*),
whereas the self is desired for its own sake and not for the sake of anything else.
A person does not desire the destruction of wealth and other such things merely because they are desired.

What is intended for this self? Alternatively, if there is an absence of a self, what is liberation as a human goal—is it in the form of the attainment of something desired, or in the form of the cessation of something undesired?
It is not the first [option].
The reason for this is: "of that which is desired."
Since the self is the ultimate limit and the basis for everything desired other than the self itself—
for everything is desired for the sake of the self— if that self did not exist, then for whom would this human goal (puruṣārtha) be? This is the meaning.
Not the second;
the reason for this is: "of that which is desired."
The cessation of the undesirable also constitutes a human goal only if it does not obstruct what is desirable;
or, even if it does obstruct that, it must be the subverter of a great undesirable,
as is observed in the world.
Indeed, no discerning person is ever observed to bring about the cessation of a minor benefit after having destroyed a great benefit.
And since the self is the most desirable of all things,
how could the cessation of undesirable states resulting from its destruction constitute a human goal?
If it is argued that those afflicted by disease and other ailments are seen to bring about their own destruction through such means as hanging, we say no;
for their activity is directed solely toward making themselves free from suffering by abandoning the body, which is the locus of disease and the like.
Indeed, the aspiration of everyone is: "May I be free from suffering."

If it is argued that they do not strive with the thought "may I not cease to exist," because those who lack the knowledge of the distinction between the body and the self strive only for the destruction of the self, we say no; for such people, being devoid of discernment, are not fit to be cited as examples here.
And this has been established:
that even animals possess the knowledge of the distinction between the body and the self.
Now, it must certainly be accepted that there is an absolute cessation of suffering.
And that [cessation] occurs only through the cessation of its cause, and not otherwise;
for the cause of suffering is the self itself,
both because of the acquisition of unrighteousness (adharma) and because of being its substratum.
If it is asked, "How then can the attainment of emptiness not be accepted through the destruction of the self?"—
it is not so;
for the self alone is not the cause of suffering.

However, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—namely, because [the self] exists during the waking state and is absent during sleep—even the body, senses, objects, and sensations [are shown to be distinct from it].

Therefore, when karma is exhausted through knowledge and experience, the body and so forth, being without seed, do not arise; since the non-arising of suffering is possible due to the deficiency of causal conditions (*sāmagrī-vaikalya*), what is the point of postulating the destruction of the self?
If you ask, "What is the criterion for this determination? [the answer follows].

We say this because everything exists for the sake of the self, and because the self is the most highly esteemed of all. For when a distant expenditure fails to accomplish the goal, wise people undertake a proximate expenditure.

Therefore, according to the maxim, "One should abandon the earth for the sake of the self," we consider it logical that one who desires to relinquish suffering should seek the liberation of only that which is limited by the self as its cause, and not of the self itself.
Indicating this, he states the refutation of the opposing view with the words, "If... (*yadīti*).
If liberation were not bounded by the self, then liberation would be the emptiness of a jar.
The meaning is: if liberation, which has the self as its limit, were not to occur in the desired manner;

that is to say, if there were no position according to which there is merely the cessation of the causes of suffering—such as the body and so forth—which are distinct from the self, while the self remains in its own essential nature;
[in other words], if even the self were to fall into emptiness (śūnyatā).
In that case, even the emptiness of the jar would constitute liberation for Devadatta;
and thus, the performance of the means [to liberation] would be useless,
because the emptiness of the jar does not depend upon causes such as renunciation and the like.

Now, one might object: "Why does this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) follow, given that there is no distinction? If this is asked, we say no; for you yourselves have stated the distinction between "the emptiness of the self" and "the emptiness of the pot. To this, he says: "Because it is conceptually constructed (kalpitatvāt)."
Because particularities are merely imagined... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.53e]

Indeed, in this context, the word "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) does not denote non-existence; for it has been stated: "That which [is characterized by] being the counter-correlate of an existent object, or which possesses the nature of an existent, does not exist in reality. Rather, (vi)
The self and the jar have perished,
and both are devoid of any means of valid cognition;
nor can specific qualities belonging to such things possibly be established through valid cognition.
For it is not possible for both a horse's horn and a rabbit's horn to possess the property of being a differentiator.
Therefore, one must accept that distinctions such as "the emptiness of the self" and "the emptiness of the pot" are merely conceptualized by speakers for the sake of conventional usage.
Thus, it is not the case that the lack of distinction is unestablished.
The similarity to the previous position was established for the purpose of extending the refutation [to the latter].
Therefore, he extends the refutation of the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins) to the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins) with the words: "Of the illusionists as well."
... for even that of a deceitful person is indeed equal to it.
The word "that" refers back to everything previously stated in the passage beginning with "the personal existence" (*ātmabhāva*).
One might object:
"The proponent of illusion (*māyāvādin*) does not assert the destruction of the self."
By this, liberation would not be a non-human goal due to the destruction of what is desired,
nor would it result in the fall into emptiness;
for if that were so, even the emptiness of a jar would be liberation.
Is it not the case that the manifestation of the state of Brahman occurs through the departure from the state of being a living soul (*jīva*),
and since Brahman consists of supreme bliss, that state indeed constitutes the goal of human life?
Not so.
What is this so-called state of being a *jīva*, and what is the state of being *brahman*?

If it is asserted that being bound by ignorance (*avidyā*), desire (*kāma*), action (*karman*), and so forth constitutes the state of being a *jīva*, while being the enjoyer of supreme bliss constitutes the state of being *brahman*, then we shall proceed with your permission.
But this is not the path for another [the opponent],

because they maintain that the form established by the witness— which is endowed with the powers of agency and enjoyership, possesses attributes, is distinct from the body and so forth, and is apprehended as "I"— is precisely what is to be eliminated by the supreme [Self].
And since it is this very form that is experienced as the supreme goal, how can the aforementioned fault not apply?
For even by the opponent, in order to establish its nature as bliss, it has been demonstrated that this very form is the object of supreme love;
indeed, no one in the world, conceiving of any formless nature distinct from this [blissful] form, hopes, "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist.
As for one who closes his eyes and says "so be it," who could possibly be his rival?
It is also incorrect to say that this aspiration exists within the form of the composite [of causes and conditions],
because that [composite] is in no way present to the mind,
and an aspiration must necessarily possess a formal object.
Because it is impossible for that [love] to exist in something formless;
and since unconditioned love toward one thing for another thing is not possible, this alone is most desirable.

If it is argued: "In that case, since even the state of being accompanied by the body and so forth is desired, then for you too, liberation would result in the loss of a human goal (apuruṣārtha) through their destruction," we say: No.
For in the world, even the destruction of a minor desire is seen to be a human goal when it serves as the cause for attaining a supreme object;
furthermore, it has been established that the state of Brahman does not differ from the state of emptiness,
and it has already been stated that its nature as bliss is a mere matter of words.
Furthermore, Ānanda, even bliss (*ānanda*) is not the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
For no one aspires, "May I become bliss"; rather, [one aspires], "May I experience that."
Furthermore, being an object of experience is not accepted by the opponent,
because there is no experiencer other [than the experience itself], and because one does not admit the status of both object and agent within the same thing. *12,191*
Furthermore, bliss (*ānanda*) is already established [by its very nature], and thus it is not something to be sought after by the person.

If it is argued that it does not shine forth because it was previously veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), but shines forth later when the veil of ignorance has been removed—and therefore the objection does not apply—that is not so;
for even prior [to such removal], the self-luminosity of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is admitted.
Furthermore, it is impossible for bliss to exist in its mere essence without being manifest.
If it is argued that even when bliss is manifest, it does not appear clearly, we say no;
for it is devoid of distinctions.
Furthermore, clarity and lack of clarity are based on specific distinctions:
for that which manifests together with specific qualities is called "clear," whereas that which manifests together with common characteristics is called "unclear."
And what is the meaning of the statement "it shines forth upon the removal of the veil of ignorance"?
Does it mean that it is perceived, or that it perceives?
Neither of these is the case.
Because it is not admitted [that a lamp acts].
If it is asked, "What is the meaning of 'the lamp shines'? [the answer is:
"It exists possessing a luminous form"—this amounts to nothing more than that.

This very point is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed). Now, we maintain that liberation is emptiness devoid of all distinctions; even the conceptual cognition (*pratyaya*) of that [emptiness] is employed solely for the sake of conventional usage and does not establish any dharma whatsoever.
If it is argued that the emptiness of a jar (*ghaṭa-śūnyatā*) is indeed qualified because it is specified by the jar,
and therefore there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the definition], we say no.

For even the intended emptiness would likewise be seen as qualified by being specified as "emptiness of self" (*ātma-śūnyatā*), which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that liberation could not be attained.

Now, even though such a distinction in the emptiness of the self is thus observed, if someone were to claim it is without distinction due to some underlying intention, [the author] says in response: "While being observed."
If there were non-distinction even when a distinction is being perceived,
then the absence of a jar would be indistinguishable from its future state.
The phrase "of the state of emptiness" (*śūnyabhāvasya*) is to be understood as that which is intended to be liberation; the word *cet* has the sense of "if";
and the word *bhāva* functions as an agentive noun (*kartṛsādhana*).

"In that case, then, even the emptiness of the jar would be non-distinct from that very same intention [of the jar], and thus the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains as it was. He exposes the opponent's underlying intention with the words: "If it is posterior... (pāścātyaśced iti).

The meaning is: [the opponent argues that] the state of being empty of self is a subsequent [state] devoid of specific qualities; and here, "subsequentness" is relative to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). *12,196*
And thus, this is what is meant:

at the present time of investigation, by means of a distinction that is merely conceptualized for the sake of conventional usage, the state of being empty of self appears as if it were possessed of distinctions;
however, when no such investigation is performed, it is in its own nature entirely without distinction.
He reveals the intention of the proponent [of the thesis] with the words: "residing in the self."

In that case, the meaning is as follows: even the state of being empty of a jar is seen to possess specific qualities only when it is investigated; however, when not investigated and not yet attained, it is indeed devoid of specific qualities—this can be asserted by us as well. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the liberation conceived in the manner described by the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*) and the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādin*).
For instance:
first of all, perception is not a means of valid cognition here,
because this object is not within the domain of perception.
Nor is there scriptural authority [for this],
because the scripture of the Vedas and so forth is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge by the proponent of emptiness, and we do not accept his own scripture as authoritative.
However, we shall speak to the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin).

Therefore, one must state the following inference: "The emptiness of the self is the human goal because it serves as a means for the cessation of suffering, just like the emptiness of the body and so forth.
As it has been said:

"If the self is not the cause of suffering without them, then they too must be of that same nature; thus both are faultless, and from that, there is detachment from both. This [argument] is not a valid inference because it is countered by a valid opposing argument; thus he says: "There is no liberation. (12.198)

Liberation is not something subject to dispute, because it is bodiless, like the emptiness of a jar; what could one who relies solely on inference as his authority say when this is stated? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.55)

The thesis (*pratijñā*) is that the state of emptiness or the state of Brahman, when conceived as distinct [from the self], is not liberation. The reason (*hetu*) is "because it is bodiless" (*adeha*), meaning "due to being bodiless.
The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "just like the emptiness of a jar."

When it is said, "He who has inference as his sole means of knowledge," by the phrase "what would he say? [the author] indicates, through this method, the absence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and, consequently, the fact that his own inference possesses an uncontradicted object. Furthermore, the deceiver (*māyī*) should not state a refutation there based on scripture (*śruti*) regarding the subject matter of inference.
The meaning is that, in this regard, one would not at all cite scripture as a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) for liberation as conceived by oneself.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the previous... [pūrveti].
...by the very path previously described;
because that [Veda] is not an object of measurement, according to the Śruti... // Manu 4.2.56bc //
In the view of that proponent of illusionism (māyāvādin), the Veda lacks authority.
How so? [Because of the statement:
"And the authority of the Veda... and so forth.
[This is] by the very path previously described in such passages.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that not the entire Veda is non-revealing of reality, but rather only that which consists of injunctions and prohibitions?
As for the Vedāntas, being of a different nature, they are indeed revealers of reality. If this is argued, we say no.

Since scripture has no authority regarding this reality by the very path previously stated—beginning with "What is to be understood from scripture for one who is devoid of all dharmas?"—let us grant, for the sake of argument, that scripture is somehow a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even so, our inference is not sublated by it; thus he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
... nor does it maintain that there is no body. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 4.2.56d)
A certain sacred revelation (śruti) states... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.57a]
The word "in liberation" (muktau) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; likewise, it should also be understood as referring to those who propound liberation according to their own views. [As it is said:
"Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who exists without a body."
Since such scriptural passages exist, how can it be said that there is no scripture teaching bodilessness? To this he says: "Bodilessness... [etc.]
...the state of being bodiless, which resides in a non-material body.
That which is described as "bodilessness" (*adehatva*) in this scripture refers precisely to the absence of a material body (*prākṛta-śarīra*);
it does not mean bodilessness in every respect.
By the word "material," the insentient (*jaḍa*) is indicated.
And that absence [of duality] is to be understood in the manner taught in the fourth quarter [of the verse].
Thus, having raised the doubt regarding such scriptural passages as, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed," and so forth...
And it must be explained:
why is the scope of the scriptural teaching on bodilessness restricted? To this, he says: "Liberation."
For the Śruti declares that there is enjoyment in liberation, saying: "Eating, playing... and so forth.
"He wanders there, laughing, playing, and delighting with women, or with vehicles, or with kinsmen, or with non-kinsmen"—
this Śruti text declares the enjoyment of women and other such things in liberation (*mokṣa*).
Since this [enjoyment] is not possible for one who is bodiless, the meaning is that [the scriptural teaching] must be restricted [to a specific state].

He states another counter-argument against the opponent's inference: "Because it is free from suffering" (*nirduḥkhatvāt*), and "because that [state] is not recognized as liberation, just as [the state of a living being is not]" (*nirduḥkhatvān na tan mokṣaḥ pratipannaṃ yatheti*).
What kind of refutation of the inference could there be between two disputants who maintain the doctrine of emptiness? (MAnu 4.2.58)

If one were to infer that "that emptiness or Brahmanhood is not liberation because it is devoid of suffering, just like the emptiness of a jar that has been discarded," what would be the refutation? None at all.
By the word "empty" (*śūnya*), one who accepts that [state] is indicated.
And [the word] "empty" (*śūnya*)...
"Śūnya" and "māyin" form a *dvandva* compound; or alternatively, "śūnya" and "māyā" form a *dvandva* compound.
The suffix *ini*, according to the rule for words such as *vrīhi*, is applied in the sense that those two [qualities] exist in them.
And in that case, the rule regarding the final element of the compound is intended.
He states another counter-argument: "Suffering.
Because it is non-different from suffering, liberation too would undoubtedly be suffering. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.59ab)
"Liberation" (mokṣa) is said to be the void (śūnya) and Brahman;
for it is accepted as such by both disputants.
That liberation would be of the nature of suffering, because it is non-different from suffering.
The meaning is that [the Self] is like well-known suffering because it is devoid of the distinction (i.e., difference) that is the counter-correlative of suffering;
for if the void (*śūnya*) and Brahman were suffering, then the attainment of their state would not constitute the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). Thus it is established.
The word "api" (also/even) serves to include another counter-argument.
The term "asaṃśayam" (without doubt) expresses the certainty of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
To the question, "Why is there an absence of difference that would serve as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to suffering? he says: "Difference... [and so forth].
In the case of difference, there would be nothing but duality... // Mānava 4.2.59c //

The remainder [of the phrase] is "from suffering, [and] from emptiness and Brahman. Thus, the sense is that there would be a fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta). Furthermore, since the removal of suffering is possible even through the destruction of the body and so forth, without the destruction of the self, the inference is also subject to the fallacy of being established otherwise (anyathāsiddhi).
Even the emptiness of the body and so forth is not the human goal because it merely serves to destroy suffering;
rather, it is the cause for the self's state of being free from suffering. For no one aspires with the thought, "May suffering perish."
"Rather, [the goal] is that one should be free from suffering.
If it is argued: "If for you the state of emptiness or the state of Brahman is established, then there is a deviation from your own tenet (apasiddhānta);
if it is not, then there is a lack of a locus (āśrayāsiddhi)," we say no.

Even in the case of inference for others (*parānumāna*), since the emptiness of the self (*ātmaśūnyatā*) is not established [for the opponent], there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
However, this is the distinction:
that the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) is possible by means of what is merely established for the other party.
If it is argued that the scriptural mention of enjoyment must refer to liberation with attributes (saguṇa-mukti), we say no;
for this would contradict what was stated [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]: "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own true form."
If it is argued that liberation cannot exist because of the absence of suffering, then that is a contradiction;
for how is it not a contradiction to hold that the destruction of the supreme self is the goal of human endeavor?
Furthermore, if there were a difference between the existent and suffering, there would be a duality of existence.
If it is argued that suffering is false, we say no;

for reasons such as its contradiction with direct experience have already been stated. Furthermore, since the final inference does not apply to one who maintains the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), there is no room for further objection.
Having taken all this into account, he concludes: "and so forth."
...due to such immeasurable faults, the wise should reject the doctrine of emptiness along with the doctrine of illusion. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.2.59d–f)
The connection is with the word "simultaneously" (*sahaiva*).
He extends the aforementioned fault to the nature of liberation as conceived by the Vijñānavādin by saying "in this same way" (*evam*).
In this same way, the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*) is also... // MAnuv_4.2.60a //
The meaning is that the liberation intended by the Vijñānavādin is also to be abandoned, just like the liberation favored by the Śūnyavādins and Māyāvādins.

Now, one might object: "The Vijñānavādins assert that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the ultimate reality (*tattva*); they maintain that it is momentary and possesses self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), characterized by its own illumination of its own objects. Since these [attributes] do not belong to the two previous [schools], there is a disparity; how, then, can there be an extension [of the critique]? To this, he says: "Knowledge... (*jñāna...*).
...due to the distinction of being mere consciousness;
for if one were to set aside even its specific qualities such as transience, the doctrine of non-duality would directly incur the aforementioned fault. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.60b–f)

"Jñānamātra-viśeṣa" means that which is both mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) and a particularity (*viśeṣa*). The suffix *-tasi* is used here in the sense of the accusative case; therefore, it means "having abandoned even that particularity of that cognition, such as its transience (*bhaṅgurattva*) and so forth, the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*) should also be understood as the view of non-duality (*advaitatā*)."
That reality in which duality does not exist is non-duality (*advaita*); its state is non-duality (*advaitatā*).
The view concerning that is the "view of non-duality" (*advaitatā-mata*).
For that reason, even the aforementioned fault would be equal [in both cases]. (12.212)
This is what is meant:
let there be some distinction of the Vijñānavāda from the former [position];
nevertheless, it is not to be respected because it is irrelevant to the present subject.
However, the essential nature of liberation is the same as that under discussion;
for even the Vijñānavādins accept that liberation consists in the attainment of non-dual consciousness after abandoning the state of being a transmigrating soul (jīva).
Therefore, this extension of the principle (atideśa) is indeed appropriate.

Alternatively, by stating that even the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*)—having set aside the specific qualities of mere cognition as well as its specific qualities such as transience—is to be understood as the doctrine of non-duality itself, he intends this:
there is no distinction whatsoever between the doctrine of consciousness and the two preceding ones;
for the specific quality of "cognition" is to be discarded, being a mere word.
For the opponent does not admit that there is a property called "cognitiveness" (jñānatva);
rather, since it has been stated that fragility and so forth are merely imagined by him, that [alleged difference] is indeed to be rejected.
It is not, in reality, a cause for a difference of opinion.
As it has been said: "In that regard, there is a distinction in the continuum," and so forth.
Therefore, the extension [of the rule] is logical;
moreover, the manner of this extension is quite clear. *12,213*
He states another inference for the purpose of refuting that [position]: "Time," etc.
Time is not possessed of perfect knowledge because it is time, like that which has been previously established;
since this is blocked by such an inference, liberation does not possess that nature.
The meaning is that the time of liberation does not possess non-dual knowledge; "pratipannavat" means like the present time;
"rodhāt" means due to opposition.
The state of being one whose nature is such liberation is "tādṛṅmokṣarūpatā.
If it is argued that even the present time is characterized as "possessing perfect knowledge" (kevalajñānin) because anything other than knowledge is merely imagined, we say no;
for this would result in the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between liberation and saṃsāra.
However, as for the specific distinction that is accepted, its very absence is what is being proven by this [argument].
In the view that nothing exists apart from cognition, time itself does not exist at all.
Therefore, on what basis could inference proceed? To this, he says: "If... (*yadi*).
If it is asked, "Is time also not [an obstacle]?", he says: "When?"—this is the answer to the question.
What will he say? ... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.62a-c]
The Vijñānavādin says:
when the opponent asks, "Then at what time is it not [present]?", what answer will he give?
Since it is impossible to determine a non-existence that lacks a locus, even the statement "time does not exist" would become indefinable; this is the meaning.
Anticipating the objection that "I shall state later that time does not exist in the state of liberation," he says: "When... (yadā).

... when one speaks of that state, it shall become the subject (*pakṣatā*) [of the inference]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one would speak of it as being the locus characterized by the absence of time.
In that case, that state of liberation (*mokṣāvasthā*) would become the subject in the aforementioned inference.
By the word "pakṣa" (the subject), its constituent part, the locus (*dharmin*), is indicated.
The meaning is that the thesis to be maintained is that the state of liberation does not possess exclusive knowledge (*kevalajñāna*).
If this were so, then the reason "because of being time" (*kālatvāt*) would be unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); therefore, he says: "because of being a state" (*avasthātvāt*).
For the reason is precisely "because it is a state," and so forth. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.63ab)

When a particular state is made the subject (*pakṣa*), then the reason (*hetu*) is stated simply as "because it is a state" (*avasthātvāt*), and not "because it is time" (*kālatvāt*); therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Likewise, it should be said that the state of saṃsāra itself is used as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), so there is no fault regarding the example either.
If it is argued that abandoning the subject, reason, and example stated at the outset would constitute a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), [we reply: no.
Not so;
