by asserting that the non-existence of time has "state" (avasthā) as its locus (adhikaraṇa), you have not done anything beneficial for yourself,
because the contradiction with another inference remains unavoidable.
The true nature of reality is not established merely by the defeat of the opponent;

for it must not be the case that when a certain inference is refuted by two valid objections and the opponent is defeated by a superior argument, that [original] inference would thereby be shown to be a valid one. It is precisely for the purpose of demonstrating this that another inference is presented.
However, with the intention of actually refuting the non-existence of time itself, he says: "That too... (sāpi).
...and when asked, "When will that [liberation] be?", the time must be stated; thus, there can be no state of being "untimely.

By stating that the state of liberation (*mokṣāvasthā*) is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the absence of time, [the author implies that] when someone asks, "When will this state of liberation be?", the time—namely, the period following the ripening of cultivation (*bhāvanāparipāka*)—is indicated as the locus of that state.
It must be stated thus:
for there is no restrictive rule that one should never ask such a question.
Therefore, since time can never be avoided in every respect, the state of being "non-time" (akālatva) would not mean the absence of time.
And thus, by relying upon that [time], the first inference will also proceed.

Now, it might be argued that because time does not exist, the first inference suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). However, what was stated here—namely, "at what time?"—is incorrect.
For the locus of an absence is indeed the very locus of its counter-positive;
and time does not have time as its locus,
such that its absence could have time as its locus.

Therefore, the question "When? is itself untenable. If you ask, "What is the point of an answer?", then in that case, by negating time without specifying a particular time as the locus, a general negation would have been made.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "No."
By the general prohibition "not at the wrong time," the rule regarding the time for study is set aside... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.64a-c].

For if a general negation were made, such as "time does not exist," the very nature of time itself would be negated; and thus, it would contradict the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), which is defined as "that which goes toward" or "takes as its object" time— that is, valid cognition (*pramā*).
For he apprehends the existence of time by virtue of its being devoid of prior and posterior limits.
Thus, this contradiction with direct perception applies not only to the Vijñānavādin, but indeed to all three including the two preceding ones; so he says: "and it is equal."
...he should be told [this], so that there would be no untimeliness on his part. // MAnu 4.2.64cd //
They have been stated and answered.
But how can this contradiction with witnesses apply to the proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin) and the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin),
since those two do not accept the existence of time?

For just as in the world, when many people are looking at various illusory elephants, horses, and so forth, he alone for whom the illusion has departed by means of a specific cause does not see them, while others indeed continue to see them; likewise, he alone for whom ignorance—the cause of the perception of duality—has departed does not perceive it, whereas for others, the perception of the manifold world (prapañca) such as time and so on continues just as before. Since this is indeed accepted by those two [the Māyāvādin and the Śūnyavādin], he says: "One... (*eketi*).
But under the view that there is only one living soul, this cognition is corrupted due to the absence of time. 4.2.65a-c.

It is true that this is the view of those who maintain the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), as well as the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) and the proponents of illusion (*māyāvāda*). However, we have not asserted that these two [views] contradict the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Rather, in the position of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*)—where the liberation of one is the liberation of all, and when one is liberated nothing remains—this valid cognition in the form of the witness-consciousness becomes incensed because of the acceptance of the non-existence of time (*kāla*) at the moment of liberation.
It is indeed contradictory;
therefore, the statement regarding contradiction with witnesses directed against the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādin) and the proponents of illusion (māyāvādin) is irrelevant.
Furthermore, even if one accepts the non-existence of time, it is not the subject under discussion at present. To this, he says: "Time."
... by taking time as the basis, one would only establish duality.
This term "measure" (pramā) continues [to apply].
Having established [it], having produced it—
this is the intended meaning.
To the extent that those two proponents of the doctrine of the single self (ekajīvavāda) declare that liberation is the state of abiding within the speech of the non-dual, empty Brahman,
we reply:
because of the existence of time, non-duality is not logically tenable.

In that context, when one asserts that even the subsequent time does not exist, then what is called "contradiction with the witness" (*sākṣivirodha*) is stated; it is on the basis of this connection that the extended application (*atideśa*) is made, and not because of the consequence of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
He states another inference common to the three types of disputants: "The subject of dispute... (*vimata iti*).

Furthermore, the inference: "The subject under dispute, time, possesses manifoldness because it is time, like that which is already established," would exclude the oneness of the individual soul (jīva).
If it were stated that "time is characterized by conceptual proliferation," it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Therefore, it is said to be "under dispute" (*vimata*);
the meaning is "the time of liberation."
To clarify this, the term "time" (kāla) has been stated.
Since the non-existence of time has just been refuted, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of space and so forth, is perceived as existing in the present time.
To dispel the doubt as to why this, which has already been stated previously, is mentioned again, it is said: "and another inference.
Although the subject matter (*dharmin*) and so forth, as well as the purpose, are the same for both, nevertheless, the former proceeded by way of negating non-duality (*advaita*).
However, the distinction is that this [is taught] by way of the method of phenomenal elaboration (*prapañca*).
Regarding the liberated soul (*jīva*),
he refutes other non-dualist doctrines by means of the previously stated extended application (*atideśa*), beginning with the verse "Time" (*kāla*).
Indeed, the doctrines of Time, Sound, the Lord, and Monism have likewise been refuted. 4.2.67a-c.
Whatever is perceived as permeated by something else is superimposed upon that thing,
just as silver is superimposed upon this [shell] in the form of "this.
And everything appears as permeated by time.
Therefore, it is superimposed upon that very [reality];
that alone is the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Hence, for those who maintain the doctrine of the oneness of time, liberation consists in abiding in that alone.
In this very way, the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas), who maintain the oneness of the word (śabdaikatvavādinaḥ), have said:
"There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge is perceived as if permeated by speech."
The partial Śaivas, relying upon their own scriptures, assert the oneness of Īśvara. To the question of how [those arguments] are refuted, he says: "And of those... [teṣāṃ ca].
...and because of the equality of those two, namely, the position and the fault. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.67cd)
The position of these [schools], beginning with the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādin), is indeed the same as that of the others;
for the difference in terminology, such as "emptiness" and so forth, is irrelevant,
since all accept the destruction of the soul (jīva) whose essential nature has been realized.
Therefore, the defect that liberation would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) due to the non-destruction of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and so forth, applies equally [to our position].

As for inference, it is indeed flawed because it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge; likewise with scripture (*āgama*), though this is not explicitly stated here as it is self-evident. *12,223*
He defines liberation as it is conceived by the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas: "Knowledge."
Knowledge is held to be eternally continuous by means of its own inherent flow,
whereas it is [held to be otherwise] by the two other schools of Buddhism.
By the word "eva" (only/alone), he excludes connection with an object;
it is desired in liberation.
This is the meaning.
Knowledge alone is the self;
and that knowledge is, by its very nature, subject to decay,
and for that very reason, it is momentary.
However, its continuum is eternal.

Due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the arising of that [continuum] colored by objects is *saṃsāra*; when those impressions are destroyed through the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*), the arising of that which is purely pure, even without the affliction of objects, is *mokṣa*. Thus, both [systems] are the same in this regard.

The Sautrāntikas, however, state that the distinction is that there is "having form" (*sākāratva*) in saṃsāra and "being formless" (*nirākāratva*) in liberation. [The author] refutes this with the words: "In that case also... (*tatrāpi*).
...even there, the enemy is said to be inference. (Manu 4.2.68d)

The time under dispute does not possess a continuous stream of this [present] cognition devoid of objects, because it is time, like the present time; such is the meaning of the "opposing inference" (anumā ripuḥ) of the aforementioned type that has been stated.
He states another inference: "Liberation... and so forth.
"Liberation is not for one who possesses a stream of pure consciousness after death;
it is attained in this way"—this is the inference that constitutes the reply.
One whose continuum of consciousness is pure is connected to a continuum of consciousness that is devoid of objects,
because of having passed away— that is, because of being connected to time.
Saṃsāra has been refuted; following that, the critique of its position is presented:
this liberation is also devoid of any valid authority.
Since, as before, there is an absence of both perception and scripture, only inferences must be stated.
To this, he says: "The inferences."
All inferences have been refuted by means of counter-arguments through the very same method of refutation already stated... MAnu 4.2.70a-c.
With the very same refutation already stated, and by way of connecting it to the counter-argument,
he says "And the Śrutis," with the intention that [the opponent's position] is also subject to the fallacy of *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) due to its contradiction with the Veda.
...and the Vedic revelations follow our teaching. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.70d)
"Ucyate" means "it is said. Those which go toward our statement—that is, those which establish it—are "asmaduktigāḥ.
The meaning is that they establish the very nature of liberation as we intend it.
Furthermore, the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*) has already been established previously. *12,226*
He restates the liberation favored by the Sāṅkhyas and others with the words: "The Sāṅkhya... and so forth.
The followers of Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and other schools, however, declare that liberation is devoid of happiness.
By the mention of "the first," the Vaiśeṣikas are intended.
The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of indicating that, just as the former were speakers of what is untenable, so too are these.
To the question "Why did they speak thus? he says: "Because they desire... and so forth.
One should also bring about the complete dissolution of desire, aversion, effort, and so forth.
Regarding this, they say: ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.72a //
In that state, they say there is also the dissolution of desire, aversion, effort, and so forth.
The phrase "in every respect" (*sarvātmanā*) is used to show the distinction from deep sleep and cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).
Dissolution in every respect is the non-arising again within that very self of that which belongs to the same class [of phenomena] as previously ceased.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of intellect (*buddhi*), suffering (*duḥkha*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), as well as the body (*śarīra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*).
Consequently, this is the intended meaning:
it is not tenable that the pleasure of one who is liberated is beginningless.
If it is argued that it must indeed appear [in liberation] because otherwise it would follow that it appears even in *saṃsāra*, we say no;
for if that which appears were beginningless, it would follow that the employment of a means of realization (*sādhana*) is useless.
If it is argued that it does not appear in *saṃsāra* because it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), whereas it appears in liberation because it is manifest (*vyakta*), we say no.
For non-manifestation is the absence of appearance, and manifestation is appearance.
Consequently, it would be said that something does not appear because of its non-appearance, and it appears because of its appearance.
Furthermore, even when the internal organ—the cause of cognition—exists, [the object] is not cognized in the state of saṃsāra.
It is well said that it is perceived upon liberation when that [obscuration] has departed;
however, if it is argued that it is not perceived because it is obscured, we say no,
for since it lacks material form (*mūrtatva*), obscuration is impossible.
And because that [object] cannot be determined:
if its cognition, like pleasure, is beginningless, what is the function of an obscuration?
If it is argued that the relationship between object and subject is obstructed, we say no.
Since a cognition devoid of an object is untenable,
this conceptual construction is only logical if the beginninglessness of both pleasure and its cognition has already been established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
yet we see no such means of knowledge in that regard.
Therefore, it must be said that there is indeed the production of happiness and its cognition in liberation;
yet even that is not possible,
due to the absence of a cause.
When the body exists, there is the presence of the sense faculties which depend upon it; through them, there is the observation of objects;
from that, there follows the inference of the capacity to achieve what is desired or avoided by way of similarity with what was previously experienced.
Therefore, there arise desire and aversion; from these two, effort arises; and from that, the acquisition of the means for what is desired.
The abandonment of that which accomplishes what is undesirable, followed by the arising of happiness,
and immediately thereafter the cognition of that [happiness]— this indeed is the sequence of observed causes.
And the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) prevails everywhere;
furthermore, this stream of causes does not exist in liberation.
For if it were present, it would follow that suffering also exists, which would contradict the state of being liberated.
Therefore, liberation is indeed devoid of happiness.

If it is asked, "How is this the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*)? we reply: because it is the absolute cessation of suffering which consists of twenty-one varieties—the body, the six sense organs, the six objects, the six types of cognition, pleasure, and pain.
It is not that the cessation of suffering alone is the goal of human endeavor; [rather, it is so because it is the ultimate end].
This is because its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is conditional (*sopādhika*).
If it is argued that since pleasure occurs only when suffering is absent, the absence of suffering is sought for the sake of pleasure, and not because it is itself what the person desires, [we reply:
no, for the reverse is also the case.

It might be argued that since the suffering of hunger and so forth ceases only when the pleasure of eating and so forth exists, it is for the sake of the cessation of suffering alone that the pleasure of eating and so forth is sought; however, one should not assume that this [pleasure] itself is what is desired by the person. This is not so, because pleasure is desired even in some cases where there is no cessation of suffering.

The cessation of suffering is also desired in some cases even in the absence of pleasure. If it is argued that there is at least the intention that "when suffering has ceased, pleasure itself will arise," [we reply] that such an intention exists there as well, because one intends that the separation from suffering is certain during a state of pleasure.
Therefore, although the absence of suffering is necessarily concomitant with happiness, and happiness is necessarily concomitant with the absence of suffering,
nevertheless, these two possess the status of human goals independently of one another,
because their respective objects of desire are not conflated.
[Objection: The cessation of suffering is the human goal (puruṣārtha), but only insofar as it is being experienced.

For wise people do not exert themselves toward that state where suffering has ceased during a condition of delusion produced by poison and the like, because [the cessation] is not being experienced there.
Therefore, since the cessation of suffering is not being experienced in liberation (mokṣa), it cannot be the human goal. [Reply: This is not so.
For we observe that some people, desiring to eliminate the suffering born of separation from sons and others, even engage in such acts as taking poison, using weapons, or hanging themselves.
If it is argued that discerning persons do not act in this way, we say no;
for there is no contradiction with its being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

For wise people do not turn toward another's wife when restrained by the goad of scriptural prohibition; thus, in that case, desire is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Rather, because the pleasure is slight while the harm is great, they desist. Similarly, even regarding poison and the like, one who would engage in them is turned away from them because they are censured in scripture; since the harm incurred is great while the benefit is slight, they do not proceed.

For this indeed is the mark of a discerning person (*prekṣā*): that even regarding what constitutes human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), one reflects upon whether it contradicts worldly convention or scriptural authority;
because being a human purpose depends solely on the fact that something is desired for its own sake.

For this very reason, where there is no contradiction with the world or the scriptures, even discerning people are seen abandoning their bodies through methods such as leaping from a precipice, falling into water, or fasting, when they are tormented by disease and other afflictions.
People do not engage in the means for its attainment with the thought, "I shall experience the cessation of suffering somewhere," but rather with the thought, "I shall abandon suffering.
Furthermore, what is intended is merely the fact that the cessation of suffering is being experienced.

Or even the existence of the cessation of suffering. If it is the former, let the wicked man be satisfied; in the latter case, it is indeed experienced in the final birth through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Even the absolute cessation of suffering, though belonging to the future or the present, is indeed experienced without delay.

In the second case [of the opponent's view], however, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cessation of suffering caused by thorns and such— which is already present— would not be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*),
because it is never being experienced.

Or, if that were the case, it would follow that there could be no transition to other objects, because cessation would remain in that same state forever. Therefore, liberation devoid of happiness is not the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). *12,264*
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so."
... even this is not appropriate here... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.72ab //
In this regard, even this view that liberation is devoid of happiness is not tenable.
Why? To this he says: "It is heard... [and so forth].
...for the Vedic scriptures invariably declare both great bliss and enjoyment [to result from it]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.72b–d)
The word "here" (atra) is understood [from the previous context].
"Experience" (bhoga) means the enjoyment thereof;
"by rule" (niyamena) means without contradiction.
Thus he declares the well-known status of the Śrutis;
these shall be cited.
[Objection: But is it not said, "Verily, when one is bodiless, neither pleasure nor pain touches him"?
Thus, it is heard that for one who is liberated, there is the loss of pleasure just as there is the loss of suffering;
likewise, because of the absence of cognition, [it is said] "after death, there is no consciousness."
To explain how this is so, he first interprets the scriptural passage concerning the "touching of bliss" with the words: "Prākṛta... (pertaining to the primordial nature).
The loss of what is dear to common folk is called "contact with the beloved. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.73ab)

In this scriptural passage, that which is "dear" (*priya*)—consisting of the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—its very loss is what is expressed by the term "non-contact with the dear" (*priyāspṛṣṭi*).
It does not, however, mean the absolute absence of happiness.
If this is so, then "non-contact with the unpleasant" (*apriyāspṛṣṭi*) should likewise be explained through such a distinction.
Because there would be no distinction [between the two states], it would follow that suffering exists even in liberation; therefore, he says: "the unpleasant."
That which is unpleasant and contrary is designated by that term [“unpleasant”] without distinction.
Since everything unpleasant— that is, suffering—
is contrary to and undesired by one seeking liberation,
it is therefore designated here without distinction as "the unpleasant."
This is what is meant:

that liberation is the cessation of all undesirable states in every respect is a point of no dispute among all proponents [of philosophical systems]. As for suffering, however, it is undesirable regardless of its specific nature.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to explain it through such a distinction.
Alternatively,
if the same principle by which a distinction is made regarding what is pleasant were to apply without exception to what is unpleasant, then that too would have to be explained through a distinction.
But it is not so;

for if [pleasure] were to perish entirely, there would be the loss of what is desired, and upon the attainment of what is undesired, liberation would cease to be the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Therefore, a distinction is postulated regarding pleasure.
And so we shall explain later.
Nor is the total elimination of suffering undesirable;
for since all suffering is undesirable, its elimination is indeed desired.

If it is argued that since all happiness is desired, even the abandonment of ordinary happiness should not be accepted, we say no; for its nature is such that it is invariably accompanied by suffering, and thus, like honey mixed with poison, it must be rejected as undesirable—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, he states "it does not exist" to show that the term "ordinary" (*prākṛta*) should not be used as a qualification for what is unpleasant.
For there is no suffering whatsoever that is not natural to a living being who exists.
If non-material suffering existed, the qualification "material" would have to be applied in order to exclude it.
However, for the soul that is capable of liberation,
there is no non-material suffering, as there is a lack of evidence [for its existence].
Therefore, the qualification is redundant;

the remainder of the sentence implies that this has been stated in some *Śruti* or *Smṛti*. [Objection: If that is so, since even non-material (*aprākṛta*) happiness is not established as a known entity, it is improper to provide an explanation by inserting a qualification there as well. To this, he says: "the beloved" (*priyam*).
His very nature is what is dear to him, according to such statements as "strength, bliss," and so forth.

From the scriptural statement, "O Ānanda, strength, vigor, endurance, and untroubled knowledge— these very natures of the individual soul (jīva) are manifested from the Supreme Lord," it is understood that the beloved nature of this existing soul is indeed its own essential form.
Furthermore, its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not the subject under discussion;
therefore, it is appropriate to provide an explanation by adding a qualification in order to exclude that [nature].
By this, it should be understood that the objection raised against pleasure having an origin is refuted by the fact that it is not accepted [as a subject here].
Because beginninglessness has been stated as being their very nature (*svarūpa*),
that which was said here is also incorrect;
for it is stated in scripture that they, while being obscured, are manifested.
And the obscuration is indeed primordial nature (prakṛti), which is designated as illusion, ignorance, and so forth;
nor is there any logical inconsistency in a matter established by clear scriptural testimony.
Although knowledge is beginningless by virtue of being its very essence, its relationship as object and subject is obstructed by ignorance.

Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable, because that [cognition] is not obstructed with respect to the nature of the self and so forth. Summarizing the point already stated, he says: "Because it is to be abandoned" (*heyatvāt*).
Since that which is unpleasant must be abandoned, and since the loss of what is pleasant is undesirable,
it is not logical to say that liberation consists in the absence of all that is pleasant.
By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "precisely because the unpleasant and painful [is] to be abandoned," he indicates that this applies in every respect.
It is not appropriate to explain the absence of all that is pleasant in liberation as it is described in the scriptural passage: "Verily, for one who exists bodiless... (*aśarīraṃ vāva santam*).
Why? Because the loss of what is dear is undesirable.

However, the word "but" (tu) indicates that this is qualified by the addition of the attribute "natural" (prākṛta). It should be supplemented by the observation that the abandonment of the unpleasant, however, is to be explained as being without such qualification.
In this context, the reason is that what is unpleasant must be abandoned in every respect;
and this is merely an illustration,
for it should also be understood that for an existing soul (*jīva*), there is an absence of non-material suffering.
But surely, even for one who possesses a body, there exists an unlovely nature that is intrinsic and non-material;
how then can this be so? To this he says: "Of the unlovely... (apriyasya).
For it is heard in scripture that the nature of the unpleasant exists only among the Asuras.
The sense is that the Asuras are not fit for liberation. He recites that Śruti in its literal meaning: "The Asuras... and so forth.
The Asuras say, "It is thus," and all humans say, "It is not thus, nor is it thus.
... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 4.2.76c–e]

By this, he cites the scripture: "The Supreme Self is eternal bliss, eternal knowledge, and eternal power; the Asuras are not so, and humans are neither so nor otherwise. By the statement of eternality, its nature as the essential self (svarūpa) is established.
Because the mental modifications (vṛtti) are impermanent;
[it refers to] the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Supreme Lord (parameśvara),
or the individual soul (jīva).
"Not thus" means that they possess a nature contrary to this.
"Thus and not thus" refers to both these modes.
The meaning is that they possess both natures;
whereas the asuras are not so,
and all humans are neither "so" nor "not so"— this is the construction.
The connection is: "Thus it has been heard.

By preventing the over-extension [of the argument]—namely, that one should exercise restraint even in the abandonment of what is unpleasant—the doubt as to why the general hearing of the non-contact with the pleasant is restricted to a specific instance is also resolved, because the restrictive factor has been indicated.
He states that very same regulating principle clearly: "The Self."
...and what wise person would strive for the loss of their own well-being? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.76ef)
"Self and that which is dear to it" constitutes "self-dear";
or alternatively, it means "that which is dear to the self. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that one also desires that [self-dear]. *12,272*
If contact with the beloved were not distinct [from ordinary pleasure], then no discerning person would desire liberation,
nor would they exert effort for its sake;
even though, by the force of aversion, a desire and so forth might arise toward the destruction of another's happiness.
Nevertheless, no intelligent person desires the loss of their own happiness,
nor do they strive for that purpose;
this is because the happiness consisting of [mental] activity is predominantly undesirable, and thus there is a desire to abandon it.
It is appropriate to sing and so forth;
but why should the thornless happiness of one's own nature be abandoned?
And it is not non-existent.
Because it is established by scripture;
for the association of pleasure with pain is caused by the unity of their cause,
and there is no cause for the pleasure of the Self.
Furthermore, the abandonment of one's own happiness is impossible;
nor can desire and effort directed toward an impossible object occur in an intelligent being.
Indeed, the abandonment of the self—characterized by destruction or non-arising—is impossible, because the self is eternal.
Nor does it have the characteristic of separation,
because according to the view of others [the self] is all-pervading,
and according to our own view, there is a contradiction in an action being directed toward oneself.
Nor can it be characterized by ignorance, because [the Self] is self-luminous.
Thus, since there exists this subverting argument, the phrase "not touching the beloved" must be explained as referring specifically to a particular state.
And so it is said: "Verily, for one who exists bodiless..."
Thus, the reasoning stated in the Śruti is consistent.

Having thus explained the scriptural passage concerning the lack of contact with pleasure (*sukhāsparśa*), he now explains the scriptural passage concerning the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*) with the word "cognition" (*saṃjñā*).
For even the notion that "there is no [object]" is not for him a case of the knowable being unexpressed. Thus it is said. (MĀnuv 4.2.77ab)
The phrase "the Śruti says" connects here as well to what is about to be stated:
the Śruti passage, "There is no consciousness after death," also declares that for this liberated one, there is no state of being an object of knowledge for those who are not liberated.
It is not that the liberated one does not know;
for the first word "hi" has the sense of "only," while the second indicates that the meaning stated by oneself does not exceed the power of the words.
For instance:
the literal meaning of the statement "after passing away (pretya), there is no perception (saṃjñā) [or] knowledge" is simply that it follows immediately after death.
In this context, however, by virtue of the specific topic under discussion, the term "after passing away" should be explained as referring to the period immediately following liberation from death.
However, when knowledge related to one who is liberated is being negated, we see no restrictive factor that would lead us to conceive it as having that [liberated person] as its agent;
therefore, this negation is understood to pertain to knowledge belonging to that very agent. Or, in every respect, [it pertains to] the state of being unknowable.

It is postulated that the denial of the knowability of the Unliberated (amukta) implies the non-existence of vehicles (yāna), as this would otherwise entail the consequence that vehicles do not exist.
This denial, however, refers to direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) even for those who are not liberated, such as ourselves;
for while Nārada and others possess such direct perception, we and others like us acquire knowledge of it through scripture (*śāstra*).
"For this very reason, the word 'saṃ' is employed.

[Objection: But in a general statement, why is it assumed that this negation applies to knowledge whose object has been abandoned, and not to that which is produced by such a person? To this, he says: "Dharma... etc.
For it is precisely because of the non-extinction of dharmas that the scripture provides a further answer.
For this reason, the subsequent scriptural passage, “This self is of a nature not subject to destruction,” declares precisely the non-destruction of the attributes of this liberated self.
Those whose destruction does not exist are described as such.
"One whose nature is non-cessation is 'anucchittidharma';
therefore, it is explained in this way.
This might be so.
It can also be said that the term *anucchittidharma* expresses the non-destruction (*anucchitti*) of properties such as number and so forth;
or alternatively, that *anucchitti* is the absence of destruction, and that which has this as its property is *anucchittidharma*.
To dispel the doubt as to how this [term] serves as a definitive restriction, he explains the sentence from the very beginning with the words: "having raised the doubt" (*āśaṅkaya*).
Fearing that his knowledge might be lost, Yājñavalkya said to Maitreyī,
who had addressed him as "Sir," "I am not speaking of delusion to you";
by saying this, he indeed spoke of the non-destruction of one's true nature.
"A mass of consciousness alone, arising from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death.

This self, whose form is consciousness, though beginningless, arises in its final birth from these elements; having become an object of empirical usage solely for the purpose of producing a body composed of elements, it—though eternal—perishes along with those very elements upon their destruction. *12,279*
The sphere of worldly activity becomes destroyed;
that is to say, one goes forth into homelessness.

Then, having heard the indistinct words of Yājñavalkya—that after passing away and attaining liberation, there is no consciousness or knowledge for this liberated one—and suspecting a loss of knowledge for this liberated being, Maitreyī thought that by this statement it was being said that the liberated one does not know; thus she said: "In this very matter, do not lead me into the depths of delusion."
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "Thus urged by her who had said that what you told me in this statement—that one who is liberated does not know—is merely delusive.

Yājñavalkya, having made the declaration—"Indeed, O beloved, I do not speak delusion"—in order to instruct her in knowledge, saying, "I do not tell you, my dearest, anything that is delusive," and then, in response to the doubt as to how that could be so, stated the indestructibility of the nature of the Self with the words, "Indeed, O beloved, this Self is indestructible."
Alternatively, the form "āśaṅkaya" is derived from the causative (ṇijanta) root with the suffix *lyap*.
The construction is as follows: Yājñavalkya spoke because he suspected that Maitreyī’s knowledge might be lost due to his obscure speech.

To the question, "What is the proof that such a suspicion arose in her? it is stated: by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of her words, namely, "For [you have] said to me... (*moham āha māṃ bhavān*...), her suspicion is established.
The meaning is "it is understood.
The second occurrence of the word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates that this meaning is indeed explicit in the Śruti.

In response to the objection that the statement regarding the destruction of knowledge is delusive, [the author] says—since the destruction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is inconsistent—how was it stated? To this, he replies: "of the essential nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpasya*).
"Since the non-destruction of consciousness—which is of the nature of knowledge—is itself its destruction...
(Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.79a-c).
Since the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of knowledge, its so-called "destruction of consciousness" is simply its destruction;
however, there is no destruction of the self,
for if that were the case, it would follow that liberation (*mokṣa*) would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).
Therefore, there is no destruction of knowledge;
for this very reason, my statement is not for that purpose,
but rather [it means] that for those who have been liberated, there is no conceptualization regarding the liberated state.

The connection is as follows: intending that the very meaning of my statement is that for those who are liberated there is no designation (saṃjñā) consisting of mental activity (vṛtti), and so forth, [the author] spoke of the non-destruction of intrinsic nature (svarūpa).
Even if such a consistency exists, one might ask: "Since he did not explicitly state that 'knowledge does not perish,' for what purpose was this said? To this, he replies: "Śūnya... (It is empty).
... for the sake of severing the view of emptiness... // MAnuv_4.2.79c //
Yājñavalkya did not proceed here merely for the sake of defining the object of knowledge (*prameya*), but rather for the purpose of examination (*parīkṣā*).

For this very reason, instead of stating explicitly that "it is not known after death," he uttered the general statement, "there is no consciousness after death," in order to provoke doubt. And examination consists in the refutation of what is not accepted by oneself.

Thus, when this answer has been given, the refutation of the view of emptiness—which is characterized by the destruction of the self—is also accomplished; for that purpose, he stated that [the self] does not perish in its own nature.
Now, he explains the phrase "of a nature not subject to cessation," for which the initial statement was previously interpreted, beginning with the word "furthermore" (punar).
... furthermore, O Ānanda, having taught the dharmas preceded by joy, which are unsevered... // MĀnuv 4.2.79de //
Having stated that the essential nature [of the self] is not destroyed, Yājñavalkya further declares that the attributes of the liberated one, beginning with bliss, remain uninterrupted.

Since the non-interruption of these attributes is already established by the very statement that the essential nature is not destroyed, this repetition might seem redundant; therefore, it is specified that they "begin with bliss.

At the commencement of the passage, it was stated that "he is indeed a mass of consciousness," thereby declaring that consciousness is the essential nature of the self, but it was not stated that they "begin with bliss."

At the beginning of the passage, by the statement "a mass of consciousness alone," it is stated that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the very nature of the Self, but not so for bliss (*ānanda*) and the others.
Therefore, since the non-destruction of the essential nature is stated, the non-destruction of consciousness itself is easily understood, whereas the non-destruction of bliss and the rest is not.
Consequently, this sentence is intended to convey the meaning that these [qualities] as well—like consciousness—are indeed the very nature of the Self and are thus not subject to annihilation.
He indicates another intended meaning with the words "by the logicians" (*tārkikaiḥ*). ... [those] who have been refuted by the logicians. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.79f)
This has already been stated in the *Parīkṣā* that Yājñavalkya proceeded [to speak].

Therefore, there is no fault of redundancy in this statement, as it is intended to demonstrate that those logicians who, while accepting the non-destruction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless deny the existence of attributes (*dharma*) such as cognition and pleasure for the liberated one, are proponents of an incorrect doctrine.
[Objection: But surely, by the mention of the non-destruction of the essential nature, the non-destruction of the attributes is also already established.
True;
that is according to our own school's view.
However, the logicians do not consider cognition, pleasure, and so forth to be of the very nature of the self.
Therefore, what is the point now of establishing their nature as the Self in the context of liberation?
With the intention that this too must be stated within the exposition on the nature of the Self, it was said that there is "indeed no cessation. This is the underlying implication here.
Regarding the term *anucchittidharma*: if this were said to mean that qualities such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth are indestructible, then this statement would become incoherent.

For, in response to the objection that "the statement regarding the destruction of cognition is delusion," one would see no logical connection in asserting the indestructibility of number and the like.

Furthermore, if it were claimed that the indestructibility of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is what is stated here, then because that has already been stated by the preceding sentence, it would entail the fault of tautology.
In our view, however, all these statements possess their efficacy according to the manner described above.
Therefore, it is understood that this statement teaches the non-cessation (*anucchitti*) of qualities such as knowledge and bliss alone.
And by virtue of that, the statement "there is no consciousness after departing" (*na pretya saṃjñāsti*) also has its meaning already explained.
And for this reason as well, he says that this has already been stated: "only," etc.
He has likewise declared that one should avoid even contact with a woman during her menses.

Just as he spoke of the non-cessation of phenomena (*dharmānucchitti*), so too he spoke of their "measure" (*mātrā*)—namely, the objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—and their conjunction, characterized by experience, through the statement: "But his conjunction with the measures occurs.
Therefore, it cannot be explained as a loss of knowledge.
Since this statement is not found in the Śruti, it is said: "the Mādhyandina Śruti."
...is the Mādhyandina Śruti. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.79h)
This section, in the form of a dialogue between Maitreyī and Yājñavalkya, is common to both the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions of the Śruti.
Although this particular statement does not exist in the Kāṇva Śruti, it certainly exists in the Mādhyandina Śruti.
Therefore, he says "he censured" (*ācikṣepa*) to show that even from this point on, the statement "there is no designation" (*saṃjñā nāsti*) has already been explained.
And he rejected that doctrine in which there is no consumption of sense-objects.
The scripture will state this later.

For the subsequent scripture beginning with "Where there is, as it were, duality" has censured— that is, condemned— that view according to which it is accepted that for one who is liberated there is no enjoyment of objects, such as the experience of forms and other sensory objects.
Consequently, that statement does not establish the absence of knowledge in one who is liberated.
For it is not possible for one devoid of knowledge—who is like a mere jar—to have contact with objects or to be censured for the absence thereof.
If it is asked, "How then does it imply [this]? [the answer follows].

It is said: having stated the pervasion by means of the passage beginning with "Where, if duality exists, then indeed one sees the other," and having declared its established validity through the word "hi" (for), [the text continues] "But where, if..."

If everything desired by this self were to become the self itself, such that nothing existed apart from it, then by what means would it perceive what object? It is stated that there would be the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) that nothing whatsoever could be perceived by anything at all. *12,285*

In that case, it is argued that if there were no duality in liberation, then the perception of forms and so forth would not occur; thus, by this [argument], the doctrine of the non-existence of duality is refuted, but not the doctrine of the non-existence of the enjoyment of objects. To this, he says: "The sense of smell, etc. (ghrāṇādi).
But the scripture [prohibits] the absence of enjoyment through the sense of smell and so forth, because such an absence is undesirable.

The enjoyment of odors and so forth by means of the nose and so forth is "enjoyment by the nose and so forth. This is because both the instrument (the sense organ) and the object (the sensory field) have been mentioned [in the preceding verse]. The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of specification.
This is by way of the intention of the heart;
the connection is with what precedes.
This is true: having refuted both the doctrine of emptiness and the doctrine of the logicians, non-duality is here refuted by this scripture.
And that [absence] is to be demonstrated by showing the consequence of the absence of enjoyment of objects.
Furthermore, that which is undesirable is what must be demonstrated.
Therefore, it is understood that in the Advaita system, the Śruti intends to show its undesirability by demonstrating the absence of enjoyment through the sense of smell and so forth.
And that which is said to be "undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*) is that which lacks authoritative basis and is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the censure of the absence of enjoyment of sense objects is indeed pervaded by the intended meaning of the Śruti.

This would be so through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) regarding the understanding of the censure of the absence of enjoyment of sense objects, provided that the absence of enjoyment of sense objects were to be adduced as a consequence here in the Advaita system.
But it is not so;
rather, this is a statement of the actual state of things.
For instance:
This self is indestructible; for that very reason, its nature is non-annihilation.
In liberation, it becomes dissociated from the subtle elements (mātrās).
Why?

For where in saṃsāra there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another, and so forth. But where in liberation all has become the Self alone for him, and nothing exists apart from himself, there by what could one see whom? By nothing at all, and nothing at all—thus say the Advaitins. To this, he replies with the words "by which."
"By what means does one know this entire world, as well as oneself, the knower?
And by what would one know that [means]?"—for such a thing is in every way impossible. (Manu Smṛti 4.2.81)

By the phrase "and by what should one know Him by whom all this is known? And by what should one know the knower? [the author] takes up two statements: "by what should one know Him by whom all this is known? and "O, by what should one know the knower? He explains that "the knower" refers to oneself alone.
The author will state that the subject matter of the first sentence is the Sūtra;
thus, what is expressed by the two sentences is the lack of knowledge of Viṣṇu and the lack of self-knowledge.
This is what is meant.
At the end of this [passage], the two statements "by whom this... and "this world... are heard.
Their meaning is as follows: the absence of knowledge of the Supreme Lord and the absence of self-knowledge are neither undesirable nor real;
therefore, it is understood that these are merely stated as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*).

By association with that [teaching], it should be understood that statements such as "by what should one see whom? are merely logical consequences (*prasañjana*) and not descriptions of the actual state of reality.
Now, is it not the case that the Lord (*īśvara*) is in every respect entirely without distinction, according to the scriptural passage beginning with "from which speech [turns back]"?
Furthermore, the individual soul (jīvātman) is not self-knowing, because it is contradictory for a single entity to simultaneously possess the status of both agent and object within a single action.

Therefore, since the absence of knowledge of the Supreme Lord and the absence of self-knowledge would otherwise follow, [the author] first refutes the notion that the Supreme Lord is in every way unknowable by stating: "No."
For Viṣṇu is not the knower of all things, since he is necessarily unknowable.
Here, by the phrase "the knower of all," the referent of that [phrase] is shown to be Viṣṇu, after having restated the meaning of the sentence "by whom this" (*yenedam*);
for it has not been explained previously,
and because the meaning of this sentence is impossible without Viṣṇu.
The word *hi* has the sense of "at least" (*tāvat*).
It is not the case that Viṣṇu is absolutely and in every way unknowable. Why? To this he says: "That... (*tad*). 12.288.
For it is for the sake of that knowledge that the entirety of the Vedas was set forth.
The phrase "of [the passage] beginning with 'All the Vedas'" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The intention is that since Viṣṇu would otherwise be entirely unknowable, which would result in the futility of all the Vedas, passages such as "From whom speech [turns back]" must be interpreted differently.
Having thus established that the Supreme Self is knowable, he establishes the individual self's knowledge of itself with the words: "It is perceived."
Moreover, because it is experienced as not contradicting perception, scripture, or self-knowledge,
no contradiction whatsoever is perceived regarding one's own state of consciousness.
This is an adverbial modifier.
"Self-cognition" (*ātmavijñāna*) and "non-contradiction" (*avirodha*) form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
Furthermore, by implication, non-contradiction is simply self-cognition itself.
The experience of those two is of the nature of direct perception; therefore,
by the word "also" (api), the inclusion of scripture and so forth is intended.
No contradiction whatsoever is perceived regarding the soul’s self-cognition,
nor is any logical inconsistency observed.
Indeed, the experience of self-knowledge is well known as being of the nature of a witness (*sākṣin*), expressed as "I know myself."
Just as in the case of "I know the pot," no inconsistency whatsoever is perceived;
rather, by means of the Witness (sākṣin) accompanied by non-apprehension, the very absence of inconsistency is directly realized.
So it is likewise in the cognition "I know myself," which is not distinct from that [previous case].
The scriptures as well state: "He who is to be known as 'I' alone," and so forth.

Furthermore, if the self did not know itself, then, due to the absence of cognitions such as "this is mine" or "this is the means to achieve my desired end," there would likewise be an absence of the corresponding desire and effort, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all engagement in action or cessation from it.
Moreover, its self-luminosity and its manifestation as the substratum of cognition cannot be established apart from its own cognition.

He refutes the objection that was stated—that the acceptance of their identity is contradictory because a difference between agent and object is observed in the case of cutting and so forth—by saying "agent-object... [kartṛkarma].
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction between the agent and the object, as well as a contradiction with constant experience;
how could such a position even reach a conclusion? Contradiction is a sublation by what is perceived.
The contradiction between the status of being an agent and that of being an object within a single action is "contradiction between agent and object.
"Constant experience" refers to the experience of the aforementioned witness.
"Place" means the locus; the word "in the present context" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
This is the intended meaning:
this has been stated in the Liṅgapāda;
namely, that the distinction between agent and object is the general rule (autsargika).
It may be argued that even when there is a denial, a distinction [between the two] still exists;
however, in this case, because it contradicts the experience of direct perception—namely, "I know myself"—this is not the proper scope of that logical principle.
Rather, this contradiction applies only where there is no sublation by unseen factors and no conflict with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Just as when one fingertip touches another fingertip,
or as when a sword’s edge cuts the sword’s edge;
let it be so that Īśvara is an object of knowledge.
And the soul possesses self-knowledge;
nevertheless, if it is asked how the absence of that knowledge in liberation is not undesirable,
it is said in reply:
"The wise one perceives nothing at all—neither self nor others, neither truth nor falsehood; he is the Fourth (turya), the eternal seer of all.
Having thus stated in this Śruti that both self-knowledge and knowledge of the Lord do not exist [in the state of deep sleep], it is then declared that these do exist for the liberated one.
Therefore, since its absence contradicts the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how could it not be undesirable?

It is understood that the absence of enjoyment of objects is undesirable not only because of this context of what is undesirable, but also because the enjoyment of objects is established by scripture (*śruti*); thus he says: "He... (sa).
"He attains all desires and, being a master of his own will, can assume any form at will"—such scriptural passages indeed express this very same meaning. (Manu 4.2.85)
Now, the phrase "immediately after liberation" is connected to the beginning of the two scriptural passages.
This has already explained the fact that for one who is liberated, there exists the enjoyment of objects;
therefore, the interpretation that "there is no contact with the subtle elements (*mātrās*)" is indeed incorrect. *12,292*
It might be argued:

since the phrase "for where there is, as it were, duality" uses the word "as it were" (*iva*) to indicate the non-existence of duality, how can this statement regarding the contingency of non-perception apply when duality is absent? To this he says: "Because of lack of independence," meaning it was stated "as it were because of lack of independence," and not because of the actual absence of duality anywhere. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.86ab)
The phrase "as if dual" was stated with the intention that duality lacks independence;
it was not stated with the intention that duality does not exist.
Why?
The meaning is that in some instances, such as in the case of *abhidhāna* (denotation), the word *iva* is not stated to have the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Furthermore, here "independence" (*asvātantrya*) refers merely to its own essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*).
He states the sublation (*bādhaka*) against the view that the word *iva* has the meaning of non-existence with the words "the Self alone" (*ātmaiva*).
For from this [notion] would follow the undesirable consequence of non-distinction, namely that "the Self alone existed. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 4.2.86cd)
If the word *iva* were to have the sense of non-existence, then the phrase "it becomes as if dual" (*dvaitam iva bhavati*) would mean "duality does not exist.

In that case, there would be no distinction between this [phrase] and the passage "but where for him everything has become the Self alone" (*yatra tv asya sarvam ātmaivābhūt*), the meaning of which is clearly the absence of duality.
Therefore, there would be no difference between the two.

And thus, if duality were non-existent, the two statements— "one would see another"— and "in the absence of duality, who could see whom?"— would follow as a logical consequence. Consequently, the Veda would fall into the status of being the speech of a madman.
To the question, "From what [source] does the word *nanu* signify lack of independence (*asvātantrya*)?", he says: "Asvātantrya... etc.
As it has been stated regarding the varieties of non-independence and similes, that which is called "the essence of speech" (śabdatattva) is thus proclaimed... // MAnu 4.2.87a-c //
The expression "non-difference and difference" (*abhedabheda*) is an illustration of two counter-correlates (*pratīyogin*).
The meaning is that when one [counter-correlate] ending in "like" (*iva*) is mentioned, the second, which is its counter-correlate, is also obtained.
Now, for us, the word *iva* occurs only in the context of simile (*upamā*).
If it is argued that the absence of duality is established by implication—
just as when it is said, "The gavaya is like a cow," the absence of cowness in the gavaya is understood—
then one must state what it is that resembles duality.
If it is argued that duality is merely imagined (*kalpita*), we say no;
for since it lacks existence (*sattā*), its "coming into being" (*bhavati*) is untenable. If it is further argued that even its coming into being is itself imaginary, [we respond as follows].

In that case, if there were the perception of duality, then the statement "one sees another" would be nothing other than that very same thing; thus, the relationship of cause and effect cannot be established. Accepting the meaning of the sentence "there is no consciousness after death" as "the liberated one does not know," [one must likewise interpret] the sentences beginning with "indestructible" (*avināśī*) and so forth.
He states the refutation for one who explains it otherwise: "Maitreyī," etc.
And what is the answer joined with loving-kindness? MĀnuv 4.2.87d.
Having heard the statement, "There is no consciousness after death," Maitreyī said, "In that case, sir, do not [say such things]," and so forth.
That [objection] is certainly not to the point, because it would entail the consequence of [the Self] being insentient if one were to negate all [consciousness].

Therefore, the intended meaning must be inferred as follows: having first declared the nature of the Self to be pure consciousness with the words "a mass of consciousness" (*prajñānaghana*), you now state the absence of consciousness; thus, your statement is delusive.
Or else, there would be the consequence that it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*).
As it has been said: "If there were the destruction of consciousness, what need would we have for liberation? You have led me into delusion here"—thus was he addressed.
Otherwise, if explained differently, the statement addressed to Maitreyī would result in being without a reply;
for by these [other] statements, neither the contradiction with one's own words is avoided nor is the status of human purpose established.
Having thus stated that the liberation favored by the Sāṅkhyas, Naiyāyikas, and others lacks scriptural authority, [the author proceeds].
He elaborates on the point that was stated—that liberation would result in not being a human goal—by saying: "Pleasure and so forth..."
Moreover, if qualities such as happiness were lost, what would be the purpose of liberation?
The phrase "when the abandonment of dharmas such as pleasure is accepted as liberation" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The word *tu* (but) distinguishes this from our own position (*svapakṣa*).
The intention is that the fault being leveled against the opponent does not exist in our own system.
The genitive case in "of liberation" (mukteḥ) expresses mere relationship.
The word "what" (kim) is used in the sense of an objection.
The particle "ca" has the sense of conjunction, implying that [the following] is not based on authoritative means of knowledge.
"Prayojana" (purpose) is that by which a person is applied or set in motion.
[The question is: "What is the purpose of liberation?
The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that sets a person in motion for the sake of liberation.
The purpose is twofold:
the attainment of the desired and the cessation of the undesired.
In this regard, although liberation does not consist in the attainment of something desired, it nonetheless consists precisely in the cessation of what is undesired.
Therefore, he raises the objection that "it is sought after by the person" with the words "yadi" (if).
If the goal were the destruction of suffering...
If you say that liberation, consisting in the cessation of suffering, is the goal to be sought by the person (*puruṣa*),
it is replied:
the cessation of what is undesirable is indeed the goal of the person.
Liberation is the destruction of all suffering; nevertheless, one might ask how it is not a human goal (puruṣārtha). To this, he says: "It is a non-goal" (anartha).
... misfortune, the destruction of happiness. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.88d)
Since there is also an evil in the form of the destruction of happiness,
this is what is meant:
the ultimate cessation of suffering alone constitutes the purpose of human life.

But how can this absolute cessation of pleasure, like that of pain, be the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*)? For if one engages in activity with the intention of ceasing what is undesirable, there arises the contingency of withdrawing from it out of fear of ceasing what is desirable;
furthermore, upon the abandonment of pleasure interspersed with pain, there follows the acquisition of pain interspersed with pleasure.

As for what was stated here— "For one for whom suffering is to be accepted, what could be said to be abandoned? For one devoid of anything to be abandoned, what liberation is there, and by whom would it be taught?"— this is inconsistent.
We do not, however, establish that suffering is something to be pursued;
rather, we say that because there is no determining factor due to the fact that the result is equal to the expenditure, activity [toward it] is not possible.
As it has been said: "They are unreal, they have miserable ends, and their results are equal to the expenditure."
"A wise person should not undertake tasks that are impossible.
Having accepted the fact that the result might equal the expenditure, this was stated;
however, in reality, expenditure is even greater than income, as he says: "Of those two... [referring to the verse beginning with *tayośca*].
And because of the destruction of those two [pleasure and pain], the loss of pleasure would indeed be greater.

Between the abandonment of pleasure and the abandonment of pain—indeed, kings and others do not, upon the loss of their kingdom and so forth, experience the agony of the loss of pleasure by means of the abandonment of pain.
Therefore, the implication is that liberation is simply cessation (*nivṛtti*). *12,301*
Where the suffering being averted is small and the happiness is great, it is thus in that case; but here,
while great suffering is averted, the happiness is very slight— how then is this not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)?

“But for one who fears even the flickering fireflies of pleasure within the dense darkness of suffering and the continuous wilderness of saṃsāra— to such a person, this easily traversed path is taught, since its dangers have been dispelled.”
It has been shown [in the previous verse].
To this, he says: "Even having reached... (prāpyāpi).
Even after undergoing very great suffering, people strive merely to obtain a tiny fragment of pleasure;
for who would strive for liberation when it involves the loss of pleasure? (Manu 4.2.89c–f)

Since even people such as those born blind strive to obtain a mere fragment of happiness even after undergoing immense suffering, what person would not strive for the liberation from great suffering even at the cost of losing a small amount of happiness? None indeed would.
And this is a statement made on the basis of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*).
For it has not been established that worldly happiness is small in comparison to suffering;
for in some birth, this person [is] poor [or] unfortunate.
A universal monarch becomes miserable at times, sometimes experiencing hell and sometimes heaven.

Furthermore, the disparagement of worldly happiness found in the treatises on liberation is intended with reference to its insignificance when compared to the supreme bliss of liberation, which is devoid of all suffering.
By the phrase "and from the small," [the author] establishes in another way that even a small amount of pleasure is more significant than the great destruction of suffering.
For people fear the loss of even a small amount of pleasure exceedingly, and they undergo great suffering in order to prevent the loss of their pleasure. (Manu 4.2.90)
The smallness of the destruction of loss is caused by the smallness of its counter-positive;
that is to say, it is because even a small pleasure [is destroyed] through its loss and so forth.
"Regarding the phrase 'for the cessation of the destruction of happiness':
the meaning is for the cessation of that which has arisen as a cause for the destruction of happiness.
As for the examples, they are indeed clear in the world. How then [is it] like eating food mixed with honey and poison?"

If it is argued that this constitutes renunciation, we reply: because it results in the loss of much greater happiness; otherwise, the other [party] would also have to establish such a position. *12,304*
This may be so:
there are two kinds of persons, those with passion and those free from passion.
Among them, those with passion experience even suffering for the sake of pleasure.

For they, considering that even food mixed with honey and poison is initially delightful due to its sweetness—whether it kills because of contact with the poison or not—they consume it, thinking, "Let us enjoy it; let us partake of this immediate pleasure! For who would take what is in their hand and place it at their feet? Thus they enjoy it.

But those free from passion, contemplating your state, abandon even their own bodies—perceiving them as resembling the shadow of the expanded hood of an enraged serpent; therefore, he says "and not... (na ca).
And that [act] is not a cause for passion... // MĀnuv 4.2.91a //
As for what was stated,
beginning with "even having attained," that is a cause for attachment;
however, those seeking liberation are free from attachment, and therefore, disregarding pleasure, they strive solely for the destruction of suffering.
And that is not so; this is the meaning.
Why? To this he says: "Because it is free from... (vīta).
...even those free from passion, such as Nārada and others, clearly endure suffering directly for the sake of happiness. (Manu 4.2.91b–d)
The word "clearly" (sphuṭam) means that the state of being free from passion (vītarāgatva) of Nārada and others is well-known from the Śrutis and other sources.
The word "directly" (añjasā) is to be construed with the phrase "for the sake of a small amount of happiness.
The word "since" (yasmāt), which will be mentioned later, is also connected here.
To explain why this is so, he says:
"Because the sight of battle and such [occasions] occurs even with great difficulty in an evil age. (Manu 4.2.91ef)
The phrase "for the sake of happiness" continues [from the previous context],

as does the expression "Nārada and others. By the word "others," the sight of the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage ceremony), which is to be accomplished by traveling to a distant place and so forth, is included.
To the question "Why is this so? he says: "When..."
"When Indra and Virocana were scorched by the Brahmā-missiles of Brahmā, even Nārada and the others did not abandon the delight of battle.
Thus says the Skanda Purāṇa... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.92a-e].
They did not at all desire to witness the battle—for the sake of the passion for battle, that is, for the cause of the pleasure derived from witnessing the battle;
the word "yadā" (when/since) connects either with what precedes or with what follows.
The word "yasmāt" (because/since) is also connected here.
This is the underlying intention here:
in this context, what is intended by the word "passion" (*rāga*)? Is it the desire for pleasure, or is it non-discrimination (*aviveka*) through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
This is true in the first case;

however, even those seeking liberation are indeed possessed of passion. If it is asked how there can be liberation for those possessed of passion, [we reply: how could there be [liberation] for those possessed of hatred either?
For they abandon suffering precisely because of their hatred of suffering. If you argue that hatred is misplaced and thus binding, then the same applies to attachment as well; it is identical.
Furthermore, even an opponent must admit that there is attachment toward the eradication of suffering.
If you argue that this is not hatred for suffering but rather a form of world-weariness (*nirveda*),
then we reply that this is not attachment to pleasure, but rather faith (*śraddhā*) itself.
If it is argued that in the second [case], Nārada and others are the illustrations, and that they too were non-discriminating at that time,
how is this known— whether they were worldly or Vedic?
Regarding the phrase "by one with inferior wisdom" (*kottaraprajñena*),
he concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "nor by passion" (*na ca rāgeṇa*) with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, who would strive for the absence of happiness?
The phrase "even one who is free from passion" (*vītarāga*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, having accepted the absence of suffering in liberation as defined by others, the undesirable consequence of the lack of engagement in that state was stated.
Now, however, he says "the object of dispute" (*vimata*) to show that even the absence of suffering is not tenable.

Since one who is conscious, being in a state of suffering, is nonetheless established in happiness, by what means can this inference—that he has attained [the goal]—be prevented? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.93)
In this context, the subject (*pakṣa*) is one accepted by the opponent as being liberated; that which is to be established (*āpādya*) is "being joined with suffering";
and the reason for its establishment (*āpādaka*) is "because, while being conscious, he is devoid of happiness."
The term "being conscious" (*cetanaḥ san*) is stated in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and the like.

Here, "conscious" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), so there is no failure to establish the probans (*apādaka*). The phrase "residing in heaven" (*sukhokhita*) is used to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with respect to those dwelling in heaven.
Even for Īśvara, there is no deviation [from the rule] because of his means of happiness,
just like a recognized inhabitant of hell;
the word "eva" (only/just) is connected with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
And this is not an independent inference (*sādhana-anumāna*) for which there would be occasion for sublation (*bādhā*) and so forth; rather, it is simply a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-anumāna*).
Thus he says: "By what could such an inference be prevented?

One should also observe other over-extended consequences (*atiprasaṅga*), such as: "If the liberated one were not happy, then he would either be non-self or he would be suffering, like [anyone] commonly agreed upon."
He now elaborates upon what was stated previously—that "the Vedas [arise] from whom"—with the verse beginning with "All... (sarva...).
Since all the Śrutis and Purāṇas likewise describe liberation as being of the nature of bliss,
the wise should not accept this view that liberation is an absence of happiness.
The word "tathā" (likewise) signifies a conjunction.
He cites those [means of knowledge], such as direct audition and so forth, with the words "sa" (he).
Thus, being liberated from non-bliss, he clearly becomes blissful;
fixing his mind clearly upon me, the quality-less Brahman,
he attains supreme bliss wherein all desire ceases.
There is no deity equal to Viṣṇu, no happiness equal to liberation,
no word equal to the Veda, and no syllable equal to the letter *a*.
Where joys, delights, pleasures, and raptures abide,
where all the desires of the heart are attained— there, O Lord, make me immortal.
By this, he cites the scriptural passage: "Released from non-bliss, he becomes blissful.
Since bliss is established as his very nature, one might ask how it can be said that he "becomes" it; therefore, the word "manifestly" (sphuṭam) is used.
"From that which is devoid of bliss, from suffering.
"He is without qualities," says the Blessed One in the *Bhāgavata*.
When supreme bliss has been attained, desire—that is, thirst—[ceases].
"Maḥ" is understood as "desire";
it goes to its cessation.
"There is nothing equal to Viṣṇu"—this also is a statement from the Purāṇa.
In this world,
words such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth are designators of specific types of happiness;
"desires of desire" (*kāmasya kāmāḥ*) refers to the objects of longing.
*Āptāḥ* means "sufficient.
*Kṛdhi* is an imperative form meaning "do" or "make," which is a prayer directed toward Vāyu.
[This is derived from] the rule: *śru-śṛṇu-pṛ-kṛ-vṛ-bhyaḥ chandasi*.
The reading of the Purāṇas between the two Vedic recitations (śrutis) is for the purpose of demonstrating its status as being equivalent to the Vedas.
He concludes with the result of the cited Vedic passages and so forth: "Thus, the Veda... and so on.
For thus do the Śrutis and Purāṇas declare in various places;
therefore, the claim that there is an absence of happiness in liberation is indeed trivial.
In various places they speak of the bliss of the liberated one; for the first word "hi" has the sense of "because," while the second is used for emphasis.
The meaning is that it is something utterly trivial.
Furthermore, as for the absence of a body attributed to the liberated one by the Sāṅkhyas and others in order to establish the non-existence of pleasure—
that has been refuted as being useless, since the existence of intrinsic bliss (*svarūpasukha*) has already been stated.
And with the intention that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The head."
Furthermore, the absence of a head, hands, and so forth would never occur for one who is liberated.
The word "and" (ca) indicates that it is not merely the absence of pleasure and so forth [that is meant].

Because the head, hands, and other limbs exist in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), but not in the state of supreme liberation (paramamukti), the term "in some cases" (kvacit) was used.
To the question "Why?", he says: "And the Śruti texts... (śrutayaśca).
And there are many Śrutis and Purāṇas that serve as authority in this matter.

The phrase "it is not the absence of head, hands, and so forth" refers back to the presence of the head and other parts that has been established; the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "because," and the words "they exist" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The word "ca" (and) also implies that the transition [to liberation] due to bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) and so forth has already been explained.
In this regard, because its meaning is clear, he first cites the Purāṇa, beginning with the words "it does not exist":
"That wherein neither rajas nor tamas exists, nor sattva mixed with them, and wherein there is no passage of time..."
Where there is no illusion, much less others who are devoted to Hari, who is worshipped by both gods and asuras.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with eyes like lotus petals, clad in saffron-colored garments, beautiful in luster and well-formed;
all were four-armed, adorned with necklaces and ornaments of choice gems that seemed to sparkle, and possessed of great splendor.

It shines all around with the radiant celestial chariots of the great-souled ones, who possess the luster of coral, lapis lazuli, and lotus stalks, and who wear shimmering earrings, crowns, and garlands.

Where Śrī, in embodied form, pays homage in many ways with her manifold splendors at the feet of the Wide-striding One, as the sky is graced by rows of clouds accompanied by lightning along with the most excellent women who are radiant.
One, having nourished it, sits reciting the nourishment of the *ṛc*s; another sings the *gāyatra* song upon the *śakvarī* verses;
one as a *brahmán* priest speaks the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice.
In this world,
the word "sattva" has multiple meanings;
in some contexts, it denotes a specific transformation of primordial matter (prakṛti).
In some cases, there is goodness (*sādhutva*);
yet, when it is said that "existence (*sattva*) is not found there," it is not known what is being negated.
Therefore, it is stated that those two, *rajas* and *tamas*, are associated with one another.
If it is argued that [the meaning] will be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*) beginning with "passion" (*rajas*),
[we reply that] this is because one searches for context and so forth only when there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
The "non-functioning" (*avṛtti*) of passion and the other qualities means the absence of their activity as bondages.
The progression of time refers to the transformations of entities produced by the power of time;
illusion is the fundamental nature.
What more need be said? Even the Mahat and other principles do not exist there; for where the followers of Hari reside, even the Asuras are virtuous.
They were pure white,
polished, well-adorned, and handsome; they wore necklaces and ornaments of the finest shimmering gems, and they were decorated with excellent strings of radiant jewels.
"Ruk" means radiance;
"varcas" means vigor; and "balam" means strength—these are to be connected with the phrase "anuvratāḥ of Hari."

"The world shines all around with the rows of radiant celestial palaces (vimāna) of such great-souled beings"—some [of whom] have the luster of coral, and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "those who possess shimmering earrings and crowns, and who wear garlands."

Alternatively, one may form a *karmadhāraya* compound of "those which are sparkling" (*parisphurantyaḥ*) and "the earrings, crowns, and garlands" (*kuṇḍalamaulimālāḥ*), and subsequently apply the suffix *ini*. [The phrase] "by those [rows of celestial chariots] in which the most excellent women are shining" is thus explained. Or else, there is a construction based on grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*), connecting it as: "by the most excellent women who are shining, that is, resplendent."
The supreme women are the lightning flashes; the circles of celestial palaces are the circles of clouds; the embodied form is directly perceived;
and "māna" means worship.
