The connection with the preceding clause is: "He showed the world to be thus constituted by his own forms, which exist as manifold manifestations.
"He moves about in embodied form according to his desires... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.105a).
By the phrase "he moves about in a form free from desire," he cites the scriptural passage: "moving about according to his will in the realm of desire.
He states the result of the cited statements as follows: "Thus, previously... and so forth.
Thus, there is no fault [in this view] according to the aforementioned Vedic revelation and also by the statements of the Purāṇas;
for indeed, even of those who have attained liberation, the body is understood to be of the very nature of their true self.
Thus, that [view] which has this as its predecessor is described as such.
Since there would be a contradiction with liberation due to the occurrence of suffering and so forth in the state of having a body, it is said: "there is no fault."
To the question "How is it the cause of defects?", it is said: "It consists of its very own nature."
The Self is that whose very nature is the nature of the individual soul (jīva); thus it is so described. To the question, "Of whom? it is said: "and even of those who have attained liberation.
For in the Purāṇic passage, by the words "dark-complexioned," "fair-complexioned," and so forth, the body is perceived.

And here, by the statement that there is no "functioning" (na vartate) due to the absence of the primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth, there is the state of supreme liberation, the body's being its own true nature, and consequently, the absence of any defect.
In the scripture, embodiment [is established] through the utterance of the syllable "Ṛ" and so forth;
here he also states an inference: "the head."
Since even those who possess heads, hands, and so forth are now endowed with liberation,
and since inference preceded by such [perception] establishes that the nature of the living soul is distinct from the limbs and other parts.
The meaning is that those persons [are so] because they possess selfhood (*ātmatva*).
Now,
"just as" means "like us and others."
There is no fault, because [the arguments regarding] Īśvara and others are equivalent to the position [being refuted].
By the mention of "prior," there is the inclusion of the following: "Liberation resides in the embodied one, because it is a state of the individual soul (jīva), just like saṃsāra."
The nature of the living being (jīva) refers to the nature of the liberated soul;
"limb" means the body;
by the word "etcetera," the sense organs are included.
The term "āvayanti" (they cause to enter) is a metaphorical attribution of agency to the instrument;
some manuscripts read "āpayanti" (they cause to reach).

Having thus refuted the doctrine of the Sāṅkhyas and others, he now refutes the view of those who believe that upon liberation, the individual soul—whether previously distinct or both distinct and non-distinct from the Supreme Brahman—attains absolute oneness with it: *12,323* [He refutes their view as follows:]... Now, wishing to explain the arguments for the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding these sections, [the author], as an incidental digression (*prasaṅga*), first states the arguments of the previous two sections and then says this regarding the present section: "Grandeur" (*audārya*)—meaning manifold power and firmness in one's own nature—is the innate character (*nijasvabhāva*).
Sovereignty (*svātantrya*), the capacity for full excellence, and the removal of contradictions belong to the fourth section. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.114)
In the third chapter of the fourth quarter (pāda),
the phrase "the arguments of the prima facie position" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Establishment" (vyavasthiti) refers to the non-distinction, and "stability" (sthiti) refers to the general rules, prohibitions, and ritual actions.
The distinctness and the very accomplishment of the path are the reasons that contradict the attainment of the opposing side.
The cessations are those produced by the attainment of the opposing side;

they are the reasons that ward off the arguments which bring about the attainment of the prima facie position. In some places, the reading is "reasons contrary to the attainment of the opposing side."
In this context, the word "attainment" (*samprāpti*) is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).

Easy feasibility, constant renown, discernment, arrangement, deliberation, various activities, and the state of having accomplished what was to be done—these are the arguments against the opposing views in the section on "That Which Has Been Transcended. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.116)
Regarding the past foot and the immediately preceding past foot:

great fruitfulness, seclusion, the grasping of the connection, the means, the fulfillment of the task, the specific purpose, the establishment of the action, and well-reasoned conclusions regarding one's own position [are explained]. *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 4.2.117.

Regarding one's own position and the subject matter of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there are the grounds for determination (*nirṇaya*)—namely, sound arguments (*suyukti*). These consist of:
being well-integrated, efficacy in producing the result, consistency with the purpose, firmness, and dependence on [the established doctrine].
Similarity of properties, the state of having a remainder, worldly analogies, and following previous opinions; these are the [criteria for] comparison.
The arguments following the previous views are pursued in this chapter; thus, they are called "pursuits" (anusārāḥ).

These are: the scriptural mention of distinction and similarity, abundance, equal elision, greatness, distinction, fulfillment of purpose, and eternal persistence—these are the specific reasons for the determination of the established doctrine.

The specific reasons for determining the established tenets [are as follows]: "Oṃ, for [the two paths] do not show [the goal] in one [and the same way], Oṃ. (12.339) *12,339* // Oṃ naikasmin darśayato hi oṃ //

In this regard, there arises a doubt due to the contradiction between two scriptural passages: "All the gods dissolve into fire" and "The gods dissolve into the elements. Is it that all the gods dissolve into fire alone, or into all five elements? [The conclusion is: the dissolution of all the gods occurs in fire alone.

Since the scriptural mention of fire (*agni-śruti*) is without any other possible application (*niravakāśatva*), whereas the scriptural mention of the elements (*bhūta-śruti*) has other possible applications (*sāvakāśatva*), and since when all things dissolve into the single fire, and that fire into air, and the air into space, the use of the plural "into the elements" (*bhūteṣu*) is justified, such was the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been formulated as follows: [the dissolution is not into the gross elements].
The dissolution of all the gods does not occur in a single fire,
but rather in all five elements as well.
Why is this?
“The Ṛbhus dissolve into the earth; the Aśvins into Varuṇa;
the fires into Agni.”
"In the wind are Indra, Soma, Āditya, and Bṛhaspati; in space itself the Sādhyas dissolve"; [and] "the Ṛbhus in the earth. (The Deaths: "The Ṛbhus in the earth..."
Varuṇa is in the waters; Agni is in the brilliance; the Maruts are in the wind.
For the two scriptural passages— "The Vināyakas dissolve into space"— and "In space," show the dissolution of the deities into all five elements as appropriate;
here, it is understood that in the phrase "Indra into wind," the word *vāyu* is intended to denote the elemental wind (*bhūtavāyu*) rather than the secondary [deity].

Because the mention of earth and the other elements serves as the cause for the context of the primary elements (*bhūta*), and because the author of the Sūtras— beginning with the statement "In the elements, on account of their capability"— has adopted this scriptural passage [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.22] to mean that the dissolution of the gods occurs within all the elements.
To prevent the misconception that even air is subordinate to that [space], he says: "the primary," and so forth.
For [the scripture] does not show [the creation] in a single [instance];
indeed, the primary wind here is called "Vāyu," and it is logically established as having entered into the elements, as it has been declared.
The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis.
Here, the phrase "even one who has gone to what is declared in the Śruti as being among the elements" is a restatement of the seed of doubt.
It means: even one who has gone to that which was declared by the Śruti with the intention of teaching dissolution (*laya*) into the elements, such as earth and so forth.
Alternatively, regarding the point that the dissolution of the gods occurs within the elements, the Vedic passage cited by the author of the Sūtras has also been taken up here.
Why? [Because...]
The meaning is that, by logical reasoning, it is impossible for the highest beings, such as Indra and others, to dissolve into the lowest element, air.
To the question of how their dissolution could even be possible in the primary air (*pradhānavāyu*), he says: "Because... (yasmāt).
For it is stated extensively in the Śruti: "He purifies... and so forth. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 4.2.120c)

For this reason, because the Śruti states, "That deity which blows here is indeed beginningless," and by the word "ca" (and), it is declared in other Śrutis as well that the primary Vāyu is the Bhūḥ, being the supreme among all living beings;
therefore, the dissolution of Indra and the others within him is logically established.

The connection here is that the "pradhāna-vāyu" (the primary wind) is what is meant by the term "vāyu. Alternatively, the intended Vedic scripture here is: "This indeed is Brahman who blows; around him these five deities revolve: lightning, rain, the moon, the sun, and fire."
In that context, it has been stated that the destroyer of the sun and other [elements] is clearly the Earth (bhū).
If this were so, however, there would be a contradiction with the section concerning the elements (bhūta-prakaraṇa); therefore, he says: "Because... (yataḥ).
... for he too is one who considers himself superior to what actually exists. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.120d)
The meaning of "and" (ca) is that it is not only the subordinate wind, but this principal wind as well is named after the elements because it consists of the elements.
Therefore, since there is no contradiction with the context, it is the principal wind alone that is designated by the name "wind" here.
He elaborates on what has already been stated: "the Great Ego" (mahāmānin).
Since he who is highly conceited is also called "one of little conceit" by that very word, he too [is included]. (Manu 4.2.120ef)
"Great and he is conceited," thus "greatly conceited" (mahāmānī), meaning one who possesses all forms of conceit (*abhimāna*).

Just as a king who is the sovereign of an entire kingdom is also the sovereign of a small village included within it, so too the primary wind, possessing all conceit, must necessarily be the conceited owner of the minor wind that has come into being.
The word "that" (tat) refers to the word "element" (bhūta);
the sense of "also" (api) is that it is not only by the word "air" (vāyu).
Thus ends the section on the multiple layers (*anekalayādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. *12,341*

Oṃ! Those [are] supreme; for thus it has been said: Oṃ!
This is the sūtra.
Its meaning is as follows:
those divine beings, such as the earth and others who possess the conceit of being elemental beings (bhūta-abhimānin), dissolve into the Supreme Self; for thus says the Śruti.
In this [passage], the direct dissolution of all the gods into the Supreme Self is perceived;
to avoid that [conclusion], the Commentary states, "by way of the vital breath" (*prāṇadvāreṇa*).
Even there, the direct dissolution of all [the gods] into the vital breath would still be perceived.
Therefore, he explains it clearly with the words "in that" (*tasmin*).
For it is said by the other [author]:
"In that [Brahman], all beings dissolve without contradicting the sequence of their respective orders; that very [Brahman] [dissolves] into Viṣṇu. (Manusmṛti 4.2.121ab)
Without contradicting the sequence in its entirety, following all the sequences prescribed by the Śruti and other authorities,
the elements— beginning with the gross elements (bhūtas) and including the divine ones— dissolve into that primary wind;
and that very wind dissolves into Viṣṇu.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the Śruti, "And he [becomes] as far as Indra," which declares that Indra and the others dissolve into the primary wind (*pradhānavāyu*), he states that even this is not direct: "Of Indra and the others..."
The dissolution of Indra and the other deities therein occurs according to a specific sequence; it is not otherwise.
In that context, regarding the primary wind (*pradhānavāyu*),
the ablative case in *viśeṣāt* is used in the sense of the instrumental;
it should be explained by following what has been stated in the specific explanatory passage (*viśeṣavākya*).
However, there is no other explanation [of this] than that dissolution occurs therein directly;
the sense is that it would otherwise contradict specific scriptural statements (*viśeṣavākya*).
He states that very sequence in brief, beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, all living beings, having entered the Daughter of the Mountain together with her, and having reached Vāṇī together with her [and Rudra] along with him,
attain dissolution in Hari together with him.
The sense is that the specific authority must be followed in every respect.
In this context, the word *girijā* should be explained as referring to Vāruṇī and Sauparṇī;
likewise, the word *rudra* refers to Śeṣa and Garuḍa.
And so he will say:
"Having reached Rudra together with that Girijā, [she became] the wife of Vāṇī."
"Aśeṣāḥ" (all without exception) is a gloss upon "samastajīvāḥ" (all living beings).
Alternatively, it may be explained by supplying the word "praviśanti" (they enter) after "rudram. The subsequent series of sentences constitutes an elaboration of this very point. *12,344*

In this regard, that which was stated—that the four [deities] beginning with Indra mentioned in the Vedic revelation "Vāyāv indraḥ," as well as the elements beginning with earth, enter into the wind in a sequential manner—is now elaborated upon.
Here, there are two paths: the path of Śeṣa and the path of Garuḍa. Of these, he first describes the path of Śeṣa, beginning with the words "But Soma... (somastu).
Soma, joined with Varuṇa, enters Aniruddha; he [Aniruddha] enters Kāma, and he [Kāma] enters Vāruṇī.
She [Vāruṇī] enters the god Śeṣa, she enters Gira, and she indeed enters Vāyu directly—this is the conclusion here.
By the phrase "joined with Vārīśa," the dissolution of the lunar deity Soma into Varuṇa is stated.
Here, the determination is made regarding the entry of Soma, as well as the waters, into the wind within the fourfold group beginning with Indra.
Previously, it was stated that [Soma] goes to Rudra after Girijā.
And now, regarding the words "giraṃ" and "vāyuṃ":
he says "umeti" in order to prevent the notion that these four words have well-known conventional meanings.

Even Umā and the Lord of the Mountain, as well as Bhāratī and her consort, are spoken of by the Vedic voice at the time of liberation as the wife of the Serpent King and the Serpent King himself, and the wife of Viriñca and Viriñca himself. (Manu 4.2.124)
"Umā and Girīśa," as well as "Bhāratī and Īra"— here,
*īra* means wind (*samīra*);
thus, the entire collection of synonyms for speech (*vāc*) is understood.
To the question, "What is the contradiction [in the meaning being already established]? it is said: "at the time of liberation.
This means at the occasion of demonstrating liberation.
By this, the contradiction is indicated that there is no liberation for these four—Umā and the others—in this present life.
The sense is that we too have employed [the words] in exactly that same manner, following the injunctions of the Vedas.
To the question, "What is the basis for the application of words such as 'umā' and others to Vāruṇī and so forth?", he says: "Those very [words]."
Those very ones attain that state... // MAnu 4.2.125a //
Since Umā and the others attain that very status—the status of Vāruṇī and so forth—in a future kalpa, therefore [they are identified as such]; this is the connection with what precedes.
By this, it is stated that the basis for the metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is the relationship between Umā and the others with Vāruṇī and the others within a single substance.
What is the purpose of abandoning well-known terms and employing unfamiliar ones?
To explain the purpose [of this], he says: "At that time."
"At that time, having worshipped these, living beings enter them at the time of becoming Brahman"— thus does the Vedic word attain such a state.

"At that time" means at the time of [their becoming] Umā and so forth; "these gods," namely Umā and the others; "at the time of their being Brahman" means at the time when those very ones, such as Vāyu and the rest, attain the state of Brahman and so forth.
"These," namely Vāruṇī and the others;
"ca" (and) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt); thus, "iti" means "therefore" (tasmāt).
Speech is the voice of the Vedas; "suchness" refers to the state of possessing words such as "Umā" and so forth.
This is what is meant.

For one who is thoroughly familiar with a particular [name], even when it acquires another name through reaching a different stage of life (*āśrama*) and so forth, its usage still occurs; thus, what is the point of searching for a specific purpose?

That which resides in this [Sūrya] resides precisely in Vāṇī.
By this, the dissolution of Indra, Āditya, and Bṛhaspati into Indra and the others; of fire into the elements; and of wind into Vāyu is explained.
But surely this contradicts the Vedic scripture: "Indra dissolves into Umā, and Umā into Rudra.

For even though the words *umā* and *rudra* have abandoned their primary meanings, they have been explained as referring to the remnants of the wine (*vāruṇī*) and the liquor itself (*śeṣa*). To this, he says: "Indra... etc.
When it is stated here that there is an entry into Indra, then *Umā* is indeed the wife of *Suparṇa*;
and since *Suparṇa* is also mentioned by the name *Girīśa*, there is no contradiction whatsoever here. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.127)
The words "when" (*yadā*) and "then" (*tadā*) are indicative of the locus alone; where [these] are heard, here the entry of Indra into Umā is stated.
And of that Umā, [it is said] in Rudra:
"Like one whose husband is Suparṇa."

The word "girīśa" is used as a synonym for "girīśa. The particle "hi" is employed because the attainment of power by Indra’s dissolution [into Śiva] is well-established through the Suparṇī [mantra]. Now, he describes the manner of dissolution into Hiraṇyagarbha for those previously mentioned as "those others," beginning with the words "Bhṛgu and the rest."
Bhṛgu and the others, having obtained Dakṣa, and through him Indra, and through him the wife of Suparṇa;
those Manus and chief kings who enter Manu, having entered him here, go to Mahendra.

Those Manus beginning with Vaivasvata, and those chief kings beginning with Priyavrata—having entered the Svāyambhuva Manu, they have gone to and reside here in Mahendra during this Svāyambhuva Manvantara.

because he is an incarnation of Kāma.

the disciples [are dissolved] in those [elements] already mentioned.

they enter the highest [realms],

"Then" means from the time of dissolution (*layakāla*).

For all this has been stated, indeed proclaimed in the supreme revelation.
It has been stated that "its dissolution is in this";
the supreme scripture (*paramaśruti*) has not been cited here for fear of prolixity.
The word "and" (*ca*) is connected with the subsequent sentence.

the meaning is that it must first be accepted that for whatever has arisen from something, its liberation occurs within that very thing;
and this should be understood to hold true provided there is no exception.
And so it is stated in the Nyāyavivaraṇa:
"From what [source] is this known? To this he says: 'Laya' (dissolution)."
... just as when [one takes] clay ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.2.133c //
The meaning is that in the universal dissolution (sādhāraṇapralaya), there exists a reversal of the order of creation.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Moreover" (atho).
"...and likewise, lethargy [arises] from the opposite," so spoke the Lord of Speech.
Furthermore, the word "atha" (then) signifies a different meaning;

and he "spoke," that is, he established [this].

The Lord of words—that is, of the Vedic utterances—is the author of the Sūtras. As it is said: "But here, the sequence is established by reversal. Since this dissolution is the liberation of the gods... // MAnu 4.2.134a //
Because this liberation is indeed the dissolution of the gods, and not—as it is for humans—the departure from the body beforehand;
therefore, what has been stated is logical.
Due to the relationship between the general and the particular, there is no fault of the probandum being undifferentiated.
The meaning is that creation is indeed consistent with what has been stated, as established by the Śruti and other authorities.
Now, an objection is raised: previously, the experience of enjoyment and so forth for those already liberated was established;
yet now it is said that liberation is simply dissolution (laya).
To the question of how there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows, he says: "Enjoyment" (*bhoga*). ... "And enjoyment especially... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.134b).
"Especially" means even more than from the state of a god (*devapada*).
The point is that liberation, characterized by the abandonment of the body, is not distinguished from dissolution (*laya*)—but this does not apply to every kind of liberation;

To the question, "Why should 'enjoyment' (*bhoga*) and 'liberation' (*mukti*)—which were not mentioned by the author of the Sūtras—be added? he says: "That which... (*yam iti*).

That enjoyment which the author of the Sūtra will describe in the fourth quarter as liberation is [now addressed].
He states another means of knowledge: "And it has been stated" (*uktaśca*).
"And the relationship between the original form and its reflection has been stated in the Piṅgalā Śruti, according to the dissolution [of the breath] therein. (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra 4.2.134cd)

"The state of being the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) for the deities is according to their dissolution (*laya*)," means that whichever [deity] has been stated by us to be dissolved into which [other], the former is the *bimba* and the latter is said to be the *pratibimba*.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The *bimba*..."
The dissolution of the images [of objects] is certain for those liberated in that state, and the consciousness-selves are always subject to its power.
This applies at all times, even after liberation;
it will be useful later on,
and is mentioned here incidentally.
Since it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the dissolution of a reflection into its original object (*bimba*) is certain upon liberation,
and since those [reflections] are other than that [original], what was stated is logical.
As for the claim that "the dissolution of all beings occurs in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and that [vital breath] dissolves into Viṣṇu," that is incorrect.
This is because it would contradict the Vedic scripture: "The vital breath [merges] into heat, and heat into the supreme deity.
Furthermore, the claim that the reflection merges into the original object is untenable.
For the vital breath is not a reflection of one who has become fire; therefore, he says: "designated as fire."
Having attained the glory designated as "splendor" (tejas) from Viṣṇu at the outset, Vāyu was then obtained as a son;
having been born again by entering Viṣṇu, he remains here liberated during the dissolution of the world.
At the time of dissolution, the wind, having attained the splendor designated as fire, becomes dissolved therein and reaches Viṣṇu;
then, when the time of creation has arrived, it emerges first from all others, and from Viṣṇu.
He is born as the son by way of being Hiraṇyagarbha;
furthermore, at the time of dissolution or liberation, having entered Viṣṇu, he abides here within Viṣṇu.
This is what is meant.
Since the word *tejas* denotes *lakṣmī* (prosperity/glorious power), there is no contradiction with what was stated.
If it is argued that, in that case, air would follow the consequence of transmigrating— based on the scriptural statement, "For when dissolved in *prakṛti*, one enters into *saṃsāra*"— it is not so.
This is because it is accepted [as such],
and because rebirth as Hiraṇyagarbha is admitted.
If it is argued that even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of liberation for those who know Brahman, we say no.
This is because liberation is accepted immediately after [the state of] Hiraṇyagarbha.
And this has been stated by adopting the position that the word *prāṇa* denotes air (*vāyu*);
however, in the case of the position that it denotes Hiraṇyagarbha, one should refer to what is stated in the Bhāṣya.
It has been stated that for those who are liberated, there is entry into and abiding within their own supreme deities;
however, this is not all, for there is also entry into the Blessed One.
And it has been stated that enjoyment is not the producer of bliss, but rather its manifestor;
bliss itself, however, is the very nature of the self. Thus he says: "All [of these]... and so forth.

All those hosts of liberated beings, while experiencing their own intense and dense bliss in its entirety, remain as if non-existent within the body of the Lord; yet at the time of dissolution or creation, they go forth once again into the external world.
When it was said "all," since the gods were the subject under discussion, there might have been the impression that they alone were meant; to prevent this understanding, he said "without exception.
"Enjoying" means experiencing.
He states another exception to the rule "the remainder [goes] to the carrier of oblations" with the word "prayāti" (he goes forth).
Nirṛti goes to Dharma; Śakra and the hosts of Maruts likewise go to their attendants; and all the commanders of the armies and others go to Aniruddha... Nirṛti, however, goes to Dharma.
The hosts of Maruts go to Śakra;
the word "tathā" (likewise) serves as a conjunction.
The commanders of the armies and others, Viṣvaksena and others—all the attendants of the Blessed One—go to Aniruddha.
The phrase "for the sake of dissolution into Deha" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is precisely that the dissolution of Aniruddha into Kāma has already been stated. He states the authority for this: "turu," etc.
... thus says Turaśruti... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.137cd //
For this very reason, this was not stated in that very place, because it was not mentioned in the *Paramaśruti*. He concludes the meaning of the quarter-verse with the words "this" (*iyam*).
... this is liberation. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 4.2.137d)
It has been stated that for gods and others, liberation consists in the dissolution of the body.

Thus ends the section on the departure [of the soul] in the fourth chapter of the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the *Anuvyākhyāna*—the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda—composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which explains the meaning of difficult words and sentences. *************************************************************************************************
Regarding this fourth chapter and third section (*adhyāya 4, pāda 3*), the commentary states: "The path and that which is to be reached are discussed in this section.

Although that has already been explained previously in connection with the relevant context, here, specifically regarding the attainment of the lower state, he explains it further, beginning with the words: "As for the departure... (*utkrānteti*).
And the path of departure, which is to be reached by the liberated, arises from the feet... // MAnu 4.3ab //
For those humans who have departed from the body, the path is for the purpose of going to the world of the Blessed One;
and to dispel the notion that it is accessible only to them, it is said: "liberated."
This [state] is accessible to all those who are liberated from both karma and the body;
this pair is set forth by these two quarters.

In these topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), he states the arguments for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the arguments for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The auspicious path" (*sukrameti*).
... as well as *sukra* and *avikrama*. Regarding *sāntānika*, *prāpti*, *abhīṣyatā*, and *saukaryam*, these are the logical arguments for another opinion.
The attainment of excellence, the acquisition of greatness, sequential passion, and the continuation of what has been told—
these bring about the determination of the final doctrine.
The term "of other doctrines" (*anyamata*) is used in the singular to denote a class;
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "reasonings that establish the determination of the tenet."
"Oṃ. Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the leader] leads those who have no reliance on symbols; for there are faults in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve. Oṃ.
This Sūtra is intended to establish that [the Self] is to be reached by those who are liberated.

Since this is not clearly stated in its commentary, the author, wishing to clarify it, first states the meaning of the word *pratīka*: "*pratīkam* // *12,364*. "Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the Lord] leads those who do not have a *pratīka* as their object of meditation; for there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of one's resolve (*tatkratu*). (BBs 4.3.15)
... the body and so forth are the physical form (pratīka) ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 4.3.2cd //
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the Blessed One’s images such as the mind and so forth is intended.

Although it is stated in the Sūtra that those who take the non-concrete (*apratīka*) as their object of focus proceed [to the higher realms], while for those who take the concrete (*pratīka*) as their object, this is established by elimination (*pariśeṣasiddha*); nevertheless, because this treatise is composed for the purpose of clarifying what is unclear, and because a negation (*abhāva*) must be preceded by an affirmation (*bhāva*), he states at the outset the very meaning established by elimination: "directed toward that" (*tadgata*).
...those men who are devoted solely to that. (Manu 4.3.2d)
Those who worship them before [the gods] shall attain Brahmā; having attained us, they shall reach Viṣṇu.
They shall obtain... // MAnu 4.3.3a-c //
They [meditate] on Viṣṇu as residing in the symbols alone; they are those who have the symbols as their support (pratīkālambana).
"In front" means prior to the time of dissolution (pralaya).
From this Brahmā,
they will obtain *mati*— the specific knowledge of the Blessed One— at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).
Now he elaborates upon the destiny of those who do not take anything as a support, which was briefly stated [in the sūtra], beginning with "Therefore": *ataḥ*.
Others as well, having reached him, go from there to Hari and become partakers of liberation at the end.
Other than those who take hold of symbols (pratīkālambana), there are those who worship by pervasion (vyāptopāsaka) and do not take hold of symbols;
having first attained that Viṣṇu, at the time of their final end,
they go from that Viṣṇu to that Brahmā and then reach Hari.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the section on the attainment [of Brahman], in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, specifically in the exposition of the meaning of the words of the difficult verses.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.

Since the subject matter to be established by the words and their mutual connection are already well-known, he states the reasoning for the prima facie and final positions as follows: "Atikrama... etc.

Transgression, speech, action, acquisition of wealth, the supreme goal, reaching the further shore, that abode, the accomplishment of all tasks, mastery, and universal esteem—these are the arguments for the other side. (Manu 4.4.1)

General appearance, eloquence, wonder, artlessness, freedom from faults, the discernment of particulars, and tirelessness—these are the characteristics of greatness, established for the sake of certain determination. (Manu Smṛti 4.4.2)

Regarding other positions, among the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*), those logical reasonings (*yuktis*) which have a well-determined conclusion as their purpose—that is, whose aim is the determination of the established tenet (*siddhānta*)—are "those with well-determined purposes. *12,367* // Oṃ, for this very reason, he has no other lord. Someone explains this very sūtra;
and for that very reason, because his resolve is not in vain, he becomes a wise lord over others.

with the intention that this [opponent's view] is incorrect, he says: "ananyā" (not other).

his state of having no other servant is declared here in order to exclude the servitude of anyone else.

In this sūtra, the statement that "for the liberated one there is no other master" (muktasyānanyādhipatiḥ)— which expresses the state of being without another servant— is intended to demonstrate that the liberated one does not become a servant to anyone other than those who are declared in the scripture to be masters over that liberated one;
it is not, however, for the purpose of precluding all masters whatsoever.
Why?
Because no other word is employed; otherwise, he would have said "the impossibility of another. *12,368*
And for this reason, he says "the husband" to show that it is exactly so.
For it is said that even Viṣṇu is the Lord of these [worlds], since there is a scriptural statement that Hari is the Lord of immortality.
Since Hari possesses lordship over immortality— meaning that his word is the Vedic revelation, "And he is the Lord of immortality"—
this [scripture] declares Viṣṇu to be the lord of these liberated ones.
Therefore, it has already been stated that this alone is the meaning of the Sūtra and no other.
He also establishes this point through inference with the words: "These too... (*ete 'pi*).
Moreover, these [beings] also possess the sovereignty of another, as men do through having Viṣṇu as their other mind;
they partake in established renown—indeed, inference alone serves here for the sake of establishing what is desired, according to certainty.
Furthermore, in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, it says:
"These are liberated;
those for whom there is another as their sovereign are 'other-sovereigns' (*anyādhipatayaḥ*)."

Their state is "other-superintendence" (anyādhipatitva); they are endowed with that [state] by way of being Viṣṇu, by way of being the mind (cittatva), and by way of being the living soul (jīvatva). The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of distinction.

however, in our own system, the assertion is simply that they are endowed with sovereignty.
If someone should disagree with the meaning of the cited scripture, for him it is sufficient [to respond] by means of inference alone.
In this case, it is inference alone that serves to establish the coexistence of the lord (*adhipati*) with those who are liberated.
How so?
[Through] pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
The word "hi" (for) indicates that those two [the liberated soul and the Lord] are established as real entities.

If it is argued that this is contradicted by the following inference—"The liberated souls are devoid of sovereign power because they are liberated, and therefore their volitions are not unfailing, like the Lord"—we say no; for such a reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the primordial material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*).
And because there is no subverting argument against the contrary position, this has been stated as "due to certainty.
Intending to show that the Blessed One is not only the sovereign lord for those who are liberated, but that others also may be so according to the circumstances, he says: "liberated."

"Even when others are liberated in another kalpa, [he is] liberated; even when those superior to him in his own kalpa are liberated, he is equal to them"—since there is no one higher than him, it is said "liberated," and so forth.

In this context, it should be understood that "by this" refers to those belonging to the world beyond, while "by that" refers to those belonging to this world.
By this [is meant]: "Now, he who, knowing thus..."
